    For simulations based on this integrator, temperature, potentials and mobility coefficients must be defined as an auxiliary variable of problem.

    This integrator concerns the following vectorial expression:

    Mi(∇⋅[λi∇φi]−∂Fi∂φi)i \begin{align} M_i{\left(\nabla \cdot \left[\lambda_i \nabla \varphi_i\right] - \displaystyle\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial \varphi_i}\right)}_i \end{align} Mi​(∇⋅[λi​∇φi​]−∂φi​∂Fi​​)i​​​

    where MiM_iMi​, λi\lambda_iλi​, and FiF_iFi​ are mandantory SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Mobility, GlossaryType::Capillary and GlossaryType::FreeEnergy, respectively.

    This integrator concerns the following vectorial expression:

    (η−∇⋅(λ∇φ)+∂F∂φMη) \Biggl( \begin{array}{c} \eta - \nabla \cdot \left(\lambda \nabla \varphi\right) + \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial \varphi} \\ M \eta \end{array} \Biggr) (η−∇⋅(λ∇φ)+∂φ∂F​Mη​)

    where MMM, λ\lambdaλ, and FFF are mandantory SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Mobility, GlossaryType::Capillary and GlossaryType::FreeEnergy, respectively.

    This integrator must be associated with the SplitTimeDerivative integrator.

    This integrator concerns the following vectorial expression:

    (μ−∇⋅(λ∇φ)+∂F∂φ∇⋅(M∇μ)) \Biggl( \begin{array}{c} \mu - \nabla \cdot \left(\lambda \nabla \varphi\right) + \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial \varphi} \\ \nabla \cdot \left(M \nabla \mu\right) \end{array} \Biggr) (μ−∇⋅(λ∇φ)+∂φ∂F​∇⋅(M∇μ)​)

    where MMM, λ\lambdaλ, and FFF are mandantory SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Mobility, GlossaryType::Capillary and GlossaryType::FreeEnergy, respectively.

    This integrator must be associated with the SplitTimeDerivative integrator.

    This integrator concerns the following mathematical expression:

    Mαp′(φ) \begin{align} M \alpha p'(\varphi) \end{align} Mαp′(φ)​​

    where MMM, ppp are mandantory SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Mobility and GlossaryType::PhaseFieldPotential, respectively.

    α\alphaα is the enthalpy of melting. It is constant and equal to the value of parameter named melting_factor.

    This integrator can be used to simulate melting phenomena based on an ad-hoc melting contribution.

    For these simulations, it must be associated with the AllenCahn integrator.

    This integrator concerns the following mathematical expression:

    Mαp′(φ) \begin{align} M \alpha p'(\varphi) \end{align} Mαp′(φ)​​

    where MMM, ppp are mandantory SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Mobility and GlossaryType::PhaseFieldPotential, respectively.

    α\alphaα is the enthalpy of melting defined by:

    α=Hm ? T≥Tm:0 \begin{align} \alpha&=&H_m\, ?\, T\geq T_m : 0 \end{align} α​=​Hm​?T≥Tm​:0​​

    where HmH_mHm​ is the enthalpy of melting, TTT the temperature and TmT_mTm​ the temperature of melting.

    This integrator can be used to simulate melting phenomena based on an ad-hoc melting contribution.

    For these simulations, it must be associated with the AllenCahn integrator.

    Two mandatory parameters are requested by this integrator. They are listed in the table 1.

    Parameter Name Type Default Value Description melting_temperature double melting temperature melting_enthalpy double melting enthalpy Table 1 - parameters allowed with MeltingTemperature

    For simulations based on this integrator, temperature must be defined as an auxiliary variable of the phase-field problem.

    This integrator concerns the following mathematical expression:

    Mα[p′(φ)+S] \begin{align} M \alpha \left[ p'(\varphi) + \mathcal{S}\right] \end{align} Mα[p′(φ)+S]​​

    where MMM, ppp are mandantory SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Mobility and GlossaryType::PhaseFieldPotential, respectively.

    S\mathcal{S}S is an optional seed value mimicking a nucleus calculated by a CALPHAD problem.

    α\alphaα is the enthalpy of melting calculated by a CALPHAD problem.

    This integrator can be used for CALPHAD-informed phase-field simulation1. For these simulations, it must be associated with the AllenCahn integrator.

    Two mandatory parameters are requested by this integrator. They are listed in the table 1.

    Parameter Name Type Default Value Description primary_phase std::string name of the phase before melting secondary_phase std::string name of the phase after melting Table 1 - parameters requested by MeltingCalphad

    For simulations based on this integrator, CALPHAD outputs -driving forces and nucleus- must be defined as auxiliary variables of the phase-field problem.

    This integrator concerns the following mathematical expression:

    1M[∂φ∂t]2 \begin{align} \dfrac{1}{M}\left[ \dfrac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} \right]^2 \\ \end{align} M1​[∂t∂φ​]2​​

    where MMM is a mandantory SLOTH coefficient of type GlossaryType::Mobility.

    This integrator can be only associated with the Fourier integrator to solve heat transfer equation for two-phase problems.

    The phase field φ\varphiφ is an auxiliary variable of the heat problem. Its time derivative is computed from its current and previous values with the physical time step:

    ∂φ∂t≈φ−φoldΔt \begin{align} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} \approx \frac{\varphi - \varphi_{\mathrm{old}}}{\Delta t} \end{align} ∂t∂φ​≈Δtφ−φold​​​​

    Accuracy of the time derivative

    This approximation is first order in time, whatever the time scheme: a coupling with latent heat is first order, even with TimeScheme::BDF2. Moreover, it depends on the position of the phase-field problem in the partitioned coupling: if the phase-field problem is solved before the heat problem, the derivative is computed over the current time step; otherwise, it is the derivative of the previous time step.

    This integrator concerns the following vectorial expression:

    (fi)i \begin{align} {\left(f_i\right)}_i \end{align} (fi​)i​​​

    where fif_ifi​ is a mandatory SLOTH coefficient of type GlossaryType::SourceTerm (Glossary::SourceTerm), defined for every unknown iii of the problem (use a zero constant for an equation without source term).

    fif_ifi​ can be a constant, a function of the unknowns, of the auxiliary variables, of the time ("constants": "(t:T)") and of the spatial coordinates ("coordinates"), or read from a file (see Coefficients). The Jacobian ∂fi/∂uj\partial f_i/\partial u_j∂fi​/∂uj​ is only assembled for source terms that can depend on the current solution (neither constant, explicit nor file-based). In axisymmetric geometry, the radial weight is applied by the integrator.

    Coefficient no_source(Glossary::SourceTerm, 0.);
Coefficient source(Glossary::SourceTerm, Scheme::Explicit, SourceCoefficient());
Coefficients coef_pb0(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy, no_source);
Coefficients coef_pb1(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy, source);
TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"CahnHilliard", "SourceTerm"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "SplitTimeDerivative");

    This integrator can be combined with any other differential operator. It replaces the former definition of source terms on the Operator.

    This integrator concerns the following mathematical expression (conservative form):

    −∇⋅(φ v) \begin{align} -\nabla\cdot\left(\varphi\,\mathbf{v}\right) \end{align} −∇⋅(φv)​​

    where v\mathbf{v}v is an imposed velocity field (not necessarily divergence-free), defined in one of the two following ways:

    • velocity components: SLOTH coefficients of type GlossaryType::Velocity: Glossary::Velocity_X, Glossary::Velocity_Y and Glossary::Velocity_Z (all the components of the space dimension are required),
    • gradient of an auxiliary variable v=α ∇a\mathbf{v} = \alpha\,\nabla av=α∇a: a SLOTH coefficient of type GlossaryType::VelocityPrefactor (Glossary::VelocityPrefactor) for α\alphaα, and the parameter velocity_gradient giving the symbol of the auxiliary variable aaa (set with set_additional_information).

    The velocity can depend on the spatial coordinates, the time and the auxiliary variables, not on the unknowns (no ∂v/∂φ\partial \mathbf{v}/\partial \varphi∂v/∂φ in the Jacobian). In the gradient mode, α\alphaα and aaa are frozen in the Jacobian (staggered coupling).

    Each unknown holding the velocity coefficients is advected. The weak form reads:

    −∫Ω∇⋅(φ v)ψ dΩ=∫Ωφ v⋅∇ψ dΩ−∫∂Ω(v⋅n)φ ψ dΓ \begin{align} -\int_\Omega \nabla\cdot\left(\varphi\,\mathbf{v}\right)\psi\, d\Omega = \int_\Omega \varphi\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\psi\, d\Omega - \int_{\partial\Omega} \left(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}\right)\varphi\,\psi\, d\Gamma \end{align} −∫Ω​∇⋅(φv)ψdΩ=∫Ω​φv⋅∇ψdΩ−∫∂Ω​(v⋅n)φψdΓ​​

    The boundary term is handled by the AdvectionBoundary integrator, added automatically on each boundary holding an Inflow coefficient (see Boundary conditions). On boundaries without Inflow coefficient, the advective flux vanishes (wall), which ensures mass conservation in a closed domain.

    Velocity componentsGradient of an auxiliary variable 
    Coefficient velocity_x(Glossary::Velocity_X, Scheme::Explicit, VelocityX());
Coefficient velocity_y(Glossary::Velocity_Y, Scheme::Explicit, VelocityY());
Coefficients coef_pb(density, heat_capacity, conductivity, velocity_x, velocity_y);
TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"Fourier", "Advection"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "HeatTimeDerivative");

    // v = alpha grad(a), a being an auxiliary variable of the problem
auto a_var = VAR(&spatial, bcs, "a", Glossary::Temperature, 2, a_initial_condition);
a_var.set_additional_information("a");
auto aux_vars = VARS(a_var);

Coefficient alpha(Glossary::VelocityPrefactor, 1.);
auto params = Parameters(Parameter("velocity_gradient", "a"));
Coefficients coef_pb(density, heat_capacity, conductivity, alpha);
TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"Fourier", "Advection"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "HeatTimeDerivative");
TransientPB heat_pb("Heat", oper, heat_vars, {coef_pb}, pst, aux_vars);

    The gradient is the gradient of the finite element field aha_hah​: it is piecewise constant with Q1\mathcal{Q}_1Q1​ elements, which limits the accuracy of the advection to order 1. A Q2\mathcal{Q}_2Q2​ discretization of aaa is recommended when the accuracy of the velocity matters (see tests/HeatTransfer/2D/test9).

    This integrator concerns the following vectorial expression:

    (0−∇⋅(φ v)) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -\nabla\cdot\left(\varphi\,\mathbf{v}\right) \end{pmatrix} (0−∇⋅(φv)​)

    It is the counterpart of Advection for the split (φ,μ)(\varphi, \mu)(φ,μ) Cahn-Hilliard formulation: the advection of φ\varphiφ (first unknown) is added to the second equation, which holds ∂φ/∂t\partial\varphi/\partial t∂φ/∂t. The velocity coefficients (Glossary::Velocity_X, Glossary::Velocity_Y, Glossary::Velocity_Z, or Glossary::VelocityPrefactor with the parameter velocity_gradient, as for Advection) must be given in the Coefficients of φ\varphiφ.

    This integrator must be associated with the CahnHilliard and SplitTimeDerivative integrators. On open boundaries, the AdvectionBoundaryCH integrator is added automatically on each boundary holding an Inflow coefficient (also given in the Coefficients of φ\varphiφ).

    Coefficient velocity_x(Glossary::Velocity_X, 0.);
Coefficient velocity_y(Glossary::Velocity_Y, Scheme::Explicit, PoiseuilleVelocity());
Coefficients coef_phi(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy, velocity_x, velocity_y);
Coefficients coef_mu(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy);
TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"CahnHilliard", "SplitAdvection"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "SplitTimeDerivative");
    See the Cahn-Hilliard example 6 (rising bubble in an imposed flow).

On the inheritance from BlockNonlinearFormIntegrator instead of NonlinearFormIntegrator

For SLOTH integrators, inheriting from BlockNonlinearFormIntegrator maximizes the generality of the implementation, as it allows solving both single-unknown problems and problems with several unknowns.

docs.title: Operators
Problems
docs.text:
As already mentioned, Problem for SLOTH is a template class instantiated with three template parameters: first, an OPERATOR object, second, a Variables object, and third, a PostProcessing object.

Alias declaration for Problem class template

The aliases SteadyPB and TransientPB are provided by SLOTH namespaces (see the Aliases page) for steady and unsteady problems, respectively.

The SteadyPB and TransientPB problems must be defined by:

  • a TransientOPE/SteadyOPE [required],
  • primary Variables [required],
  • a vector of Coefficients [required],
  • a set of parameters (see Parameters) [optional],
  • an PostProcessing object [optional],
  • a set of auxiliary Variables [optional].

On the size of the vector of Coefficients objects

The size of the vector of Coefficients objects must be equal to the number of variables.

On the order of the vector of Coefficients objects

The order of coefficent in the vector of Coefficients objects corresponds the order unknowns in the Variables object.

Definition of a Cahn-Hilliard problem

SPAS spatials{&spatial, &spatial};

// Variables: phi, mu
auto phi = VAR(&spatial, bcs_phi, "phi", Glossary::PhaseField, 2, phi_initial_condition);
auto mu = VAR(&spatial, bcs_mu, "mu", Glossary::ChemicalPotential, 2, mu_initial_condition);
auto vars = VARS(phi, mu);

// Operator
TransientOPE phasefield_ope(spatials, {"CahnHilliard"}, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "SplitTimeDerivative");

// Coefficients
//  Interface thickness
const double epsilon(0.02);
// Two-phase mobility
const double mob(1.);
// Gradient coefficient
const double lambda = (epsilon * epsilon);
Coefficient grad_energy(Glossary::GradEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, GradientEnergy(lambda));
Coefficient double_well(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, W(omega));
Coefficient capillary(Glossary::Capillary, lambda);
Coefficient mobility(Glossary::Mobility, mob);

Coefficients coef_phase_field(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy);

// Problem (pst is PostProcessing object not detailed here)
TransientPB phase_field_pb(phasefield_ope, vars, {coef_phase_field, coef_phase_field}, pst);

This example assume an two-phase problem solved by Cahn-Hilliard equations with two unknowns (phi and mu).

(0∂φ∂t)=(μ−∇⋅(λ∇φ)∇⋅(M∇μ)) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \dfrac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mu - \nabla \cdot \left(\lambda \nabla \varphi\right) \\[1ex] \nabla \cdot \left(M \nabla \mu\right) \end{pmatrix} (0∂t∂φ​​)=(μ−∇⋅(λ∇φ)∇⋅(M∇μ)​)

The TransientOPE object, denoted by phasefield_ope, is well declared with a vector of two spatial discretization objects (see the alias SPAS provided by a SLOTH namespace), the CahnHilliard integrator for the right-hand-side of PDEs and the SplitTimeDerivative for the left-hand-side.

For this example, the Backward Euler method is considered (see TimeScheme::EulerImplicit).

For this problem, a vector of two Coefficients is considered for phi and mu, respectively. Here, the same Coefficients are used for both variables accordingly with the CahnHilliard integrator. As expected by this integrator, coefficients of type Glossary::FreeEnergy, Glossary::Capillary and Glossary::Mobility are defined. The coefficient of type Glossary::GradEnergy is only used to compute the gradient terms in the output of the density of energy.

This example has no parameters or auxiliary variables.

docs.title: How to perform simulations on axisymmetric geometries?
docs.text:
To enable simulations on axisymmetric geometries, the current definition of the Problem class needs to be enhanced. The proposed modification is as follows:

    TransientPB phase_field_pb(phasefield_ope, vars, {coef_phase_field, coef_phase_field}, pst);
    phase_field_pb.setGeometry(Geometry::Axisymmetric);

By default, the geometry will be set to Geometry::Cartesian if no specific geometry is defined.

Defining source terms on axisymmetric geometries

Source terms are defined with the SourceTerm integrator, which applies the radial weight automatically, as all the other integrators. The source term coefficient must therefore not be multiplied by the radius.

docs.title: How to use Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR)?
docs.text:
Once a Problem is fully defined, an AMR driver can be attached to it so that SLOTH locally refines/coarsens the mesh — and every finite element space and variable (primary + auxiliary) built on it — as the simulation progresses. This assumes the spatial discretization used by the problem was built with enable_nc_mesh = true.

Attaching AMR to the Cahn-Hilliard problem defined above

    mfem::ConstantCoefficient amr_coef{1.0};
    mfem::DiffusionIntegrator amr_integ{amr_coef};
    SlothErrorEstimators estimator(ErrorEstimatorType::KELLY, &amr_integ);

    SingleVariableAMR<VARS> amr(*spatial.get_mesh(), spatial.is_nc_simplices(), 0);

    auto amr_params = Parameters(Parameter("max_elem_error", 1.e-4), Parameter("amr_max_level", 4),
                           Parameter("nc_limit", 0), Parameter("max_preref_cycles", 4));
    amr.SetCriteria(/*estimator*/ &estimator, amr_params);

    phase_field_pb.set_amr(&amr);
An error estimator is first built from an MFEM integrator and wrapped into a SlothErrorEstimators object, then used to configure a SingleVariableAMR driver — here based on phi (index 0 in vars). The driver is finally attached to the problem with set_amr(), exactly as setGeometry() is used above for axisymmetric geometries.

Full AMR workflow

This page only shows how to attach an already-configured AMR driver to a Problem.

  • For the complete step-by-step workflow, see the AMR tutorial;
  • For the full reference on error estimators (ErrorEstimatorType::KELLY, ErrorEstimatorType::ZZ) and AMR drivers (SingleVariableAMR, MultiVariableMaxAMR), see the Adaptive Mesh Refinement page of the User Manual.

docs.title: How to use the BDF2 time scheme?
docs.text:
TimeScheme::BDF2 is a variable-step, second-order implicit time scheme. It costs one nonlinear solve per time step, as the backward Euler method, whereas the SDIRK methods need two or three. It is well suited to stiff phase-field problems.

Definition of a transient operator with the BDF2 time scheme

SPAS spatials{&spatial, &spatial};
TransientOPE phasefield_ope(spatials, {"CahnHilliard"}, TimeScheme::BDF2, "SplitTimeDerivative");
Nothing else changes in the definition of the problem.

docs.title: Principle
docs.text:
With Δtn=tn+1−tn\Delta t_n = t^{n+1} - t^nΔtn​=tn+1−tn and the ratio ω=Δtn/Δtn−1\omega = \Delta t_n / \Delta t_{n-1}ω=Δtn​/Δtn−1​ of two consecutive time steps, the BDF2 scheme reads:

Un+1−a Un+b Un−1=β Δtn ∂U∂t(tn+1),a=(1+ω)21+2ω,b=ω21+2ω,β=1+ω1+2ω \begin{align} U^{n+1} - a\, U^n + b\, U^{n-1} = \beta\, \Delta t_n\, \frac{\partial U}{\partial t}(t^{n+1}), \qquad a = \frac{(1+\omega)^2}{1+2\omega},\quad b = \frac{\omega^2}{1+2\omega},\quad \beta = \frac{1+\omega}{1+2\omega} \end{align} Un+1−aUn+bUn−1=βΔtn​∂t∂U​(tn+1),a=1+2ω(1+ω)2​,b=1+2ωω2​,β=1+2ω1+ω​​​

For a constant time step: a=4/3a = 4/3a=4/3, b=1/3b = 1/3b=1/3 and β=2/3\beta = 2/3β=2/3.

In SLOTH, the scheme is solved as a backward Euler step on an effective state U⋆=a Un−b Un−1U^\star = a\, U^n - b\, U^{n-1}U⋆=aUn−bUn−1 with an effective time step β Δtn\beta\, \Delta t_nβΔtn​:

Un+1=U⋆+β Δtn K \begin{align} U^{n+1} = U^\star + \beta\, \Delta t_n\, K \end{align} Un+1=U⋆+βΔtn​K​​

where KKK is the time derivative solved by the nonlinear algorithm. The integrators are therefore the same as for the backward Euler method.

  • First time step: no previous state is available, so the first step is a backward Euler step.
  • Variable time step: the coefficients depend on the ratio ω\omegaω. A ratio ω≥1+2\omega \geq 1+\sqrt{2}ω≥1+2​ is rejected (zero-stability of the variable-step BDF2 method for arbitrary step sequences, Crouzeix & Lisbona, 1984): an adaptive time step must limit the growth of the time step, for instance to ω≤2\omega \leq 2ω≤2.
  • Adaptive Mesh Refinement: the previous state Un−1U^{n-1}Un−1 is taken from the history of the Variables, which is transferred by the AMR with the current solution. The scheme is not restarted after a mesh change.
  • Restart: the first step after a restart is a backward Euler step.

docs.title: Partitioned coupling
docs.text:
In a Coupling with several problems, the problems are solved one after the other. A problem sees the variables of the other problems as auxiliary variables: those of the problems already solved in the current time step are at tn+1t^{n+1}tn+1, those of the problems not yet solved are at tnt^ntn (lagged).

Problem solved sees Pb1 sees Pb2 sees Pb3 Pb1 - tnt^ntn (lagged) tnt^ntn (lagged) Pb2 tn+1t^{n+1}tn+1 - tnt^ntn (lagged) Pb3 tn+1t^{n+1}tn+1 tn+1t^{n+1}tn+1 - Table 3 - auxiliary variables seen by each problem of Coupling("...", Pb1, Pb2, Pb3)

This lag is a splitting error of order Δt\Delta tΔt: it keeps the backward Euler method at order 1, but limits higher-order schemes to order 1. With TimeScheme::BDF2, the lagged auxiliary variables are therefore automatically replaced, during the time step, by the second-order extrapolation

B~=(1+ω) Bn−ω Bn−1 \begin{align} \tilde{B} = (1+\omega)\, B^n - \omega\, B^{n-1} \end{align} B~=(1+ω)Bn−ωBn−1​​

and restored after the time step. The lagged auxiliary variables are detected automatically, whatever the order of the problems in the Coupling. With the other time schemes, they are reported once (in Verbosity::Verbose).

An extrapolated value may leave the physical range of the variable (e.g. φ~>1\tilde{\varphi} > 1φ~​>1 near a moving interface). Physical bounds can be given to the variable: the extrapolated value is then truncated in these bounds. As long as the bounds contain the exact solution, the truncation keeps the second order.

Bounds of the extrapolated value

auto eta = VAR(&spatial, bcs, "eta", Glossary::PhaseField, 2, eta_initial_condition);
eta.set_extrapolation_bounds(0., 1.);   // or (-1., 1.), depending on the formulation
auto ac_vars = VARS(eta);
The bounds must be set before the variable is added to a VARS object. They only apply to the extrapolated value of a lagged auxiliary variable (BDF2): neither the solution itself nor the other time schemes are affected.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Explicit coefficients of the unknowns

With TimeScheme::BDF2, Scheme::Explicit coefficients (and the previous value of Scheme::SemiImplicit coefficients) that depend on the unknowns of the problem are evaluated on the effective state U⋆U^\starU⋆, which is not a physical state: for a constant time step, U⋆=Un+(Un−Un−1)/3U^\star = U^n + (U^n - U^{n-1})/3U⋆=Un+(Un−Un−1)/3 may leave the physical range where the variable still varies near a bound.

This matters for coefficients only defined on a bounded range, e.g. an explicit mobility with a c(1−c)c(1-c)c(1−c) term. For such coefficients:

  • prefer Scheme::Implicit (evaluated at the end of the time step: safe and second order),
  • otherwise, bound the argument inside the coefficient function,
  • or keep the backward Euler method.

Implicit and constant coefficients, as well as explicit coefficients depending only on the time, the coordinates or the auxiliary variables, are not affected.

Time derivatives of auxiliary variables

Integrators computing the time derivative of an auxiliary variable (e.g. LatentHeat) use a first-order approximation: a coupling involving such integrators is first order, even with TimeScheme::BDF2.

docs.title: How to set auxiliary variables after construction?
docs.text:
Auxiliary variables (see Variables) can be set afterwards with set_auxvariables, exactly as set_amr is used above to attach an AMR driver:

Setting auxiliary variables after construction

std::vector<VARS*> aux_vect = {&aux_vars_1, &aux_vars_2};
phase_field_pb.set_auxvariables(aux_vect);
aux_vect is a std::vector<VARS*>. This is particularly convenient in partitioned multiphase-field simulations, where each Problem needs the other Variables as auxiliary variables.

docs.title: How to export a Coefficient in VTK output?
docs.text:
In addition to the primary Variables, quantities computed from a Coefficient — not resolved by the system, but useful for visualization or diagnostics - can be exported to VTK output. The coefficient must first be given a name, then registered on the Problem with set_vtk_coefficients:

Registering a Coefficient for VTK output

In this example, the Coefficient named Squares is exported to VTK output.

Coefficient squares(Glossary::PhaseField, Scheme::Implicit, Squares());
squares.set_name("Squares");

phase_field_pb.set_vtk_coefficients({squares});
set_vtk_coefficients takes a std::vector<Coefficient>, so several coefficients can be registered at once. Each is projected onto a grid function and saved alongside the usual Variables, using its name ("Squares" here) as the field name in the VTK output.

  1. Clément Introïni, Jérôme Sercombe, Isabelle Ramière, and Romain Le Tellier. Phase-field modeling with the taf-id of incipient melting and oxygen transport in nuclear fuel during power transients. Journal of Nuclear Materials, 556:153173, 2021. ↩

docs.title: "The remainder"
docs.text:
"The remainder" refers to everything that is neither PDEs nor 0D problems, such as the computation of physical properties or the update of variables (e.g. c∼f(μ)c\sim f(\mu)c∼f(μ) in the grand potential formulation of phase-field model).

The SLOTH development team recommends using Property_problem. This is a template class instantiated with three template parameters: first, an PROPERTY object, second, the Variables object (see VARSin the example), and third, the Postprocessing object (see PST in the example).

The users are referred to dedicated pages of the user manual for details about Variables and PostProcessing.

The PROPERTY object in Property_problem corresponds to a C++ object that inherits from the template class PropertyBase, only defined with a set of Parameter (within a Parameters object).

Alias declaration for Property_problem class template

The alias PB_PROPERTY<PROPERTY> is provided by SLOTH namespaces (see the Aliases page).

Similar to other types of problems, Property_problem take auxiliary Variables as inputs, and primary Variables as outputs.

Defintion of a fictitious Property_problem

auto property_params = FictitiousProperty(property_params);

PB_PROPERTY<FictitiousProperty> prop_pb = fictitious_property_problem(
  "Property problem", property_params, outputs_property_var, inputs_property_var);

docs.title: MPI problems
docs.text:
MPI_Problem is a diagnostic problem: at each time step, its single primary variable is set, on each MPI process, to the rank of this process. Saved like any other variable, it shows how the mesh is distributed between processes, for instance to check the load balancing of a simulation with adaptive mesh refinement.

MPI_Problem is a template class instantiated with the Variables and PostProcessing types (alias PB_MPI, see the Aliases page). It has no parameter and no auxiliary variable.

Definition of an MPI_Problem

auto mpi_init = AnalyticalFunctions<DIM>(std::function<double(const mfem::Vector&, double)>(
    [&](const mfem::Vector& x, [[maybe_unused]] double time) { return 0.; }));
auto vars_mpi = VARS(VAR(&spatial, bcs, "MPI rank", Glossary::MPI, 2, mpi_init));
auto pst_mpi = PST(&spatial, p_pst_mpi);
PB_MPI problem_mpi(vars_mpi, pst_mpi);
problem_mpi is then added to a coupling like any other problem.

docs.title: Time discretization
docs.text:
This page describes the C++ object TimeDiscretization, which enables SLOTH to manage the time loop of all multiphysics simulations.

TimeDiscretization object is simply defined by:

  • a list of parameters (SLOTH object Parameters)
  • a list of Coupling

The parameters allowed with TimeDiscretization are summarized in table 1.

Object Parameter Name Type Default Value Description TimeDiscretization "initial_time" double 0. The initial time of the simulation TimeDiscretization "final_time" double The final time of the simulation TimeDiscretization "time_step" double The time-step of the simulation (constant value) TimeDiscretization "initial_iteration" int 0 Initial iteration number used to restart a simulation from a previously saved state (constant value) Table 1 - parameters allowed with TimeDiscretization

Definition of time-step as a function of the time

The time step can also be defined as a function of the current simulation time. However, this is not an adaptative time-stepping algorithm which will be implemented in the future.

When a std::function<double(double)> is passed to TimeDiscretization, the time_step parameter is ignored and the time step is evaluated dynamically at each iteration. In the following example, the time-step increases as the simulation progresses.

auto user_time_step = std::function<double(double)>([](double time) {
    double dt;
    if (time < 0.1) {
    dt = 0.01;
    } else if (time < 0.2) {
    dt = 0.02;
    } else if (time < 0.4) {
    dt = 0.04;
    } else {
    dt = 0.05;
    }
    return dt;
});

auto time_params =
    Parameters(Parameter("initial_time", t_initial), Parameter("final_time", t_final));
auto time = TimeDiscretization(user_time_step, time_params, cc);

If no function is provided, the constant value specified by the time_step parameter is used as before.

Example of TimeDiscretization with parameters

The following example assume a multiphysics simulation based on two couplings, each composed of three problems.

The time loop starts at 000 s, ends at 111 s with a time-step of 0.10.10.1 s.

    auto coupling_example_1 = Coupling("MyCoupling1", Problem1_1, Problem1_2, Problem1_3);
    auto coupling_example_2 = Coupling("MyCoupling2", Problem2_1, Problem2_2, Problem2_3);

    const double t_initial = 0.0;
    const double t_final = 1.0;
    const double dt = 0.1;
    auto time_params = Parameters(
        Parameter("initial_time", t_initial),
        Parameter("final_time", t_final), 
        Parameter("time_step", dt));
    auto time = TimeDiscretization(time_parameters, coupling_example_1, coupling_example_2);

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
This page focuses on the Parameter and Parameters objects specially designed for SLOTH.

SLOTH provides a variety of parameter types, enabling flexible and dynamic configuration of simulation inputs. These parameters can then be passed as arguments to SLOTH problems (see Problems for more details).

docs.title: Parameter
docs.text:
Each parameter is managed by the C++ class Parameter. A Parameter is defined by its name (type std::string), its value, and optionally a description (type std::string). 

Parameter(name, value, description)

Parameter(name, value)

The type of the Parameteris deduced from the value. The basic types double, int, std::string and bool can be used

Example of definitions of Parameter with basic types

doubleintstd::stringbool 
Parameter("p1", 1.0, "Scalar Parameter of type double")

Parameter("p1", 1, "Scalar Parameter of type int")

Parameter("p1", "1.0", "Scalar Parameter of type std::string")

Parameter("p1", true, "Scalar Parameter of type bool")

but also custom-defined containers:

Example of definitions of Parameter with custom-defined types

Custom-defined types can be defined either by their standard definition or by using a C++ alias.

MapStringDoubleMap2String2DoublevStringvIntvDoublevTupleStringIntvTupleStringStringvTuple2StringDouble

MapStringDoubleis a C++ alias for std::map<std::string,double>.

MapStringDouble param_value;
param_value.emplace("value", 1.0);
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type MapStringDouble")

Map2String2Doubleis a C++ alias for std::map<std::tuple<std::string, std::string>, std::tuple<double, double>>.

Map2String2Double param_value;
param_value.emplace(std::make_tuple("value_1", "value_2"), std::make_tuple(1.0,2.));
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type Map2String2Double")

vStringis a C++ alias for std::vector<std::string>.

vString param_value;
param_value.emplace_back("value_1");
param_value.emplace_back("value_2");
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vString")

vIntis a C++ alias for std::vector<int>.

vInt param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(0);
param_value.emplace_back(1);
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vInt")

vDoubleis a C++ alias for std::vector<double>.

vDouble param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(0.0);
param_value.emplace_back(0.1);
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vDouble")

vStringis a C++ alias for std::vector<std::tuple<std::string,int>>.

vTupleStringInt param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("value_1",1));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("value_2",2));
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTupleStringInt")

vTupleStringStringis a C++ alias for std::vector<std::tuple<std::string,std::string>>.

vTupleStringString param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_1","value_1"));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_2","value_2"));
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTupleStringString")

vTuple2StringDoubleis a C++ alias for std::vector<std::tuple<std::string,std::string, double>>.

vTuple2StringDouble param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_1","value_1",0.0));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_2","value_2",1.0));
Parameter("p1", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTuple2StringDouble")

This list of parameter types can be easly extended.

Access to Parameter informations

As for deep inside the code, C++ public methods allow you to get the name, description and value of a `parameter'.

Please see the Doxygen for more details.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The C++ class Parameters allows to define a collection of Parameter objects of different types.

Example of definitions of Parameters

auto p1 = Parameter("p1", 1.0, "Scalar Parameter of type double")
auto p2 = Parameter("p2", true, "Scalar Parameter of type bool")
vTupleStringString param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_1","value_1"));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_2","value_2"));
auto p3 = Parameter("p3", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTupleStringString")

auto params = Parameters(p1, p2, p3);

In this example, params gathers three Parameter of type double, bool and vTupleStringString.

Parameters class allows to add or substract Parameter.

docs.title: Addition of parameters
docs.text:
Two `Parameters' objects can be merged.

Example of merge of two Parameters

auto p1 = Parameter("p1", 1.0, "Scalar Parameter of type double")
auto p2 = Parameter("p2", true, "Scalar Parameter of type bool")
vTupleStringString param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_1","value_1"));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_2","value_2"));
auto p3 = Parameter("p3", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTupleStringString")

auto merge_parameter = Parameters(p1) + Parameters(p2, p3);

Priority when merging

When merging two Parameters' objects, anyParameter' contained in the second Parameter' will overwrite anyParameter' contained in the first `Parameter' if they have the same name.

A Parameters' can be also be merged with aParameter' object.

Example of merge of a Parameters with a Parameter

auto p1 = Parameter("p1", 1.0, "Scalar Parameter of type double")
auto p2 = Parameter("p2", true, "Scalar Parameter of type bool")
vTupleStringString param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_1","value_1"));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_2","value_2"));
auto p3 = Parameter("p3", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTupleStringString")

auto merge_parameter = Parameters(p2, p3) + p1 ;

Priority when merging

If the Parameter' object already contains aParameter' with the same name as the `Parameter' to be merged, the latter will overwrite the existing one.

docs.title: Removing a parameter
docs.text:
A Parameter' can be removed from aParameters' object by name.

Example of Parameter removal

auto p1 = Parameter("p1", 1.0, "Scalar Parameter of type double")
auto p2 = Parameter("p2", true, "Scalar Parameter of type bool")
vTupleStringString param_value;
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_1","value_1"));
param_value.emplace_back(std::make_tuple("key_2","value_2"));
auto p3 = Parameter("p3", param_value, "Scalar Parameter of type vTupleStringString")

auto merge_parameter = Parameters(p1, p2, p3);
auto reduced_parameter = merge_parameter - p1;

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text:
This page presents all Post-processing features and describes all parameters with their default values.

Definition of a post-processing for SLOTH is made with a C++ object of type PostProcessing.

PostProcessing is a template class instantiated with three template parameters: first, the kind of finite element; second, the data format for saving results; and third, the spatial dimension.

The kind of finite element refers to a C++ class that inherits from the mfem::FiniteElementCollection. This class manages all collections of finite elements provided by MFEM. Currently, the most commonly used finite element collection in SLOTH is mfem::H1_FECollection, which corresponds to arbitrary-order H1-conforming continuous finite elements.

The dimension is simply an integer that can be 1, 2, or 3.

The data format refers to a C++ class that inherits from the mfem::DataCollection. This class manages all collections of data provided by MFEM. The development team primarily uses ParaView to visualize results, which corresponds to the mfem::ParaviewDataCollection C++ class.

Use of alternative software for visualizing results

Users are free to employ alternative visualization software such as VisIt. In that case, please contact the development team so that an interface to the mfem::VisitDataCollection class can be provided.

Alias declaration for PostProcessing class template

The alias PST is provided by SLOTH namespaces (see the Aliases page) for PostProcessing class template.

Without loss of generality, the alias PST is used in this page in order to simplify each code snippet.

The PST object must be defined by:

  • the spatial discretisation (see Meshing);
  • a set of parameters (see Parameters).

Declaration of a PostProcessing object

auto post_processing = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);
This example shows how to declare a PST object with the spatial discretisation spatial and the parameters pst_parameters.

docs.title: Optional post-processing
docs.text:
PST objects are optional when defining a Problem.

A Problem can therefore be defined either with or without an associated PST object.

Problem definition with post-processing

auto ch_pst = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);
PB ch_pb("CahnHilliard", ch_oper, ch_vars, {ch_coef, ch_coef}, ch_pst, ac_vars);

Problem definition without post-processing

PB ch_pb("CahnHilliard", ch_oper, ch_vars, {ch_coef, ch_coef}, ac_vars);

When no PST object is provided, no ParaView output or specialized post-processing output is associated with the Problem.

docs.title: Shared post-processing for multiphysics simulations
docs.text:
A single PST object can be shared by several Problem objects. This makes it possible to save the variables of several coupled problems in a common ParaView file and to use a common post-processing directory.

Two problems with separate post-processing objects

auto ch_pst = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);
PB ch_pb("CahnHilliard", ch_oper, ch_vars, {ch_coef, ch_coef}, ch_pst, ac_vars);

auto ac_pst = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);
PB ac_pb("AllenCahn", ac_oper, ac_vars, {ac_coef, ac_coef}, ac_pst, ch_vars);

In this case, the variables for the Cahn-Hilliard and Allen-Cahn problems are saved in two separate VTK files.

If specialized post-processing is enabled, the global specialized file time_specialized.csv is generated separately in each problem's post-processing directory.

Two problems sharing a common post-processing object

auto common_pst = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);

PB ch_pb("CahnHilliard", ch_oper, ch_vars, {ch_coef, ch_coef}, common_pst, ac_vars);
PB ac_pb("AllenCahn", ac_oper, ac_vars, {ac_coef, ac_coef}, common_pst, ch_vars);

In this case, the variables for both the Cahn-Hilliard and Allen-Cahn problems are saved in the same VTK file.

If specialized post-processing is enabled, the specialized files for both problems are generated in the common post-processing directory.

To avoid naming conflicts and duplicated files, generated specialized files are automatically prefixed with the name of the corresponding Problem and, when applicable, with the name of the coupling.

Each PST object is associated with one or more Problem objects, and the Variables associated with these problems are saved in the corresponding ParaView file.

docs.title: ParaView output parameters
docs.text:
The parameters allowed with PostProcessing for visualizing data with ParaView are summarized in Table 1.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description "main_folder_path" std::string Root directory for saving all results "calculation_path" std::string Directory for saving the results of the problem "force_clean_output_dir" bool false Flag to force cleaning of the root directory "frequency" int Data output frequency "iterations_list" std::vector<int> Iteration indices for data output. Used only if "frequency" is not provided "times_list" std::vector<double> Times for data output. Used only if "frequency" is not provided. Can be combined with "iterations_list" Table 1 - Parameters allowed with PostProcessing for visualizing data with ParaView

docs.title: Specialized post-processing
docs.text:
In addition to visualizing Variables with ParaView, some results can also be exported in CSV format.

The time_specialized.csv file contains:

  • The L2L^2L2 and L∞L^\inftyL∞ norms of the error for each variable with an analytical solution;
  • The energy density of the problem;
  • The surface tension of the problem (for phase-field problems);
  • The spatial average of the variable over the computational domain, if requested with the "integral_to_compute" parameter.

The parameters allowed with PostProcessing for exporting specialized values in the time_specialized.csv file are summarized in Table 2.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description "enable_save_specialized_at_iter" bool true By default, specialized values are written to the CSV files as soon as they are computed. If false, they are kept in memory and written at the end of the simulation "specialized_frequency" int 1 Frequency, in iterations, at which specialized values are computed: they are computed at iterations that are multiples of "specialized_frequency" (1: every iteration) "iso_val_to_compute" MapStringDouble Map of isovalues for each variable. The key must match the name of a Variable "integral_to_compute" MapString2Double Map of lower and upper bounds used to compute the average value of each variable. The key must match the name of a Variable "enable_compute_energies" bool true Indicates whether energies are calculated "iterations_list_save_gf" std::vector<int> Iterations at which variables are saved as MFEM GridFunction files Table 2 - Parameters allowed with PostProcessing to save specialized values in the time_specialized.csv file

The iterations_list_save_gf parameter specifies the iterations at which variables are saved as MFEM GridFunction files. By default, the files are written to a directory named GF. This location can be customized using the gf_folder_path parameter (type std::string). Each file follows the naming convention <variable_name>_<iteration>.gf.<MPI_rank>. For example, eta_2.gf.000010 corresponds to the variable eta saved at iteration 2 on MPI rank 10.

docs.title: Frequency of specialized values
docs.text:
Specialized values (errors, isovalues, integrals and energies) are computed every "specialized_frequency" iterations, independently of the "frequency" used for ParaView outputs. By default (1), they are computed at every iteration.

Computing energies can be expensive, in particular for problems with many variables or for partitioned schemes where each Problem computes its own energy. In that case, a larger "specialized_frequency" can significantly reduce the cost of the post-processing.

"specialized_frequency" controls when specialized values are computed, while "enable_save_specialized_at_iter" controls when they are written:

"enable_save_specialized_at_iter" "specialized_frequency" Behaviour true (default) 1 (default) Computed and written at every iteration true N Computed and written every N iterations false 1 Computed at every iteration, written at the end of the simulation false N Computed every N iterations, written at the end of the simulation Table 3 - Combination of "enable_save_specialized_at_iter" and "specialized_frequency"

Reading CSV files written with specialized_frequency greater than 1

Each line of a CSV file contains its own iteration (Iter[-]), time step (Dt[s]) and time (Time[s]). When "specialized_frequency" is greater than 1, consecutive lines no longer correspond to consecutive iterations: post-processing scripts must rely on these columns, not on line numbers.

The last iteration of the simulation is written only if it is a multiple of "specialized_frequency".

Specialized values of Calphad problems

"specialized_frequency" applies to the specialized values computed by PDE problems. Specialized values of Calphad problems (calphad.csv) are produced during their own resolution and follow only "enable_save_specialized_at_iter".

Isovalues are not stored in the time_specialized.csv file. Instead, the parameter "iso_val_to_compute" generates separate CSV files, one for each variable.

On the dimension of iso_val_to_compute and integral_to_compute

The parameters "iso_val_to_compute" and "integral_to_compute" must have exactly the same number of entries as the number of variables.

On the lower and upper bounds used with integral_to_compute

Lower and upper bounds are used to limit the calculation of the integral to specific values of the variables. For example, it can be useful to compute the volume of a bubble corresponding to a phase indicator lower than \(0.5\).

On the calculation of energies for phase-field problems

By default, energies are calculated. For phase-field problems, if "enable_compute_energies" is set to true, a SLOTH coefficient of type Glossary::GradEnergy must be defined in the vector of coefficients passed to the SLOTH problem. Otherwise, an exception is raised.

See the dedicated page of the user manual for more details about the definition of SLOTH coefficients.

Example of PostProcessing with parameters

The following example assumes the existence of a Variable named "phi" for Cahn-Hilliard equations.

The results are saved in the Saves/CahnHilliard directory at each time step (see "frequency").

Specialized values are also written at each time step, including the average value of "phi".

const std::string& main_folder_path = "Saves";
const std::string& calculation_path = "CahnHilliard";
const int frequency = 1;
std::map<std::string, std::tuple<double, double>> map_threshold_integral = {
    {"phi", {-1.1, 1.1}}
};
bool save_specialized_at_iter = true;

auto pst_parameters = Parameters(
    Parameter("main_folder_path", main_folder_path),
    Parameter("calculation_path", calculation_path),
    Parameter("frequency", frequency),
    Parameter("integral_to_compute", map_threshold_integral),
    Parameter("enable_save_specialized_at_iter", save_specialized_at_iter));

auto post_processing = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);

Computing specialized values every 10 iterations

For long simulations, specialized values can be computed less often than every iteration, here every 10 iterations, while ParaView outputs are saved every 100 iterations:

auto pst_parameters = Parameters(
    Parameter("main_folder_path", main_folder_path),
    Parameter("calculation_path", calculation_path),
    Parameter("frequency", 100),
    Parameter("specialized_frequency", 10),
    Parameter("integral_to_compute", map_threshold_integral));

docs.title: Post-processing Coefficients in VTK output
docs.text:
In addition to Variables, a PST object can also export named Coefficient objects — quantities computed from the solved variables, not resolved by the system, but useful for visualization or diagnostics (e.g. an interpolation function, an order-parameter norm used to check the multiphase-field normalization constraint, ...).

A coefficient must be given a name and registered on a Problem with set_vtk_coefficients:

Registering a Coefficient for VTK output

Coefficient squares(Glossary::PhaseField, Scheme::Implicit, Squares());
squares.set_name("Squares");

phase_field_pb.set_vtk_coefficients({squares});

At each post-processing step, every registered coefficient is projected onto a grid function and saved to the VTK output under its name, alongside the usual Variables.

Storage and unified/non-unified output

This feature is compatible with both unified and non-unified VTK post-processing (see Shared post-processing for multiphysics simulations).

docs.title: Profiling tools
docs.text: This page describes how to define and use profiling tools in SLOTH.

docs.title: MATools and Timetable
docs.text:
SLOTH provides a simple tool for profiling your application, consisting mainly in generating a time table of timed sections respecting the call stack (tree). The master or root timer of the call stack is initialized during the general initialization of SLOTH:

Profiling::getInstance().enable();

Displaying the time table in your terminal is done by adding the following function call:

Profiling::getInstance().print();

This is an example of an output:
