To disable the timetable or the file generation, you can use:

Profiling::getInstance().disable_timetable();
Profiling::getInstance().disable_write_file();

You can instrument each of your functions using section timers. It's important to remember that adding chronos can add extra cost, negligible for "big" functions but very costly for functions called in each element.

To time a function, place this instruction at the start of your function, the timer will stop at the end of the scope (the second time point is hidden in the timer destructor).

Catch_Time_Section("NameOfYourFunction");

To add a second timer to the same scope, you can use:

Catch_Nested_Time_Section("NameOfYourNestedSection");

To capture a specific section:

add_capture_chrono_section("NameOfYourSection", [&] {
  your_code ...
});

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
This page describes the nonlinear solvers, linear solvers and preconditioners available in SLOTH and how to overload the default choices made by the operators.

Prerequisite

  • Solvers are attached to the OPERATOR objects used to define PDEs - see the Partial Differential Equations page.
  • Solver options are passed with Parameter / Parameters objects - see the Parameters page.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SLOTH does not implement its own solvers: it relies on the solvers and preconditioners provided by MFEM (and, through MFEM, by HYPRE and MUMPS). SLOTH wraps them in a thin layer (class SlothSolver) that:

  • exposes each solver through a C++ enumeration (NLSolverType, IterativeSolverType, HypreSolverType, DirectSolverType, PreconditionerType, HyprePreconditionerType),
  • builds the underlying MFEM object with SLOTH default values (see the tables below),
  • lets the user overload these default values with a Parameters object,
  • checks the compatibility between a linear solver and its preconditioner.

Default solvers depend on the time scheme:

Time scheme Default nonlinear solver Default linear solver Default preconditioner Implicit: EulerImplicit, BDF2, SDIRK23, SDIRK33 (and steady problems) NLSolverType::NEWTON HypreSolverType::HYPRE_GMRES HyprePreconditionerType::HYPRE_ILU Explicit: EulerExplicit, RungeKutta4 (mass matrix inversion) - HypreSolverType::HYPRE_GMRES HyprePreconditionerType::HYPRE_ILU Table 1 - default solvers used by SLOTH operators

On iterative_mode

For SteadyOperator, the parameter iterative_mode of the nonlinear solver is always forced to true, so that the current solution is used as the initial guess of the Newton algorithm, even when the nonlinear solver parameters are overloaded. For TransientOperator, it is set to false by default.

docs.title: How to overload the default solvers?
docs.text:
Each operator provides the following methods. Each method exists in two versions: with the solver type only (default parameters are kept), or with the solver type and a Parameters object.

Method Available for Role overload_nl_solver(NLSolverType, [Parameters]) TransientOperator, SteadyOperator nonlinear solver overload_solver(VSolverType, [Parameters]) TransientOperator, SteadyOperator linear solver used at each nonlinear iteration overload_preconditioner(VSolverType, [Parameters]) TransientOperator, SteadyOperator preconditioner of the linear solver above overload_mass_solver(VSolverType, [Parameters]) TransientOperator linear solver used to invert the mass matrix (explicit time-schemes) overload_mass_preconditioner(VSolverType, [Parameters]) TransientOperator preconditioner of the mass solver Table 2 - methods used to overload solvers

VSolverType is a std::variant gathering all the enumerations listed in this page, so any linear solver or preconditioner type can be passed to these methods.

Overload before the problem is initialized

Solvers are built when the operator is initialized. The overload_* methods must therefore be called on the OPERATOR object before it is passed to a Problem (or at least before the initialization of the simulation).

Parameter types must match exactly

Solver parameters are read with a strict type: an int parameter (e.g. iter_max) must be defined with an int value (100, not 100.), and a double parameter (e.g. rel_tol) with a double value (1.e-10, not 1). Otherwise, SLOTH stops with the error message Parameter named ...: Invalid conversion.

Overloading the solvers of a transient operator

SPAS spatials{&spatial, &spatial};
TransientOPE phasefield_ope(spatials, {"CahnHilliard"}, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "SplitTimeDerivative");

// Nonlinear solver: Newton with user-defined tolerances
phasefield_ope.overload_nl_solver(NLSolverType::NEWTON,
                                  Parameters(Parameter("iter_max", 50),
                                             Parameter("rel_tol", 1.e-10),
                                             Parameter("abs_tol", 1.e-12)));

// Linear solver: HYPRE GMRES with a larger Krylov space
phasefield_ope.overload_solver(HypreSolverType::HYPRE_GMRES,
                               Parameters(Parameter("kdim", 200), Parameter("tol", 1.e-10)));

// Preconditioner: BoomerAMG
phasefield_ope.overload_preconditioner(HyprePreconditionerType::HYPRE_BOOMER_AMG);

Using a direct solver

// MUMPS does not use a preconditioner
phasefield_ope.overload_solver(DirectSolverType::MUMPS);
phasefield_ope.overload_preconditioner(HyprePreconditionerType::NO);

docs.title: Nonlinear solvers
docs.text:
Nonlinear solvers are selected with the enumeration NLSolverType.

NEWTONLBFGS

Newton-Raphson algorithm - MFEM class mfem::NewtonSolver. This is the default nonlinear solver of SLOTH.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description iter_max int 100 maximum number of iterations rel_tol double 1.e-13 relative tolerance abs_tol double 1.e-13 absolute tolerance iterative_mode bool false use the input vector as initial guess print_level int -1 MFEM print level Table 3 - parameters allowed with NLSolverType::NEWTON

Limited-memory BFGS quasi-Newton algorithm - MFEM class mfem::LBFGSSolver. No Jacobian matrix is inverted: the linear solver and preconditioner of the operator are not used.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description history_size int 10 number of stored correction pairs iter_max int 1000 maximum number of iterations rel_tol double 1.e-13 relative tolerance abs_tol double 1.e-13 absolute tolerance iterative_mode bool false use the input vector as initial guess print_level int -1 MFEM print level Table 4 - parameters allowed with NLSolverType::LBFGS

docs.title: Linear solvers
docs.text: Linear solvers are used either inside the nonlinear algorithm (to solve the Newton linear system) or to invert the mass matrix for explicit time-schemes. Three families are available.

docs.title: HYPRE solvers
docs.text:
Selected with the enumeration HypreSolverType. They work on HYPRE parallel matrices and must be associated with a HYPRE preconditioner (HyprePreconditionerType).

HypreSolverType MFEM class Description HYPRE_PCG mfem::HyprePCG preconditioned conjugate gradient (symmetric positive definite systems) HYPRE_GMRES mfem::HypreGMRES GMRES (default) HYPRE_FGMRES mfem::HypreFGMRES flexible GMRES Table 5 - HYPRE linear solvers Parameter Name Type HYPRE_PCG HYPRE_GMRES HYPRE_FGMRES Description iter_max int 100 5000 5000 maximum number of iterations tol double 1.e-12 1.e-12 1.e-12 tolerance kdim int - 100 100 dimension of the Krylov space print_level int -1 -1 -1 HYPRE print level Table 6 - parameters (and default values) allowed with HYPRE linear solvers

docs.title: MFEM iterative solvers
docs.text:
Selected with the enumeration IterativeSolverType. They are the native Krylov solvers of MFEM and must be associated with an MFEM preconditioner (PreconditionerType).

IterativeSolverType MFEM class Description CG mfem::CGSolver conjugate gradient (symmetric positive definite systems) MINRES mfem::MINRESSolver minimal residual (symmetric indefinite systems) GMRES mfem::GMRESSolver GMRES BICGSTAB mfem::BiCGSTABSolver stabilized bi-conjugate gradient Table 7 - MFEM iterative linear solvers Parameter Name Type Default Value Description iter_max int 1000 maximum number of iterations rel_tol double 1.e-12 relative tolerance abs_tol double 1.e-24 absolute tolerance iterative_mode bool false use the input vector as initial guess print_level int -1 MFEM print level Table 8 - parameters allowed with MFEM iterative linear solvers (same default values for all of them)

Krylov space for IterativeSolverType::GMRES

A default Krylov dimension of 50 is defined in SLOTH options for the MFEM GMRES solver but it is not yet exposed as a parameter: the MFEM default value is used.

docs.title: Direct solvers
docs.text:
Selected with the enumeration DirectSolverType. Direct solvers do not use a preconditioner: they must be associated with PreconditionerType::NO or HyprePreconditionerType::NO.

MUMPS

Parallel sparse direct solver - MFEM class mfem::MUMPSSolver.

Availability

DirectSolverType::MUMPS is only available if MFEM has been built with MUMPS (MFEM_USE_MUMPS=ON). In this case, SLOTH is compiled with the definition SLOTH_USE_MUMPS.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description mat_type int 0 symmetry of the matrix: 0 = unsymmetric, 1 = symmetric positive definite, 2 = symmetric indefinite reordering_strategy int 0 0 = automatic, 1 = AMD, 2 = AMF, 3 = PORD, 4 = METIS, 5 = ParMETIS, 6 = SCOTCH, 7 = PT-SCOTCH print_level int -1 MUMPS print level Table 9 - parameters allowed with DirectSolverType::MUMPS

docs.title: HYPRE preconditioners
docs.text:
Selected with the enumeration HyprePreconditionerType. They can only be associated with HYPRE linear solvers.

HYPRE_ILUHYPRE_BOOMER_AMGHYPRE_DIAG_SCALEHYPRE_SMOOTHERNO

Incomplete LU factorization - MFEM class mfem::HypreILU. This is the default preconditioner of SLOTH.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description type int 0 ILU type (0: ILU(k) locally and block Jacobi globally) iter_max int 1 number of iterations tol double 0. tolerance reordering int 0 local reordering: 0 = no reordering, 1 = reverse Cuthill-McKee print_level int -1 HYPRE print level Table 10 - parameters allowed with HyprePreconditionerType::HYPRE_ILU

Algebraic multigrid - MFEM class mfem::HypreBoomerAMG.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description iter_max int 100 number of AMG cycles tol double 1.e-16 tolerance print_level int -1 HYPRE print level Table 11 - parameters allowed with HyprePreconditionerType::HYPRE_BOOMER_AMG

Diagonal (Jacobi) scaling - MFEM class mfem::HypreDiagScale. No parameter.

HYPRE relaxation methods - MFEM class mfem::HypreSmoother.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description type int 0 0 = Jacobi, 1 = l1-Jacobi, 2 = l1-Gauss-Seidel, 4 = truncated l1-Gauss-Seidel, 5 = lumped Jacobi, 6 = Gauss-Seidel, 10 = OPFS, 16 = Chebyshev, 1001 = Taubin, 1002 = FIR positive_diagonal bool true assume a positive diagonal Table 12 - parameters allowed with HyprePreconditionerType::HYPRE_SMOOTHER

No preconditioner.

docs.title: MFEM preconditioners
docs.text:
Selected with the enumeration PreconditionerType. They can only be associated with MFEM iterative linear solvers.

SMOOTHERNO

Jacobi-type smoother - MFEM class mfem::DSmoother.

Parameter Name Type Default Value Description type int 0 0 = scaled Jacobi, 1 = scaled l1-Jacobi, 2 = scaled lumped-Jacobi scale double 1. scaling factor iterations int 1 number of smoothing iterations use_abs_diag bool true use the absolute value of the diagonal Table 13 - parameters allowed with PreconditionerType::SMOOTHER

No preconditioner.

docs.title: Compatibility rules
docs.text:
SLOTH checks the association between a linear solver and its preconditioner and stops with an explicit error message if the association is not allowed.

Linear solver family HyprePreconditionerType PreconditionerType NO HypreSolverType ✅ ❌ ✅ IterativeSolverType ❌ ✅ ✅ DirectSolverType ❌ ❌ ✅ Table 14 - allowed associations between linear solvers and preconditioners

Verbosity

The print_level parameters are only taken into account if the SLOTH verbosity is at least Verbosity::Verbose. Otherwise, solvers are silent. In debug verbosity, the names of the solver and preconditioner actually used are printed.

Extension of the list of solvers in SLOTH

MFEM provides many other solvers and preconditioners (e.g. through PETSc or SuperLU). They could be added in SLOTH in the future.

docs.title: Spatial Discretization
docs.text:
SLOTH uses the Finite Elements Method1 2.

On this page, the users can find instructions

  • for building a finite element mesh on the basis of MFEM features,
  • for prescribing boundary conditions.

On the future use of MEROPE to generate microstructure meshes

SLOTH can read GMSH meshes and can therefore use microstructural meshes generated by the dedicated MEROPE code of the PLEIADES platform 3.

Ongoing work aims to provide a comprehensive study based on these real microstructural meshes.

  1. Olgierd C Zienkiewicz and Robert Leroy Taylor. The finite element method set. Elsevier, 2005. ↩

  2. André Fortin and André Garon. Les éléments finis: de la théorie à la pratique. Université Laval, 2011. ↩

  3. Marc Josien. Mérope: a microstructure generator for simulation of heterogeneous materials. Journal of Computational Science, 81:102359, 2024. URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877750324001522, doi:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jocs.2024.102359. ↩

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: This page described the definition and the use of boundary conditions in SLOTH.

docs.title: Build boundary conditions
docs.text:
Definition of boundary conditions for SLOTH is made with a C++ object of type BoundaryConditions. As for the object SpatialDiscretization (see Meshing), BoundaryConditions is a template class instantiated with two template parameters: first, the kind of finite element, and second, the spatial dimension.

Currently, the most commonly used finite element collection in SLOTH is mfem::H1_FECollection, which corresponds to arbitrary order H1-conforming continuous finite elements.

The dimension is simply an integer that can be 1, 2, or 3.

Alias declaration for BoundaryConditions class template

using BCS = BoundaryConditions<mfem::H1_FECollection, 3>;
This example show how to define a convenient alias for the BoundaryConditions class template instantiated with mfem::H1_FECollection in dimension 3. This alias is often used in tests in order to simplify the code.

BoundaryConditions is roughly defined as a set of C++ object of type Boundary. Each geometrical boundary must be associated with a C++ object of type Boundary.

Number of boundaries

The number of Boundary objects inside the Boundaries object must be equal to the total number of geometrical boundary.

A Boundary object is defined by

  • a name (C++ type std::string),
  • an index (C++ type int),
  • a type (C++ type std::string) among "Dirichlet", "Neumann", "Robin", "Periodic",
  • a value (C++ type double) in case of "Dirichlet" boundary conditions only.

Inflow/outflow conditions for advection problems are not a boundary type: they are activated by a Coefficient of type Glossary::Inflow attached to the open boundaries (see the "Inflow / outflow" tab below).

Defining boundary conditions

The following examples assume that the spatial discretisation is defined. In the code snippets, it is referred to as a spatial object.

These examples show how to define Dirichlet, homogeneous Neumann and Periodic boundary conditions in a square.

DirichletNeumannRobinInflow / outflowPeriodic 

        auto list_boundaries_2 =  {Boundary("left", 0, "Dirichlet", 0.), Boundary("bottom", 1, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 2, "Dirichlet", 1.), Boundary("top", 3, "Neumann")};
        auto bcs_2 = BCS(&spatial, list_boundaries_2);
The fourth argument in the definition of a Boundary object is only required for Dirichlet boundary conditions.

To define space- and/or time-dependent Dirichlet boundary conditions, a Coefficient object of type Glossary::Dirichlet must be defined and associated with a set of Boundary objects, exactly as for non-homogeneous Neumann or Robin boundary conditions. The following example prescribes a different DirichletCoefficient on the right boundary (1) and on the left boundary (3).

        auto boundaries = {Boundary("lower", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 1, "Dirichlet"),
                        Boundary("upper", 2, "Neumann"), Boundary("left", 3, "Dirichlet")};
        auto bcs = BCS(&spatial, boundaries);

        Coefficient dirichlet_left(Glossary::Dirichlet, Scheme::Implicit, DirichletCoefficient());
        Coefficient dirichlet_right(Glossary::Dirichlet, Scheme::Implicit, DirichletCoefficient(-1));
        dirichlet_left.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{3});
        dirichlet_right.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{1});

Here, Boundary("right", 1, "Dirichlet") and Boundary("left", 3, "Dirichlet") use the three-argument constructor overload (no constant value), since the actual boundary value is provided by the associated Coefficient instead.

In this example, DirichletCoefficient() is built from the following JSON file

        [
            {
            "expression":"t*sin(pi*y)",
            "variables":"phi",
            "coordinates":"x,y",
            "constants":"(t:T)",
            "class_name":"DirichletCoefficient",
            "outputfile":"Coefficient"
            }
        ]

phi is declared as the coefficient's own variable, even though it is not used in the expression. x and y are the spatial coordinates (see Coefficients). t is mapped to the current simulation time. The prefactor passed to DirichletCoefficient(-1) flips the sign of the whole expression for the left boundary.

auto list_boundaries_1 = {Boundary("left", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("bottom", 1, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 2, "Neumann"), Boundary("top", 3, "Neumann")};
auto bcs_1 = BCS(&spatial, list_boundaries_1);
This example enables to define homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.

To define non-homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, a Coefficient object of type Glossary::Neumann must be defined and associated with a set of Boundary objects. The following example prescribes the heat_flux coefficient on the left boundary (0) and on the top boundary (3).

Coefficient neumann(Glossary::Neumann, Scheme::Implicit, heat_flux());
neumann.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{0,3});


auto list_boundaries_1 = {Boundary("left", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("bottom", 1, "Robin"), Boundary("right", 2, "Neumann"), Boundary("top", 3, "Robin")};
auto bcs_1 = BCS(&spatial, list_boundaries_1);
This example enables to define

  • homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions on the left boundary (0) and on the right boundary (2)
  • Robin boundary conditions on the bottom boundary (1) and on the top boundary (3)

Robin boundary conditions prescribes the following expression on a boundary:

n⋅∇u+a×u=b {\bf{n}} \cdot \nabla u + a \times u = b n⋅∇u+a×u=b

where aaa and bbb are two Coefficient objects of type Glossary::Robin_a and Glossary::Robin_b, respectively. These two coefficients must also be associated with a set of Boundary objects.

The following example illustrates how to define radiation boundary conditions by prescribing:

n⋅k∇T+a(T)×T=b {\bf{n}} \cdot k\nabla T + a(T) \times T = b n⋅k∇T+a(T)×T=b

with suitable coefficients on the bottom boundary (1) and on the top boundary (3).

Coefficient robin_a(Glossary::Robin_a, Scheme::Implicit, RobinCoefficient());
Coefficient robin_b(Glossary::Robin_b, epsilon * sigma * std::pow(T_inf, 4));
robin_a.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{1,3});
robin_b.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{1,3});

In this example, RobinCoefficient() is built from the following JSON file

[
    {
    "expression":"epsilon * sigma * T*T*T",
    "variables":"T",
    "constants":"(epsilon:0.7),(sigma:5.669e-8)",
    "class_name":"RobinCoefficient",
    "outputfile":"RobinCoefficient"
    }
]

For problems with an Advection or SplitAdvection integrator, the advective flux through the boundary is prescribed by an upwind boundary term:

∫Γ[(v⋅n)+u+(v⋅n)−uin]ψ dΓ \int_{\Gamma} \left[\left(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}\right)^{+} u + \left(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}\right)^{-} u_{in}\right] \psi \, d\Gamma ∫Γ​[(v⋅n)+u+(v⋅n)−uin​]ψdΓ

where (a)+=max⁡(a,0)(a)^{+}=\max(a,0)(a)+=max(a,0) and (a)−=min⁡(a,0)(a)^{-}=\min(a,0)(a)−=min(a,0):

  • outflow (v⋅n>0\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} > 0v⋅n>0): the interior value uuu leaves the domain freely,
  • inflow (v⋅n<0\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} < 0v⋅n<0): the incoming flux (v⋅n) uin(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n})\,u_{in}(v⋅n)uin​ is imposed.

uinu_{in}uin​ is given by a Coefficient of type Glossary::Inflow, attached to the open boundaries with set_bdr_index_coef. The switch between inflow and outflow is made at each integration point according to the sign of v⋅n\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}v⋅n, so the Inflow coefficient can be attached to all the open boundaries, whatever the direction of the flow. It can depend on the spatial coordinates and on the time, not on the unknowns.

auto boundaries = {Boundary("lower", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 1, "Neumann"),
                   Boundary("upper", 2, "Neumann"), Boundary("left", 3, "Neumann")};
auto bcs = BCS(&spatial, boundaries);

Coefficient inflow(Glossary::Inflow, Scheme::Explicit, InflowCoefficient());
inflow.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{0, 1, 2, 3});

The corresponding boundary integrator (AdvectionBoundary, or AdvectionBoundaryCH with SplitAdvection) is added automatically: there is no boundary type to declare. The Inflow term is independent of the boundary type and is added to it (homogeneous Neumann in the example above for the diffusive flux).

Boundaries without Inflow coefficient

On a boundary without Inflow coefficient, the advective flux vanishes (u v⋅n=0u\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}=0uv⋅n=0 in the weak sense): the boundary behaves as a wall. This is the expected behavior for closed domains, where the integral of the advected variable is conserved.

Consistency checks

  • An Inflow coefficient without Advection or SplitAdvection integrator in the operator stops the simulation with an error message.
  • With SplitAdvection, the Inflow coefficient must be given in the Coefficients of the phase-field variable (first unknown), together with the velocity coefficients.
    auto list_boundaries_3 = {Boundary("left", 0, "Periodic"), Boundary("bottom", 1, "Periodic"), Boundary("right", 2, "Periodic"), Boundary("top", 3, "Periodic")};
    auto bcs_3 = BCS(&spatial, list_boundaries_3);

This example enables to define Periodic boundary conditions.

Once defined, boundary conditions are associated with variables (see Variables). The user can define as many boundary conditions as there are variables.

Consistency of the indices of the boundaries

MFEM v4.7 provides new features for referring to boundary attribute numbers. Such an improvement is not yet implemented in SLOTH. Consequently, users must take care to the consistency of the indices used in the test file with the indices defined when building the mesh with GMSH.

docs.title: Build N boundary conditions from a vector of spatial discretizations
docs.text:
When N spatial discretizations share the same boundary layout - typically the SPAS vector built by the spatial discretization factory — building each BCS object one by one is repetitive. setBoundaryConditions builds N of them in a single call, from a spatials vector and a single, shared list of Boundary objects.

Building boundary conditions for 30 spatial discretizations

using namespace Sloth2D;

auto boundaries = {Boundary("lower", 0, "Periodic"), Boundary("right", 1, "Periodic"),
                   Boundary("upper", 2, "Periodic"), Boundary("left", 3, "Periodic")};
auto bcs = setBoundaryConditions(30, spatials, boundaries);
spatials is a SPAS object (e.g. built with setPeriodicSpatialDiscretization), and bcs[i] is the BCS object associated with spatials[i], equivalent to BCS(spatials[i], boundaries).

Number of spatial discretizations

spatials must contain exactly N elements — one Boundary list is shared across every spatial discretization, but each still gets its own BoundaryConditions object.

docs.title: Meshing
docs.text:
Definition of a finite element mesh for SLOTH is made with a C++ object of type SpatialDiscretization. SLOTH can either read a GMSH mesh file or use the meshing functionalities provided by MFEM.

SpatialDiscretization is a template class instantiated with two template parameters: first, the kind of finite element, and second, the spatial dimension.

The kind of finite element refers to a C++ class that inherits from the mfem::FiniteElementCollection. This class manages all collections of finite elements provided by MFEM. Currently, the most commonly used finite element collection in SLOTH is mfem::H1_FECollection, which corresponds to arbitrary order H1-conforming continuous finite elements.

The dimension is simply an integer that can be 1, 2, or 3.

Alias declaration for SpatialDiscretization class template

using SPA = SpatialDiscretization<mfem::H1_FECollection, 3>;
This example show how to define a convenient alias for the SpatialDiscretization class template instantiated with mfem::H1_FECollection in dimension 3.

Without loss of generality, the alias SPA is used in this page in order to simplify each code snippet.

Non-conforming refinement flags (used for AMR)

Every constructor below (except the shared-mesh one) accepts two optional, trailing boolean flags, always in this order:

  • enable_nc_mesh (default false) — builds the mesh in non-conforming mode. It must be set to true to later use Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR): a conforming mesh cannot be converted afterwards.
  • allow_nc_simplices (default false) — additionally allows non-conforming refinement on triangle/tetrahedron elements specifically. It has no effect on quadrilateral/hexahedral meshes, which natively support non-conforming refinement regardless of this flag. Its value is what is_nc_simplices() returns afterwards.

Both are illustrated as "With AMR" variants in the examples below. See the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow.

docs.title: Build a mesh from GMSH file
docs.text:
SLOTH can read a mesh file directly built with GMSH.

On the GMSH version used to export meshes

For compatibility with the GMSH file reader provided by MFEM, meshes must be exported in ASCII version 2 format.

Defining a mesh from GMSH involves creating an object of type SPA with the following parameters:

  1. A string exactly equal to "GMSH",
  2. An integer greater than or equal to 1 indicating the order of finite elements,
  3. An integer greater than or equal to 0 indicating the level of uniform mesh refinement applied to the initial mesh,
  4. A string associated with the name of the GMSH mesh file,
  5. (Optional, default false) A boolean to indicate whether the imported mesh is periodic or not,
  6. (Optional, default false) enable_nc_mesh — builds the mesh in non-conforming mode, required to use Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR),
  7. (Optional, default false) allow_nc_simplices — allows non-conforming refinement on simplex elements specifically (no effect on quadrangle/hexahedron meshes).

Defining a mesh from GMSH

Without AMRWith AMR 

const int order_fe = 1;                                // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                        // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::string& filename = "pellet2Dinclusion.msh"; // name of the GMSH file
bool is_periodic = false;                              // flag to indicate if the imported mesh is periodic

SPA spatial("GMSH", order_fe, refinement_level, filename, is_periodic);
This example demonstrates how to define a mesh from GMSH. It uses first-order finite elements without any refinement, and the mesh contained in the "pellet2Dinclusion.msh" file is not periodic.

const int order_fe = 1;                                // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                        // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::string& filename = "pellet2Dinclusion.msh"; // name of the GMSH file
bool is_periodic = false;                              // flag to indicate if the imported mesh is periodic
bool enable_nc_mesh = true;                            // build the mesh in non-conforming mode (AMR)
bool allow_nc_simplices = false;                       // set to true only if the mesh is made of triangles/tetrahedra

SPA spatial("GMSH", order_fe, refinement_level, filename, is_periodic, enable_nc_mesh, allow_nc_simplices);
Setting enable_nc_mesh to true builds the mesh in non-conforming mode, a prerequisite for attaching an AMR driver to the problem. allow_nc_simplices only matters for triangle/tetrahedron meshes. See the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow.

AMR on split GMSH meshes

To use AMR on meshes read from pre-partitioned GMSH files (see GMSH Split Meshes below), they must be converted to non-conforming mode, regardless of enable_nc_mesh / allow_nc_simplices.

docs.title: Build a mesh from MFEM meshing functionalities
docs.text:
SLOTH can build a mesh using the meshing functionalities provided by MFEM.

Here again, defining a mesh involves creating an object of type SPA with the following parameters:

  1. A string specifying the type of mesh from the following list:

    • "InlineLineWithSegments" : 1D mesh composed of segments
    • "InlineSquareWithTriangles" : 2D mesh composed of triangles
    • "InlineSquareWithQuadrangles" : 2D mesh composed of quadrangles
    • "InlineSquareWithTetraedres" : 2D mesh composed of tetrahedra
    • "InlineSquareWithHexaedres" : 2D mesh composed of hexahedra

  2. An integer greater than or equal to 1 indicating the order of finite elements.

  3. An integer greater than or equal to 0 indicating the level of uniform mesh refinement applied to the initial mesh.
  4. A C++ object of type std::tuple to provide the number of elements and maximum length in each direction.
  5. (Optional) A C++ object of type std::vector<mfem::Vector> to provide translations to apply in each direction, if the final mesh is periodic. This parameter must be entirely omitted for a non-periodic mesh — it is not defaulted; a distinct, non-periodic constructor overload is used instead (see the tabs below).
  6. (Optional, default false) enable_nc_mesh — builds the mesh in non-conforming mode, required to use Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR).
  7. (Optional, default false) allow_nc_simplices — allows non-conforming refinement on simplex elements specifically (no effect on quadrangle/hexahedron meshes).

Parameter position without periodicity

When the mesh is not periodic, parameter 5 (translations) is simply absent: enable_nc_mesh and allow_nc_simplices directly follow tuple_of_dimensions, as shown in the "Without periodicity" tabs below.

The following examples specify the use of these parameters in 1D, 2D and 3D.

docs.title: 1D mesh
docs.text:
In this example, the domain corresponds to a line of 1 mm. The mesh is composed of 30 segments. There is no mesh refinement and the finite elements are of order 1.

Defining a 1D mesh using the meshing functionalities provided by MFEM

Without AMRWith AMR 
const std::string& mesh_type = "InlineLineWithSegments"; // type of mesh
const int order_fe = 1;                                  // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                          // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::tuple<int, double>& tuple_of_dimensions = std::make_tuple(30, 1.e-3) ; // Number of elements and maximum length 

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions );


const std::string& mesh_type = "InlineLineWithSegments"; // type of mesh
const int order_fe = 1;                                  // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                          // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::tuple<int, double>& tuple_of_dimensions = std::make_tuple(30, 1.e-3) ; // Number of elements and maximum length 
bool enable_nc_mesh = true;                              // build the mesh in non-conforming mode (AMR)

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, enable_nc_mesh );
See the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow, including how to share this mesh across the other variables of the coupling.

docs.title: 2D mesh
docs.text:
In these examples, the domain corresponds to a square with a side length of 1 mm. The mesh consists of 30 quadrangles per direction. Triangles can be used by removing "InlineSquareWithQuadrangles" by "InlineSquareWithTriangles". There is no mesh refinement, and the finite elements are of order 1.

Defining a 2D mesh using the meshing functionalities provided by MFEM

Without periodicity (without/with AMR)With periodicity (without/with AMR) 
const std::string& mesh_type = "InlineSquareWithQuadrangles"; // type of mesh 
const int order_fe = 1;                                       // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                               // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::tuple<int, int, double, double>& tuple_of_dimensions = std::make_tuple(30, 30, 1.e-3, 1.e-3) ; // Number of elements and maximum length in each direction 

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions );

In case of AMR, the following modifications must be done.

bool enable_nc_mesh = true; // build the mesh in non-conforming mode (AMR)

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, enable_nc_mesh );
Setting enable_nc_mesh to true builds the mesh in non-conforming mode. This is a prerequisite for attaching an AMR driver to the problem — see the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow, including how to share this mesh across the other variables of the coupling.

For a mesh made of triangles ("InlineSquareWithTriangles"), also pass allow_nc_simplices = true as a 6th argument if non-conforming refinement of the triangles themselves is needed.

const std::string& mesh_type = "InlineSquareWithQuadrangles"; // type of mesh 
const int order_fe = 1;                                       // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                               // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::tuple<int, int, double, double>& tuple_of_dimensions = std::make_tuple(30, 30, 1.e-3, 1.e-3) ; // Number of elements and maximum length in each direction 

// Periodicity in x-direction
mfem::Vector x_translation({1.e-3, 0.0});
// mfem::Vector y_translation({0.0, 1.e-3});
std::vector<mfem::Vector> translations = {x_translation};
// std::vector<mfem::Vector> translations = {x_translation, y_translation};

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, translations );

The initial mesh is transformed to a periodic mesh by specifying a translation in the x-direction. See comments in the example to extend periodicity to the top and bottom boundaries.

In case of AMR, the following modifications must be done.

bool enable_nc_mesh = true;  // build the mesh in non-conforming mode (AMR)

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, translations, enable_nc_mesh );
Note that, with periodicity, the translations vector is a mandatory 5th argument, so enable_nc_mesh now comes 6th (instead of 5th in the non-periodic case above). Setting it to true builds the mesh in non-conforming mode. This is a prerequisite for attaching an AMR driver to the problem — see the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow, including how to share this mesh across the other variables of the coupling.

docs.title: 3D mesh
docs.text:
In these examples, one considers a cubic domain with a side length of 1 mm. The mesh consists of 30 tetrahedra per direction. Hexahedra can be used by removing "InlineSquareWithTetraedres" by "InlineSquareWithHexaedres". There is no mesh refinement, and the finite elements are of order 1.

Defining a 3D mesh using the meshing functionalities provided by MFEM

Without periodicity (without/with AMR)With periodicity (without/with AMR) 
const std::string& mesh_type = "InlineSquareWithTetraedres";  // type of mesh 
const int order_fe = 1;                                       // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                               // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::tuple<int, int, int, double, double, double>& tuple_of_dimensions = std::make_tuple(30, 30, 30, 1.e-3, 1.e-3, 1.e-3) ; // Number of elements and maximum length in each direction 

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions );

In case of AMR, the following modifications must be done.

bool enable_nc_mesh = true;      // build the mesh in non-conforming mode (AMR)
bool allow_nc_simplices = true;  // this mesh is made of tetrahedra: allow non-conforming refinement on them

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, enable_nc_mesh, allow_nc_simplices );
allow_nc_simplices is set here since tetrahedra are simplices — see the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow, including how to share this mesh across the other variables of the coupling.

const std::string& mesh_type = "InlineSquareWithTetraedres"; // type of mesh 
const int order_fe = 1;                                       // finite element order
const int refinement_level = 0;                               // number of levels of uniform refinement
const std::tuple<int, int, int, double, double, double>& tuple_of_dimensions = std::make_tuple(30, 30, 30, 1.e-3, 1.e-3, 1.e-3) ; // Number of elements and maximum length in each direction 

// Periodicity in one direction
mfem::Vector x_translation({1.e-3, 0.0, 0.0});
std::vector<mfem::Vector> translations = {x_translation};

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions,  translations);

A part of the cubic domain is transformed to a periodic domain by specifying a translation in the targeted direction.

In case of AMR, the following modifications must be done.

bool enable_nc_mesh = true;      // build the mesh in non-conforming mode (AMR)
bool allow_nc_simplices = true;  // this mesh is made of tetrahedra: allow non-conforming refinement on them

SPA spatial(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, translations, enable_nc_mesh, allow_nc_simplices );
Note that, with periodicity, the translations vector is a mandatory 5th argument, so the non-conforming flags now come 6th and 7th (instead of 5th and 6th in the non-periodic case above). See the AMR tutorial for the complete workflow, including how to share this mesh across the other variables of the coupling.

docs.title: Build a mesh from an existing mesh
docs.text:
Besides building a mesh from a GMSH file or from MFEM meshing functionalities, an SPA object can also be built directly from an existing mfem::ParMesh, typically the one held by another, already-defined SPA object. This is done with a lighter constructor that only takes the mesh, a finite element order, and an optional periodicity flag:

Building an SPA object from an existing mesh

SPA spatial_phi(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, true);
SPA spatial_mu(spatial_phi.get_mesh(), order_fe);
spatial_mu shares the same underlying mesh as spatial_phi (obtained with get_mesh()), but gets its own, independent finite element space, which can use a different order_fe if needed.

The full signature is SPA(mfem::ParMesh* existing_mesh, const int& fe_order, bool is_periodic_mesh = false). If the shared mesh is periodic, pass spatial_phi.is_periodic() as the third argument so that spatial_mu reports its periodicity correctly too:

SPA spatial_mu(spatial_phi.get_mesh(), order_fe, spatial_phi.is_periodic());

This constructor is useful in two situations:

  • To let several variables use different finite element orders while still living on the same mesh.
  • To keep several variables consistent under mesh refinement: this is required when using Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), since every variable of the coupling must follow the same sequence of refinements/derefinements applied to the shared mesh.

Requirement for AMR

When the shared mesh is meant to be refined with AMR, it must first be built in non-conforming mode (see the enable_nc_mesh / allow_nc_simplices arguments in the GMSH and MFEM sections above). These flags do not need to be passed again when building spatial_mu: this lighter constructor doesn't take them, since non-conforming support is a property of the shared mesh itself.

docs.title: Build N spatial discretizations sharing a mesh
docs.text:
For problems with many unknowns sharing the same mesh — typically a multiphase-field simulation — building each SPA object becomes repetitive. The factory functions setSpatialDiscretization and setPeriodicSpatialDiscretization build N such objects in a single call.

Building 30 spatial discretizations sharing a periodic mesh

using namespace Sloth2D;

SPAS spatials =
    setPeriodicSpatialDiscretization(30, "InlineSquareWithQuadrangles", 1, refinement_level,
                                     std::make_tuple(NN, NN, L, L), translations, true);
This builds the same mesh as done above and 30 SPA objects sharing it, equivalent to writing the first one, then 29 more from its get_mesh(). SPAS (defined by using namespace SlothND, see the Basic features page) is an alias for std::vector<SPA*>, ready to use wherever a vector of spatial discretizations is expected (variables, operators, boundary conditions).

The first argument is N, the number of objects to build; the remaining arguments are forwarded verbatim to whichever SPA constructor they match — any of the constructors described above (GMSH), above (MFEM inline meshes, periodic or not). The first object builds the mesh; the following N - 1 share it, exactly as in the manual pattern.

  • setSpatialDiscretization(N, args...) builds N objects sharing a non-periodic mesh.
  • setPeriodicSpatialDiscretization(N, args...) builds N objects sharing a periodic mesh.

Ownership

The returned SPAS does not own the underlying SpatialDiscretization objects by itself — they must be released with deleteSpatialDiscretization(spatials) once no longer needed (typically at the end of main), which deletes them in the correct order (mesh-owning object last) to avoid a use-after-free on the shared mesh.

docs.title: GMSH Split Meshes
docs.text: To read directly partitioned meshes, the MFEM miniapps called mesh-explorer must be used.

docs.title: Use the Mesh Explorer
docs.text:
Please refer to the documentation at https://mfem.org/meshing-miniapps/#mesh-explorer.

Below is a simple example of how to partition the Camembert2D mesh into four files:

    spack location -i mfem`/share/mfem/miniapps/meshing/mesh-explorer --mesh camembert2D.msh

    PRESS p // partitioning
    PRESS 1 // metis
    PRESS 4 // number of mpi processes
    PRESS T // Save par
    PRESS "camembert2D." // mesh name
    PRESS 6 // digit
    PRESS q // exit

This must generate 4 files named: camembert2D.000000, camembert2D.000000, camembert2D.000000, and camembert2D.000003.

docs.title: How to Read the Partitionned Files ?
docs.text:
To read partitionned files, the pattern of the file name, ending explicitly with ., must be specified.

Defining a 2D mesh using GMSH Split Meshes

    const int order_fe = 1;                                // finite element order
    const int refinement_level = 0;                        // number of levels of uniform refinement
    const std::string& pattern = "camembert2D.";           // pattern of the file name
    SPA spatial("GMSH", order_fe, refinement_level, pattern, false);

Number of processes

The number of processes must be equal to the number of files, otherwise reading will fail.

AMR is not available on split GMSH meshes

As noted above, to use AMR on meshes read from pre-partitioned GMSH files, they must be converted to non-conforming mode, regardless of enable_nc_mesh / allow_nc_simplices.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
This page described how to define and manage variables in SLOTH.

Definition of variables for SLOTH is made with a C++ object of type Variables that is simply a set of C++ object of type Variable.

As for the object SpatialDiscretization (see Meshing), Variable is a template class instantiated with two template parameters: first, the kind of finite element, and second, the spatial dimension.

The kind of finite element refers to a C++ class that inherits from the mfem::FiniteElementCollection. This class manages all collections of finite elements provided by MFEM. Currently, the most commonly used finite element collection in SLOTH is mfem::H1_FECollection, which corresponds to arbitrary order H1-conforming continuous finite elements.

The dimension is simply an integer that can be 1, 2, or 3.

Alias declaration for Variable class template

using VAR = Variable<mfem::H1_FECollection, 3>;
This example show how to define a convenient alias for the Variable class template instantiated with mfem::H1_FECollection in dimension 3. This alias is often used in tests in order to simplify the code.

docs.title: Variable description
docs.text: SLOTH differentiates between primary variables, that are solved directly by the problem (eg. the order parameter for the Allen-Cahn equation, the order parameter and the chemical potential for the Cahn-Hilliard equation), and secondary (or auxiliary) variables, which are derived from another problem to ensure multiphysics coupling (eg. the order parameter in the heat transfer equation, the temperature in the Allen-Cahn equation). Both kind of variables are defined in the same way.

docs.title: Mandatory parameters
docs.text:
The Variable object must be defined by:

  • the spatial discretisation (see Meshing),
  • a set of boundary conditions (see BoundaryConditions),
  • a name (C++ type std::string),
  • a type (SLOTH type GlossaryQuantity),
  • a storage depth level (C++ type int),
  • an initial condition.

The initial condition can be defined by a constant, a C++ object of type std::function or a SLOTH object of type AnalyticalFunctions. The latter enables to use pre-defined mathematical functions currently used in the studies conducted with SLOTH. If the mathematical expression is not yet available, the users can define it with a C++ object of type std::function.

Example of Variableobjects with mandatory parameters

The following examples assume that the spatial discretisation and the boundary conditions are defined. In the code snippets, the first is referred to as a spatial object, while the second is referred to as a bcs object. Without loss of generality, the alias VAR is also used.

These examples show how to initialize variables using:

  • a constant double value,
  • an AnalyticalFunction,
  • a std::function,
  • or a file in the MFEM field format.

The latter option is primarily intended for save/restart simulations, enabling calculations to resume from a previously saved state.

doublestd::functionAnalyticalFunctionsFile

In this example, the variable is named phi. Its initial value is zero.

int level_of_storage= 2;
std::string variable_name = "phi";
GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::PhaseField;
double initial_condition = 0.;
auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition);

In this example, the variable is named T. It is defined by a parabolic profile.

int level_of_storage= 2;
std::string variable_name = "T";
GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::Temperature;

auto initial_condition = std::function<double(const mfem::Vector&, double)>(
    [](const mfem::Vector& vcoord, double time) {
        const double Text = 800.;
        const double radius = 4.e-3;
        const double puissance = 20.e4;
        const double conductivity = 2.;
        const double r2 = radius * radius;
        double rr = std::transform_reduce(vcoord.begin(), vcoord.begin() + std::min(vcoord.Size(), 2), 0.0, std::plus<>(), [](double x) { return x * x; });

        const auto func = Text + puissance * (r2 - rr) / (4. * M_PI * 2. * r2);

        return func;
    });
auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition);

In this example, the variable is named phi. It is defined by a 2D hyperbolic tangent profile.

int level_of_storage= 2;
std::string variable_name = "phi";
GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::PhaseField;
const double center_x = 0.;
const double a_x = 1.;
const double thickness = 5.e-5;
const double radius = 5.e-4;

auto initial_condition = AnalyticalFunctions<2>(AnalyticalFunctionsType::HyperbolicTangent, center_x, a_x, thickness, radius)

auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition);

SLOTH provides several pre-implemented analytical functions, including the Heaviside function, sinusoidal profiles, hyperbolic tangent, and parabolic profiles. Each of these functions requires a set of parameters detailed in a dedicated page of the user manual.

In this example, the variable phi is initialized from the file phi_2.gf. The file name follows the convention <variable_name>_<iteration>.gf, where the iteration number matches the initial iteration of the simulation.

This initialization method is typically used to restart a simulation from a previously saved state. In this example, the simulation resumes from iteration 2 (see the initial_iteration parameter in the Time section of the user manual).

int level_of_storage= 2;
std::string variable_name = "phi";
GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::PhaseField;

std::string file_restart = "phi_2.gf";
auto initial_condition =  std::make_tuple(file_restart, gf_folder_path)

auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition);

docs.title: Optional parameters
docs.text:
In addition to the mandatory parameters, definition of Variable can be enhanced by an analytical solution with the same type as the initial condition.

Definition of variables with an analytical solution

The presence of an analytical solution automatically enables the calculation of the L2L^2L2 error over the domain.

The initial condition can also be asscoiated with a set of attributes names that correspond to PhysicalNames defined in the GMSH file mesh. In this case, the list of attributes (ie the PhysicalNames defined in the GMSH file mesh) must be defined in a C++ container of type std::set<std::string>, just after the initial condition.

Example of initialization based on PhysicalNames of a GMSH file mesh

Please find the following extract of a GMSH file mesh used to build an inclusion inside a fragment of material: Mesh of a fragment of material with an inclusion 

$MeshFormat
2.2 0 8
$EndMeshFormat
$PhysicalNames
5
1 1 "bottom"
1 2 "top"
1 3 "external"
2 22 "pellet"
2 23 "cluster"
$EndPhysicalNames

In the following example, the variable named phi is equal to one within the inclusion associated with the attribute 'cluster' and zero elsewhere.

int level_of_storage= 2;
std::string variable_name = "phi";
GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::PhaseField;
double initial_condition = 1.;
std::set<std::string> list_of_physical_names = {"cluster"};
auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition, list_of_physical_names);

Variable initialization within a fragment of material including an inclusion

docs.title: Additional information
docs.text:
Processing certain physical problems requires additional information to distinguish variables. This information is provided in the form of a list of strings associated with the variables using the public C++ method set_additional_information.

Example of variables definition with additional information

The following example refers to Calphad problems (see Problems for more details). The first variable, named Ma, corresponds to a mobility coefficient whereas the second one is associated with a chemical potential named mu_a.

For a Calphad problem, managing the variables requires knowing the type of each variable. By convention, the last additional information corresponds to a pre-defined symbol (e.g., 'mu' for chemical potentials and 'mob' for mobilities).

The definition of chemical potentials requires the name of the chemical element, whereas for mobilities, both the name of the phase and the name of the chemical element must be specified.

    int level_of_storage= 2;
    std::string variable_name_1 = "Ma";
    GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::Mobility;
    double initial_condition_1 = 1.e-15;
    auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name_1, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition_1);
    var_1.set_additional_information("SOLUTION", "A", "mob");

    std::string variable_name_2 = "mu_a";
    GlossaryQuantity variable_type_2 = Glossary::ChemicalPotential;
    double initial_condition_2 = 1.e5;
    auto var_2 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name_2, variable_type_2, level_of_storage, initial_condition_2);
    var_2.set_additional_information("A", "mu");

Conventions used to associate additional information with variables for each kind of SLOTH problem are detailed in Section Problemsof the user manual.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
The C++ class Variables allows to define a collection of Variable objects. As for the object Variable, Variables is a template class instantiated with two template parameters: first, the kind of finite element, and second, the spatial dimension.

Each SLOTH problem (see Problems for more details) requires a Variables object as input argument.

Example of Variables definition

    std::string variable_name_1 = "mu_a";
    GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::ChemicalPotential;
    double initial_condition_1 = 1.e5;
    auto var_1 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name_1, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition_1);
    var_1.set_additional_information("A", "mu");

    std::string variable_name_2 = "mu_b";
    double initial_condition_2 = 2.e5;
    auto var_2 = VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name_2, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition_2);
    var_2.set_additional_information("B", "mu");

    auto mu_var = VARS(var_1, var_2);

This example shows the definition of two variables that correspond to chemical potentials. These variables are gathered within a Variables object that can be used as primary variables for a CALPHAD problem and as auxiliary variables for ThermalDiffusion problems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
This section presents the example problems available in SLOTH for multiphysics simulations.

The examples are organized into the following categories:

  • Cahn-Hilliard
  • Allen-Cahn
  • Allen-Cahn/Cahn-Hilliard
  • Mass Diffusion
  • Heat Transfer
  • CALPHAD

All examples are automatically executed as part of the SLOTH continuous integration (CI) pipeline. This ensures that code regressions are detected early while maintaining comprehensive test coverage.

docs.title: Allen-Cahn
docs.text:
The following examples are used to verify the implementation of the Allen-Cahn equation in SLOTH:

  • Example 1: Analytical steady-state solution (documentation)
  • Example 2: Homogeneous nucleation from a single seed (documentation)
  • Example 3: Evolution of a polycrystalline microstructure containing 30 and 102 grains (documentation)

Additional examples

This list is not exhaustive. Additional examples and their documentation will be added as new verification cases become available.

docs.title: Example 1: steady-state solution of the Allen-Cahn equations
Files
docs.text:
• Comprehensive test file: main.cpp
  • Reference results for comparison: convergence_output_ref.csv

docs.title: Statement of the problem
docs.text:
This test consists of finding the steady-state solution of the Allen-Cahn equations. A transient simulation is performed to reach this steady-state, and a convergence analysis is carried out to ensure the consistency of the results.

The domain Ω\OmegaΩ is a square [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]\times[0,1][0,1]×[0,1]

∂ϕ∂t=−M(F′(ϕ)−λΔϕ) in Ω \begin{align} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}&=-M (F'(\phi) - \lambda \Delta \phi) \text{ in }\Omega \end{align} ∂t∂ϕ​​=−M(F′(ϕ)−λΔϕ) in Ω​​

where ϕ\phiϕ is the phase indicator, F′F'F′ the derivative against ϕ\phiϕ of the potential FFF defined by:

F(ϕ)=ωϕ2(1−ϕ)2 \begin{align} F(\phi)&=\omega\phi^2(1-\phi)^2 \end{align} F(ϕ)​=ωϕ2(1−ϕ)2​​

docs.title: Initial condition
docs.text:
The initial condition is given by:

ϕ=12+12tanh⁡(x−0.55⋅10−3). \phi = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \tanh\left(\dfrac{x-0.5}{5\cdot 10^{-3}}\right). ϕ=21​+21​tanh(5⋅10−3x−0.5​).

docs.title: Parameters used for the test
docs.text:
For this test, all parameters are equal to one.

Name Description Symbol Value mob mobility coefficient MϕM_\phiMϕ​ 1.01.01.0 lambda energy gradient coefficient λ\lambdaλ 32σϵ\dfrac{3}{2}{\sigma}{\epsilon}23​σϵ omega depth of the double-well potential ω\omegaω 12σϵ12\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon}12ϵσ​ sigma surface tension σ\sigmaσ 1.01.01.0 epsilon thickness of interface ϵ\epsilonϵ 0.10.10.1

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions are prescribed on boundary of the domain:

n⋅λ∇ϕ=0 on ∂Ωtop∩∂Ωbottomϕ=1 on ∂Ωrightϕ=0 on ∂Ωleft \begin{align} {\bf{n}} \cdot{} \lambda \nabla \phi&=0 \text{ on }\partial\Omega_{top}\cap\partial\Omega_{bottom} \\[6pt] \phi&=1 \text{ on }\partial\Omega_{right} \\[6pt] \phi&=0 \text{ on }\partial\Omega_{left} \end{align} n⋅λ∇ϕϕϕ​=0 on ∂Ωtop​∩∂Ωbottom​=1 on ∂Ωright​=0 on ∂Ωleft​​​

docs.title: Numerical scheme
docs.text:
• Time integration: Euler Implicit over the interval t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]t∈[0,1] with a time-step δt=10−3\delta t=10^{-3}δt=10−3. The calculation stops when convergence criteria are reached.

∥ϕ(t+δt)−ϕ(t)∥<ϵϕ \|{\phi(t+\delta t)-\phi(t)}\|<\epsilon_\phi ∥ϕ(t+δt)−ϕ(t)∥<ϵϕ​

where ϵϕ=10−12\epsilon_\phi=10^{-12}ϵϕ​=10−12.

  • Spatial discretization for convergence analysis: uniform grid with N=30,60,90,120N={30, 60, 90, 120}N=30,60,90,120 nodes in each spatial direction, with Q1\mathcal{Q}_1Q1​ and Q2\mathcal{Q}_2Q2​ finite elements
  • Newton solver: relative tolerance 10−1210^{-12}10−12, absolute tolerance 10−1210^{-12}10−12
  • Iterative solver: HYPRE_GMRES
  • Preconditioner: HYPRE_ILU

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The steady state solution is given by:

ϕ=12+12tanh⁡(x−0.5ϵ). \phi = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \tanh\left(\dfrac{x-0.5}{\epsilon}\right). ϕ=21​+21​tanh(ϵx−0.5​).

This test corresponds to the homogeneous nucleation test proposed on PFhub, for single circular seed.

The domain Ω\OmegaΩ is a square [0,100]×[0,100][0,100]\times[0,100][0,100]×[0,100]

∂ϕ∂t=−M(F′(ϕ)−λΔϕ−Δfp′(ϕ)) in Ω \begin{align} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}&=-M (F'(\phi) - \lambda \Delta \phi - \Delta f p'(\phi)) \text{ in }\Omega \end{align} ∂t∂ϕ​​=−M(F′(ϕ)−λΔϕ−Δfp′(ϕ)) in Ω​​

docs.title: Statement of the problem
docs.text:
This test extends to 30 and 102 grains the one presented in 1 concerning the time evolution of a polycrystalline microstructure.

Allen-Cahn equations are solved in a square Ω=[0,32]×[0,32]\Omega=[0,32]\times[0,32]Ω=[0,32]×[0,32] using an implicit monolithic algorithm.

∂ηi∂t=−LiδFδηi,i=1,…,C \begin{align} \frac{\partial \eta_i}{\partial t} &= -L_i \frac{\delta F}{\delta \eta_i}, \qquad i = 1,\ldots,C \end{align} ∂t∂ηi​​​=−Li​δηi​δF​,i=1,…,C​​

where the free energy density is defined by:

F=∫V[∑i=1N(−12ηi2+14ηi4)+∑i=1C∑j=1j≠iC(ηi2ηj2)+∑i=1Cκi2∣∇ηi∣2] dv \begin{align} F &= \int_V \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( -\frac{1}{2}\eta_i^2 + \frac{1}{4}\eta_i^4 \right) + \sum_{i=1}^{C} \sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{C} (\eta_i^2 \eta_j^2) + \sum_{i=1}^{C} \frac{\kappa_i}{2} \left|\nabla \eta_i \right|^2 \right] \, dv \end{align} F​=∫V​⎣⎡​i=1∑N​(−21​ηi2​+41​ηi4​)+i=1∑C​j=1j=i​∑C​(ηi2​ηj2​)+i=1∑C​2κi​​∣∇ηi​∣2⎦⎤​dv​​

Hereabove, CCC corresponds to the number of grains.

F(ϕ)=ωϕ2(1−ϕ)2 \begin{align} F(\phi)&=\omega\phi^2(1-\phi)^2 \end{align} F(ϕ)​=ωϕ2(1−ϕ)2​​

docs.title: Statement of the problem
docs.text:
This test is taken from Zhang & al.1. It consists of spatial convergence analysis based on a manufactured solution benchmark.

The domain Ω\OmegaΩ is a square [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]\times[0,1][0,1]×[0,1]

∂ϕ∂t=Δμ+S(x,y,t) in Ωμ=F′(ϕ)−λΔϕ in Ω \begin{align} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}&= \Delta \mu +S(x,y,t)\text{ in }\Omega \\[6pt] \mu &= F'(\phi) - \lambda \Delta \phi \text{ in }\Omega \end{align} ∂t∂ϕ​μ​=Δμ+S(x,y,t) in Ω=F′(ϕ)−λΔϕ in Ω​​

where ϕ\phiϕ is the phase indicator, μ\muμ the generalized chemical potential and F′F'F′ the derivative against ϕ\phiϕ of the potential FFF defined by:

F(ϕ)=ϕ44−ϕ22 \begin{align} F(\phi)&=\frac{\phi^4}{4} - \frac{\phi^2}{2} \end{align} F(ϕ)​=4ϕ4​−2ϕ2​​​

In equation (1), S(x,y,t)S(x,y,t)S(x,y,t) is the source term allowing the exact solution:

ϕ=(t+1)sin⁡(απx) \phi = (t+1) \sin(\alpha \pi x) ϕ=(t+1)sin(απx)

docs.title: Example 6: rising bubble in an imposed flow (advection + AMR)
Files
docs.text:
• 2D test file: main.cpp
  • 3D test file: main.cpp
  • Velocity field: coefficient.json in each test directory

docs.title: Statement of the problem
docs.text:
This test is adapted from a rising bubble problem of C. Introïni's PhD thesis1. It validates the advection integrators (SplitAdvection, AdvectionBoundaryCH) coupled with the Cahn-Hilliard equations, with adaptive mesh refinement.

A bubble is transported by an imposed velocity field v\mathbf{v}v (no Navier-Stokes equations are solved):

∂ϕ∂t=∇⋅(M∇μ)−∇⋅(ϕ v) in Ωμ=ωW′(ϕ)−λΔϕ in Ω egin{align} rac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}&= abla\cdot\left(M abla \mu ight) - abla\cdot\left(\phi\,\mathbf{v} ight) ext{ in }\Omega \[6pt] \mu &= \omega W'(\phi) - \lambda \Delta \phi ext{ in }\Omega \end{align} ∂t∂ϕ​μ​=∇⋅(M∇μ)−∇⋅(ϕv) in Ω=ωW′(ϕ)−λΔϕ in Ω​​

where ϕ\phiϕ is the phase indicator (ϕ=0\phi=0ϕ=0 in the bubble, ϕ=1\phi=1ϕ=1 in the surrounding matrix), μ\muμ the generalized chemical potential and WWW the double-well potential:

W(ϕ)=ϕ2(1−ϕ)2,λ=32σϵ,ω=12σϵ egin{align} W(\phi)&=\phi^2(1-\phi)^2, \qquad \lambda= rac{3}{2}\sigma\epsilon, \qquad \omega= rac{12\sigma}{\epsilon} \end{align} W(ϕ)​=ϕ2(1−ϕ)2,λ=23​σϵ,ω=ϵ12σ​​​

The 2D domain Ω\OmegaΩ is the rectangle [0,R]×[0,H][0,R] imes[0,H][0,R]×[0,H] with R=5rbR=5r_bR=5rb​ and H=8rbH=8r_bH=8rb​, where rbr_brb​ is the bubble radius. The imposed velocity is a Poiseuille-like profile, vanishing on the lateral walls and divergence-free:

v=vmax[1−(x−R/2R/2)2]ey \mathbf{v} = v_{max}\left[1-\left( rac{x-R/2}{R/2} ight)^2 ight]\mathbf{e}_y v=vmax​[1−(R/2x−R/2​)2]ey​

In 3D, the domain is [0,R]×[0,H]×[0,R][0,R] imes[0,H] imes[0,R][0,R]×[0,H]×[0,R] (yyy is the vertical direction) and the profile is parabolic in both transverse directions:

v=vmax[1−(x−R/2R/2)2][1−(z−R/2R/2)2]ey \mathbf{v} = v_{max}\left[1-\left( rac{x-R/2}{R/2} ight)^2 ight]\left[1-\left( rac{z-R/2}{R/2} ight)^2 ight]\mathbf{e}_y v=vmax​[1−(R/2x−R/2​)2][1−(R/2z−R/2​)2]ey​

docs.title: Initial condition
docs.text:
The bubble is centred at (R/2,3rb)(R/2, 3r_b)(R/2,3rb​) in 2D ((R/2,3rb,R/2)(R/2, 3r_b, R/2)(R/2,3rb​,R/2) in 3D):

ϕ=12+12tanh⁡(2(r−rb)ϵ),μ=0 \phi = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\tanh\left(\frac{2\left(r - r_b\right)}{\epsilon}\right), \qquad \mu = 0 ϕ=21​+21​tanh(ϵ2(r−rb​)​),μ=0

where rrr is the distance to the bubble centre. μ=0\mu=0μ=0 corresponds to the equilibrium of the planar tanh profile (ωW′(ϕ)=λϕ′′\omega W'(\phi)=\lambda\phi''ωW′(ϕ)=λϕ′′ since λ/ω=ϵ2/8\lambda/\omega=\epsilon^2/8λ/ω=ϵ2/8).

docs.title: Parameters used for the test
docs.text:
The physical data are those of the rising bubble problem with Bo=10Bo=10Bo=10 and Mo=10−2Mo=10^{-2}Mo=10−2, the radius being deduced from the Bond number: rb=0.5σBo/(g(ρ2−ρ1))r_b = 0.5\sqrt{\sigma Bo/\left(g(\rho_2-\rho_1)\right)}rb​=0.5σBo/(g(ρ2​−ρ1​))​.

Name Description Symbol Value sigma interfacial energy σ\sigmaσ 7×10−27\times 10^{-2}7×10−2 J.m−2^{-2}−2 rho1, rho2 gas and liquid densities ρ1,ρ2\rho_1, \rho_2ρ1​,ρ2​ 111, 10310^3103 kg.m−3^{-3}−3 bond Bond number BoBoBo 101010 rb bubble radius rbr_brb​ 4.226×10−34.226\times 10^{-3}4.226×10−3 m epsilon interface thickness ϵ\epsilonϵ rb/7r_b/7rb​/7 mob mobility coefficient MMM 10−710^{-7}10−7 vmax maximum velocity vmaxv_{max}vmax​ 0.050.050.05 m.s−1^{-1}−1

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
Two configurations are computed successively:

  • periodic: periodic boundary conditions on all boundaries. The bubble leaving the domain at the top re-enters at the bottom.
  • open: periodic boundary conditions on the lateral boundaries, inflow/outflow boundary conditions on the bottom and top boundaries (homogeneous Neumann conditions for ϕ\phiϕ and μ\muμ completed by the advective flux):

ϕ v⋅n=ϕin v⋅n on ∂Ωbottom(v⋅n<0, ϕin=1)ϕ v⋅n=ϕ v⋅n on ∂Ωtop(v⋅n>0, free outflow) \begin{align} \phi\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} &= \phi_{in}\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} \text{ on }\partial\Omega_{bottom} \quad (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} < 0,\ \phi_{in}=1) \\[6pt] \phi\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} &= \phi\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} \text{ on }\partial\Omega_{top} \quad (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} > 0,\ \text{free outflow}) \end{align} ϕv⋅nϕv⋅n​=ϕin​v⋅n on ∂Ωbottom​(v⋅n<0, ϕin​=1)=ϕv⋅n on ∂Ωtop​(v⋅n>0, free outflow)​​

The inflow/outflow term is activated by an Inflow coefficient attached to the open boundaries (see Boundary conditions). The velocity components are Velocity_X, Velocity_Y (and Velocity_Z in 3D) coefficients carried by ϕ\phiϕ (block 0):

Coefficient velocity_x(Glossary::Velocity_X, 0.);
Coefficient velocity_y(Glossary::Velocity_Y, Scheme::Explicit, PoiseuilleVelocity());
Coefficient inflow(Glossary::Inflow, 1.);
inflow.set_bdr_index_coef(std::vector<int>{0, 2});

Coefficients coef_phi(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy, velocity_x, velocity_y, inflow);
Coefficients coef_mu(double_well, capillary, mobility, grad_energy);

SPAS spatials{&spatial_phi, &spatial_mu};
TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"CahnHilliard", "SplitAdvection"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit,
                  "SplitTimeDerivative");

docs.title: Numerical scheme
docs.text:
• Time integration: Euler Implicit over the interval t∈[0,0.6]t\in[0,0.6]t∈[0,0.6] s with a time-step δt=10−3\delta t=10^{-3}δt=10−3 s
  • Spatial discretization: Q1\mathcal{Q}_1Q1​ finite elements, coarse mesh 15×2415\times 2415×24 (15×24×1515\times 24\times 1515×24×15 in 3D, h=rb/3h=r_b/3h=rb​/3)
  • AMR: SingleVariableAMR driven by ϕ\phiϕ with a Kelly error estimator, 3 levels of refinement (hmin=rb/24h_{min}=r_b/24hmin​=rb​/24, i.e. about 3.4 elements in ϵ\epsilonϵ), 3 cycles of pre-refinement of the initial condition
  • AMR thresholds: max_elem_error =10−6=10^{-6}=10−6 in 2D (10−1210^{-12}10−12 in 3D), scale_down_factor =10−2=10^{-2}=10−2
  • Load balancing (2D test): the mesh is rebalanced between MPI processes after each AMR pass (rebalance AMR parameter), and an MPI_Problem saves the MPI rank of each degree of freedom (Saves_<config>/ProblemMPI) to visualize the partition (see Load balancing)
  • Newton solver: relative tolerance 10−1010^{-10}10−10, absolute tolerance 10−1410^{-14}10−14
  • Iterative solver: HYPRE_GMRES
  • Preconditioner: HYPRE_ILU

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The bubble is stretched by the Poiseuille flow (faster in the centre of the domain) and takes an ogive shape, while the refined region follows the interface and the wake is derefined (Figure 1).

Figure 1: rising bubble and AMR mesh (2D, periodic configuration)

In the periodic configuration, the integral of ϕ\phiϕ is conserved. In the open configuration, it increases once the bubble leaves the domain through the top boundary, the bubble (ϕ=0\phi=0ϕ=0) being replaced by the matrix (ϕ=1\phi=1ϕ=1) entering at the bottom.

  1. Clément Introïni. Interaction entre un fluide à haute température et un béton: contribution à la modélisation des échanges de masse et de chaleur. PhD thesis, Institut National Polytechnique de Toulouse-INPT, 2010. ↩

docs.title: Statement of the problem
docs.text:
This test corresponds to a 1D simulation of the evolution of temperature in a semi-infinite solid due to constant surface heat flux.

The domain Ω\OmegaΩ is a segment [0,10−3][0,10^{-3}][0,10−3]

ρCp∂T∂t=[∇⋅k∇T] in Ω \begin{align} \rho C_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=[\nabla \cdot{} k\nabla T] \text{ in }\Omega \end{align} ρCp​∂t∂T​=[∇⋅k∇T] in Ω​​

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
Neumann boundary conditions are prescribed on Γleft\Gamma_{left}Γleft​ and Dirichlet boundary conditions are prescribed on Γright\Gamma_{right}Γright​:

n⋅k∇T=q0′′ on ΓleftT(x=L,t)=Ti \begin{align} {\bf{n}} \cdot{} k \nabla T &= q_0'' \text{ on }\Gamma_{left} \\[6pt] T(x=L,t) &= T_i \end{align} n⋅k∇TT(x=L,t)​=q0′′​ on Γleft​=Ti​​​

docs.title: Initial condition
docs.text:
The temperature is assumed to be constant at t=0t=0t=0:

T(x,t=0)=Ti \begin{align} T(x,t=0) = T_i \end{align} T(x,t=0)=Ti​​​

Parameter Symbol Value Density ρ\rhoρ 10410^4104 Heat capacity CpC_pCp​ 10410^4104 Thermal conductivity kkk 111 Initial temperature TiT_iTi​ 000 Surface heat flux q0′′q_0''q0′′​ 111

  • Spatial discretization: uniform grid with N=30N=30N=30 nodes
  • Newton solver: absolute tolerance 10−1010^{-10}10−10

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The simulated temperature is compared to the analytical solution ([1]), which can be written as:

T(x,t)=Ti+q0′′Lcπkexp⁡(−x2Lc2)−q0′′xkerfc(xLc) \begin{align} T(x,t) = T_i + \frac{ q_0'' L_c }{ \sqrt{\pi} k } \exp \left( \frac{ -x^2 }{ L_c^2 } \right) - \frac{ q_0'' x }{ k } \text{erfc} \left( \frac{ x }{ L_c } \right) \end{align} T(x,t)=Ti​+π​kq0′′​Lc​​exp(Lc2​−x2​)−kq0′′​x​erfc(Lc​x​)​​

with Lc=4αt, α=kρCpL_c = \sqrt{ 4 \alpha t } \text{, } \alpha=\frac{ k }{ \rho C_p }Lc​=4αt​, α=ρCp​k​.

The results show good agreement with the analytical solution.

T(r,z,t)=e−tcos(πr2)cos(πz)−z \begin{align} T(r,z,t) &= e^{-t} cos (\pi r^2) cos(\pi z) - z \end{align} T(r,z,t)​=e−tcos(πr2)cos(πz)−z​​

∂c∂t=[∇⋅(κ+αc)∇c] in Ω \begin{align} \frac{\partial c}{\partial t}&=[\nabla \cdot{} \displaystyle(\kappa+\alpha c) \nabla c ]\text{ in }\Omega \end{align} ∂t∂c​​=[∇⋅(κ+αc)∇c] in Ω​​

where the concentration ccc in the diffusion coefficient can be evaluated at the previous time step, as done in the MFEM example, or at the current time step to form a fully nonlinear system.

This test is a Finite Element version of the sintering test of two unequal sized particles from 1.

(CH)∂ρ∂t=∇⋅D∇(∂f∂ρ−κρ∇2ρ)(AC)∂ηi∂t=−L(∂f∂ηi−κη∇2ηi),i=1,2 egin{align} (CH)\quad rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} &= abla \cdot D abla \left( rac{\partial f}{\partial ho} - \kappa_{ ho} abla^{2} ho ight) \[5pt] (AC)\quad rac{\partial \eta_i}{\partial t} &= -L\left( rac{\partial f}{\partial \eta_i} - \kappa_{\eta} abla^{2}\eta_i ight), \quad i=1,2 \end{align} (CH)∂t∂ρ​(AC)∂t∂ηi​​​=∇⋅D∇(∂ρ∂f​−κρ​∇2ρ)=−L(∂ηi​∂f​−κη​∇2ηi​),i=1,2​​

The free energy density is defined by:

where

docs.title: HowTo
docs.text:
This page comprises two sections:

  • The first section provides a description of the basic features of a SLOTH test as implemented in a very simple simulation;
  • The second section offers tutorials that provide comprehensive explanations of the more advanced features and how to use them to run more complex simulations.

docs.title: Basic features
docs.text:
This page provides a description of the basic features of a SLOTH test as implemented in a very simple simulation. This description is based on a very simple example, but the data structure shown is common to all SLOTH simulations.

On this page, the users can find the most important parts of a SLOTH input dataset and go to the pages of the User Manual that give all the options and the instructions for using them.

General structure of an input file

For an overview of the structure shared by all SLOTH input files, including multiphase and multiphysics cases, see the tutorial SLOTH Input Files in a Nutshell.

Statement of the problem

The current description is based on a simple example code that solves the Allen-Cahn equation in a 1D domain Ω=[0,R]\Omega=[0,R]Ω=[0,R] with R=10−3R=10^{-3}R=10−3.

Governing equationBoundary conditionsParametersNumerical scheme

Let us consider the following set of governing equations:

∂ϕ∂t=Mϕ[∇⋅λ∇ϕ−ωW′(ϕ)] in Ω rac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}=M_\phi[ abla \cdot{} \lambda abla \phi -\omega W'(\phi)] ext{ in }\Omega ∂t∂ϕ​=Mϕ​[∇⋅λ∇ϕ−ωW′(ϕ)] in Ω

where WWW is a double-well potential defined by:

W(ϕ)=ϕ2(1−ϕ)2 W(\phi)=\phi^2(1-\phi)^2 W(ϕ)=ϕ2(1−ϕ)2

The objective is to recover the 1D hyperbolic tangent solution

ϕ(r,t=tend)=12+12tanh⁡[2×(r−(R/2))ϵ] \phi(r,t=t_{end}) = rac{1}{2}+ rac{1}{2} anh igg[2 imes rac{(r - (R/2))}{ \epsilon} igg] ϕ(r,t=tend​)=21​+21​tanh[2×ϵ(r−(R/2))​]

starting from hyperbolic tangent solution with a thinner interface ϵ0=ϵ/10\epsilon_0=\epsilon/10ϵ0​=ϵ/10:

ϕ(r,t=0)=12+12tanh⁡[2×(r−(R/2)))ϵ0] \phi(r,t=0) = rac{1}{2}+ rac{1}{2} anh igg[2 imes rac{(r - (R/2)))}{ \epsilon_0} igg] ϕ(r,t=0)=21​+21​tanh[2×ϵ0​(r−(R/2)))​]

Neumann boundary conditions are prescribed on Γleft\Gamma_{left}Γleft​ (r=0) and Γright\Gamma_{right}Γright​ (r=R):

n⋅λ∇ϕ=0 on Γleft∪Γright { f{n}} \cdot{} \lambda abla \phi=0 ext{ on }\Gamma_{left} \cup \Gamma_{right} n⋅λ∇ϕ=0 on Γleft​∪Γright​

For this test, the following parameters are considered:

Parameter Symbol Value mobility coefficient MϕM_\phiMϕ​ 10−510^{-5}10−5 energy gradient coefficient λ\lambdaλ 32σϵ rac{3}{2}\sigma\epsilon23​σϵ surface tension σ\sigmaσ 0.060.060.06 interface \epsilon ϵ\epsilonϵ 5×10−45 imes10^{-4}5×10−4 depth of the double-well potential ω\omegaω 12σ/ϵ12 rac{\sigma}/{\epsilon}12/σ​ϵ
  • Time marching: Euler Implicit scheme, t∈[0,50]t\in[0,50]t∈[0,50], δt=0.25\delta t=0.25δt=0.25
