docs.title: Structure of a minimal test case
docs.text:
SLOTH provides C++ packages that allows to build multiphysics simulations.

Each SLOTH test is actually defined as a main.cpp file, which consists of four main parts:

Global structure of a minimal test case

//---------------------------------------
// 1/ Headers...
//---------------------------------------
int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    //---------------------------------------
    // 1/ Namespace / Parallelism
    //---------------------------------------

    //---------------------------------------
    // 2/ Geometry and Spatial discretization
    //---------------------------------------

    //---------------------------------------
    // 3/ Multiphysics coupling scheme
    //---------------------------------------

    //---------------------------------------
    // 4/ Time discretization
    //---------------------------------------
}

docs.title: Headers, Namespace & Parallelism
docs.text:
Headers, naamespace and parallelism features are the most general information that can be find in all test files.

There are 3 main headers.

  • kernel/sloth.hpp groups all SLOTH dependencies
  • mfem.hpp groups all mfem dependencies
  • tests/tests.hpp groups all dependencies useful only for tests

Test file with headers

//---------------------------------------
// Headers
//---------------------------------------
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"
#include "mfem.hpp"  // NOLINT [no include the directory when naming mfem include file]
#include "Sloth/tests.hpp"

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {

}

There are three namespaces, Sloth1D, Sloth2D and Sloth3D, for 1D, 2D, 3D simulations, respectively. They involved aliases that facilitate the use of complex C++ types by providing a more concise alternative and pertain to all tests. They are detailed in the Aliases page.

Test file with headers and namespace 

//---------------------------------------
// Headers
//---------------------------------------
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"
#include "mfem.hpp"  // NOLINT [no include the directory when naming mfem include file]
#include "Sloth/tests.hpp"

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    //---------------------------------------
    // Namespace
    //---------------------------------------
    using namespace Sloth1D;
}

The main aliases involved by the namespace Sloth1D are:

Alias Description DIM Spatial dimension VAR A single variable VARS Collection of variables PST Post-processing object SPA Spatial discretization SPAS std::vector<SPA*> BCS Boundary conditions TransientOPE Operator for transient problem TransientPB Transient problem

SLOTH's ambition is to be able to perform massively parallel computations while logically retaining the ability to perform sequential computations.

Only three lines of code must be defined in each test file for the MPI and HYPRE libraries, and two lines for the profiling.

Test file with headers, common aliases and parallelism features

//---------------------------------------
// Headers
//---------------------------------------
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"
#include "mfem.hpp"  // NOLINT [no include the directory when naming `MFEM` include file]
#include "Sloth/tests.hpp"

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    //---------------------------------------
    // Initialize MPI and HYPRE
    //---------------------------------------
    mfem::Mpi::Init(argc, argv);
    mfem::Hypre::Init();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Profiling
    //---------------------------------------
    Profiling::getInstance().enable();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Namespace
    //---------------------------------------
    using namespace Sloth1D;


    //---------------------------------------
    // Profiling stop
    //---------------------------------------
    Profiling::getInstance().print();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Finalize MPI
    //---------------------------------------
    mfem::Mpi::Finalize();
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Spatial discretization
docs.text:
This part is dedicated the mesh (see Meshing) and the associated boundary conditions (see BoundaryConditions).

Regarding the mesh, SLOTH enables to read meshes built with GMSH or to build a Cartesian mesh directly in MFEM. The order of the Finite Elements and the level of mesh refinement must be also defined.

Definition of a Finite Element mesh for SLOTH is made with a C++ object of type SpatialDiscretization or, more specifically for tests, by using the alias SPA.

Extract of the test file with the definition of the mesh

auto refinement_level = 0;
auto fe_order = 1;
auto length = 1.e-3;
auto nb_fe = 30;
SPA spatial("InlineLineWithSegments", fe_order, refinement_level, std::make_tuple(nb_fe, length));
This example considers a 1D Finite Element mesh, without refinement (refinement_level = 0), built directly in MFEM. The length of the domain is 111 mm (length = 1.e-3), divided into 303030 first order (fe_order = 1) elements (nb_fe = 30).

All the functions used to create meshes are detailed in the Meshing section of the user manual.

Regarding the boundary conditions, SLOTH enables to prescribe Dirichlet, Neumann and Periodic boundary conditions.

Definition of boundary conditions for SLOTH is made with a C++ object of type BoundaryConditions or, more specifically for tests, by using the alias BCS.

A BCSobject is a collection of C++ objects of type Boundary. Each of them is associated to a geometrical boundary. The number of Boundary objects inside the BCS object must be equal to the total number of geometrical boundary.

A Boundary object is defined by

  • a name (C++ type `std::string'),
  • an index (C++ type int),
  • a type (C++ type `std::string') among "Dirichlet", "Neumann", "Periodic",
  • a value (C++ type double), only for uniform Dirichlet boundar condition.

Extract of the test file with the mesh and its associated Neumann boundary conditions

    //---------------------------------------
    // Meshing & Boundary Conditions
    //---------------------------------------
    auto refinement_level = 0;
    auto fe_order = 1;
    auto length = 1.e-3;
    auto nb_fe = 30;
    SPA spatial("InlineLineWithSegments", fe_order, refinement_level, std::make_tuple(nb_fe, length));

    auto boundaries = {Boundary("left", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 1, "Neumann")};
    auto bcs = BCS(&spatial, boundaries);
This example consider homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions both on the left and on the right of the domain.

Different type of boundary conditions can be mixed as detailed in the Boundary Conditions section of the user manual.

On the consistency of the indices of the boundaries

MFEM v4.7 provides new features for referring to boundary attribute numbers. Such an improvement is not yet implemented in SLOTH. Consequently, users must take care to the consistency of the indices used in the test file with the indices defined when building the mesh with GMSH.

Test file with the mesh and the boundary conditions

//---------------------------------------
// Headers
//---------------------------------------
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"
#include "mfem.hpp"  // NOLINT [no include the directory when naming mfem include file]
#include "Sloth/tests.hpp"

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    //---------------------------------------
    // Initialize MPI and HYPRE
    //---------------------------------------
    mfem::Mpi::Init(argc, argv);
    mfem::Hypre::Init();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Profiling
    //---------------------------------------
    Profiling::getInstance().enable();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Namespace
    //---------------------------------------
    using namespace Sloth1D;

    //---------------------------------------
    // Meshing & Boundary Conditions
    //---------------------------------------
    auto refinement_level = 0;
    auto fe_order = 1;
    auto length = 1.e-3;
    auto nb_fe = 30;
    SPA spatial("InlineLineWithSegments", fe_order, refinement_level, std::make_tuple(nb_fe, length));
    auto boundaries = {Boundary("left", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 1, "Neumann")};
    auto bcs = BCS(&spatial, boundaries);
    //---------------------------------------
    // Finalize MPI
    //---------------------------------------
    mfem::Mpi::Finalize();
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Multiphysics coupling scheme
docs.text:
This part is the core of the test file with the definition of the targeted physical problems (eg. equations, variational formulations, variables, coefficients) gathered inside a Coupling object.

This implies many C++ objects designed specifically for SLOTH. The main one is the Problem object defined as a collection of C++ objects of interest for SLOTH:

  • a Variables object,
  • an Operator object,
  • a PostProcessing object.

Regarding the Variables, SLOTH differentiates between primary variables, that are solved directly by the problem (eg. the order parameter for the Allen-Cahn equation, the order parameter and the chemical potential for the Cahn-Hilliard equation), and secondary variables, which are derived from another problem to ensure multiphysics coupling (eg. the order parameter in the heat transfer equation, the temperature in the Allen-Cahn equation).

Despite their different purposes, the definition of primary and auxiliary variables are consistent and made with a C++ object of type Variables (see the alias VARS). Variables is simply a collection of Variable object (see the alias VAR) defined by:

  • the spatial discretisation (ie. the SPAobject),
  • a set of boundary conditions (ie the BCS object),
  • a name (C++ type std::string),
  • a storage depth level (C++ type int),
  • a type (SLOTH type GlossaryQuantity),
  • an initial condition,
  • an analytical solution (optional).

Definition of variables with an analytical solution

The presence of an analytical solution automatically enables the calculation of the L2L^2L2 error over the domain.

Whether it's an initial condition or an analytical solution, the users can define them with a constant, a C++ object of type std::function or a C++ object of type AnalyticalFunctions.

It is recommended to read the page dedicated to Variables in the user manual for more details about the use and the different definitions of this SLOTH object.

AnalyticalFunctions enable to use pre-defined mathematical functions currently used in the studies conducted with SLOTH.

If the mathematical expression is not yet available, the users can define it with a C++ object of type std::function.

Extract of the test file with Variables

    //---------------------------------------
    // Multiphysics coupling scheme
    //---------------------------------------     
    //--- Variables
    const auto& center_x = 0.;
    const auto& a_x = 1.;
    const auto& epsilon = 5.e-4;
    const auto& thickness = 5.e-5;
    const auto& radius = 5.e-4;

    std::string variable_name = "phi";
    GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::PhaseField;
    int level_of_storage= 2;

    auto initial_condition = AnalyticalFunctions<DIM>(AnalyticalFunctionsType::from("HyperbolicTangent"), center_x, a_x, 2.*thickness, radius);
    auto analytical_solution = AnalyticalFunctions<DIM>(AnalyticalFunctionsType::from("HyperbolicTangent"), center_x, a_x, thickness, radius);
    auto vars = VARS(VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition, analytical_solution));
This example defines a single primary variable, named "phi" with two levels of storage. The initial condition and the analytical solution are of the hyperbolic tangent type.

Other major C++ objects for SLOTH is SteadyOperator and TransientOperator, which enables to solve the steady and unsteady algebraic system resulting from the discretization of the (non-linear) equations. This is detailed in the Partial Differential Equations page of the user manual. Specifically for tests, SteadyOperator and TransientOperator are accessible by using the aliases SteadyOPE and TransientOPE.

Although the input arguments provided to these objects are of interest, the focus is rather on the definition of the C++ object itself, which requires the input of the variational formulation of the equations. This specificity is implemented using objects of BlockNonLinearFormIntegrators, also detailed in the user manual in the Partial Differential Equations page. The definition of the integrators obviously depends on the targeted problem (see the dedicated page of the user manual for more details about Integrators).

In the present example, the variational formulation is defined by combining the TimeDerivative, AllenCahn and MeltingConstant integrators in order to solve the following equation:

∂φ∂t=M(∇⋅[λ∇φ]−∂F∂φ)+Mαp′(φ) \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} = M\left(\nabla \cdot \left[\lambda \nabla \varphi\right] - \displaystyle\frac{\partial F}{\partial \varphi}\right)+ M \alpha p'(\varphi) \end{align} ∂t∂φ​=M(∇⋅[λ∇φ]−∂φ∂F​)+Mαp′(φ)​​

where α\alphaα is a constant enthalpy of melting.

Extract of the test file with a transient Operator

    SPAS spatials{&spatial};
    const auto& alpha(7.e3);
    auto params = Parameters(Parameter("melting_factor", alpha));

    TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"AllenCahn", "MeltingConstant"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "TimeDerivative");

Use of Parameters and Parameter objects

Parameters is a C++ object designed for SLOTH and defined as a collection of Parameter objects. The latter is also a C++ object specially developed for SLOTH. It enables the definition of a variable which can be of different C++ types. It is based on the std::variant type. Users are referred to the Parameters page in the user manual for more details about the definition and the use of these objects.

The results of SLOTH simulations can be exported to VTK format and can be read with Paraview. This is possible by using the C++ object PSTCollection or, more specifically for tests, by using the alias PST. This C++ object requires the knowledge of the mesh and a number of parameters to define, at least, the directories in which the results are stored and the frequency of storage. All these parameters are detailed in the page PostProcessing. By default, all primary variables associated with a SLOTH Problem are saved.

Extract of the test file with PostProcessing

    //--- Post-Processing 
    const std::string& main_folder_path = "Saves";
    std::string calculation_path = "AllenCahn";
    const auto& frequency = 1;
    auto pst_parameters = Parameters(Parameter("main_folder_path", main_folder_path), Parameter("calculation_path", calculation_path), Parameter("frequency", frequency));
    auto pst = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);
In this example, the results will be saved in the Saves/AllenCahn directory (see Parameter("main_folder_path", main_folder_path) and Parameter("calculation_path", calculation_path)), at each time-step (see Parameter("frequency", frequency)).

At this stage, the SLOTH Problem can be defined and, as previously explained, collected in a Coupling object. Specially for tests, steady and unsteady problems are accessible using the SteadyPB and TransientPB, respectively.

This is illustrated in the following example (see TransientPB and Coupling("Main coupling", ac_problem)).

Test file with Variables, Operators and Integrators and Post-Processing

//---------------------------------------
// Headers
//---------------------------------------
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"
#include "mfem.hpp"  // NOLINT [no include the directory when naming mfem include file]
#include "Sloth/tests.hpp"

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    //---------------------------------------
    // Initialize MPI and HYPRE
    //---------------------------------------
    mfem::Mpi::Init(argc, argv);
    mfem::Hypre::Init();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Profiling
    //---------------------------------------
    Profiling::getInstance().enable();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Namespace
    //---------------------------------------        
    using namespace Sloth1D;
    //---------------------------------------
    // Meshing & Boundary Conditions
    //---------------------------------------
    auto refinement_level = 0;
    auto fe_order = 1;
    auto length = 1.e-3;
    auto nb_fe = 30;
    SPA spatial("InlineLineWithSegments", fe_order, refinement_level, std::make_tuple(nb_fe, length));
    auto boundaries = {Boundary("left", 0, "Neumann"), Boundary("right", 1, "Neumann")};
    auto bcs = BCS(&spatial, boundaries);

    //---------------------------------------
    // Multiphysics coupling scheme
    //---------------------------------------     
    //--- Variables
    const auto& center_x = 0.;
    const auto& a_x = 1.;
    const auto& epsilon = 5.e-4;
    const auto& thickness = 5.e-5;
    const auto& radius = 5.e-4;

    std::string variable_name = "phi";
    GlossaryQuantity variable_type = Glossary::PhaseField;
    int level_of_storage= 2;

    auto initial_condition = AnalyticalFunctions<DIM>(AnalyticalFunctionsType::from("HyperbolicTangent"), center_x, a_x, 2.*thickness, radius);
    auto analytical_solution = AnalyticalFunctions<DIM>(AnalyticalFunctionsType::from("HyperbolicTangent"), center_x, a_x, thickness, radius);
    auto vars = VARS(VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition, analytical_solution));

    //--- Operator definition
    SPAS spatials{&spatial};
    const auto& alpha(7.e3);
    auto params = Parameters(Parameter("melting_factor", alpha));

    TransientOPE oper(spatials, {"AllenCahn", "MeltingConstant"}, params, TimeScheme::EulerImplicit, "TimeDerivative");

    //--- Coefficients
    // Interfacial energy
    const auto& sigma(6.e-2);
    // Two-phase mobility
    const auto& mob(1.e-5);
    const auto& lambda = 3. * sigma * epsilon / 2.;
    const auto& omega = 12. * sigma / epsilon;
    Coefficient grad_energy(Glossary::GradEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, GradientEnergy(lambda));
    Coefficient double_well_imp(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, W(omega));
    Coefficient interpolation(Glossary::InterpolationFunction, Scheme::Implicit, H());
    Coefficient capillary(Glossary::Capillary, lambda);
    Coefficient mobility(Glossary::Mobility, mob);
    Coefficients coef_ac(double_well_imp, capillary, mobility, interpolation, grad_energy);

    //--- Post-Processing 
    const std::string& main_folder_path = "Saves";
    std::string calculation_path = "AllenCahn";
    const auto& frequency = 1;
    auto pst_parameters = Parameters(Parameter("main_folder_path", main_folder_path), Parameter("calculation_path", calculation_path), Parameter("frequency", frequency));
    auto pst = PST(&spatial, pst_parameters);

    //-----------------------
    // Problem
    //-----------------------
    TransientPB ac_problem(oper, vars, {coef_ac}, pst);

    //-----------------------
    // Coupling
    //-----------------------
    auto main_coupling = Coupling("Main coupling", ac_problem);

    //---------------------------------------
    // Profiling stop
    //---------------------------------------
    Profiling::getInstance().print();
    //---------------------------------------
    // Finalize MPI
    //---------------------------------------
    mfem::Mpi::Finalize();
    return 0;
}
In this example, a coupling, labelled Main coupling, is defined with only one SLOTH Problem associated with the solution of Allen-Cahn equation.

Each SLOTH problem used to solve PDEs must be defined with a vector of SLOTH Coefficients objects. These objects are described in Coefficients page of the user manual. They are used to define the main parameters of the equations and the energy of the system, which are then employed by the SLOTHintegrators.

Users are referred to the MultiPhysicsCouplingScheme page of the user manual for more details about the available SLOTH problems and how to use them.

docs.title: Time discretization
docs.text:
Time discretization is the last main part of a test file. It corresponds to the C++ object TimeDiscretization defined as a number of parameters and the Coupling objects specially designed for the current SLOTH simulation. Among these parameters, there are the initial time, the final time and the uniform value of the time-step. The method solve must be explicitly called to run the calculation. This is detailed in the Time page of the user manual.

Extract of the test file with TimeDiscretization

    //---------------------------------------
    // Time discretization
    //--------------------------------------- 
    const auto& t_initial = 0.0;
    const auto& t_final = 50.0;
    const auto& dt = 0.01;
    auto time_parameters = Parameters(Parameter("initial_time", t_initial), Parameter("final_time", t_final), Parameter("time_step", dt));
    auto time = TimeDiscretization(time_parameters, main_coupling);

    time.solve();
In this example, the simulation is performed during 505050 s with a time-step equal to 0.010.010.01 s.

docs.title: Comprehensive test file
docs.text:

// Headers
//---------------------------------------
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"
#include "mfem.hpp"  // NOLINT [no include the directory when naming mfem include file]

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {

    //---------------------------------------

    //---------------------------------------

    //---------------------------------------
    using namespace Sloth1D;
    //---------------------------------------
    // Meshing & Boundary Conditions
    //---------------------------------------
    auto refinement_level = 0;
    auto fe_order = 1;
    auto length = 1.e-3;
    auto nb_fe = 30;

    const auto& center_x = 0.;

    std::string variable_name = "phi";

    auto analytical_solution = AnalyticalFunctions<DIM>(AnalyticalFunctionsType::from("HyperbolicTangent"), center_x, a_x, thickness, radius);
    auto vars = VARS(VAR(&spatial, bcs, variable_name, variable_type, level_of_storage, initial_condition, analytical_solution));

    //--- Operator definition
    SPAS spatials{&spatial};

docs.title: Tutorial: Using Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR)
docs.text:
This tutorial explains how to enable Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) on a SLOTH simulation.

It builds on a standard Cahn-Hilliard simulation (see the Cahn-Hilliard examples) and highlights only the additions required to switch it on.

docs.title: Step 1 – Enable non-conforming refinement on the mesh
docs.text:
AMR relies on locally refining/coarsening a mesh, which requires the mesh to support non-conforming refinement (see the dedicated page on the MFEM website for more details). This is enabled by adding two boolean flags, enable_nc_mesh and allow_nc_simplices, as the last arguments of the SPA constructor, whatever the type of mesh (periodic or not, built from file or not):

SPA spatial_phi(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, /*enable_nc_mesh*/ true);
  • enable_nc_mesh (default false) is the flag that actually builds the mesh in non-conforming mode. It must be set to true to use AMR - a conforming mesh cannot be converted afterwards.
  • allow_nc_simplices (default false, omitted above) additionally allows non-conforming refinement on triangle/tetrahedron elements specifically; it has no effect on quadrilateral/hexahedral meshes such as the one used here. If your mesh is made of triangles or tetrahedra, pass it explicitly too: 
SPA spatial_phi(mesh_type, order_fe, refinement_level, tuple_of_dimensions, /*enable_nc_mesh*/ true, /*allow_nc_simplices*/ true);

The value passed for allow_nc_simplices can later be read back with is_nc_simplices(), which is needed to configure the AMR driver (see Step 3). See the Meshing page of the User Manual for the full constructor signatures (GMSH and MFEM inline meshes, with or without periodicity).

docs.title: Step 2 – Share the same mesh across all variables
docs.text:
All the variables involved in the coupling must live on the same mesh, so that a refinement decision taken for one variable is consistently applied to every finite element space. Additional SPA objects are therefore built from the mesh of the first one, rather than from mesh_type / tuple_of_dimensions again:

SPA spatial_mu(spatial_phi.get_mesh(), order_fe);

Building an SPA object from an existing mesh is also interesting for simulations that do not involve AMR. Such an approach lets several variables share the same mesh while using different finite element orders (order_fe) for each of them. If every variable uses the same finite element order, a single SPA object is enough — there is no need to build additional ones from get_mesh(). With AMR, this pattern becomes essential, since it is now the only way to guarantee that every variable follows the same sequence of refinements/derefinements applied to the shared mesh.

Here, spatial_mu gets its own, independent finite element space (it can even use a different order_fe), while sharing the mesh (mfem::ParMesh) held by spatial_phi. This constructor also accepts a third, optional argument, is_periodic_mesh (default false): if the shared mesh is periodic, pass spatial_phi.is_periodic() so that spatial_mu reports its periodicity correctly too.

Mesh ownership

spatial_mu does not take ownership of the mesh: it will never delete it. The SPA object that originally created the mesh (spatial_phi here) must therefore outlive every SPA object built from it.

AMR Requirements

To use AMR, the following conditions must be satisfied:

  • The SPA object driving the mesh must be built with enable_nc_mesh set to true (and allow_nc_simplices set to true as well, if the mesh is made of triangles/tetrahedra).
  • Every other SPA object used by the variables of the coupling must be built from that same mesh, using spatial.get_mesh(), rather than from a new mesh definition.
  • Boundary conditions (BCS) and variables (VAR) are then declared exactly as usual, one per SPA object.

docs.title: 2. Defining an Error Estimator
docs.text:
Refinement decisions are driven by an error estimator, evaluated on the mesh shared in Step 1. It can be built from an MFEM bilinear form integrator and wrapped into a SlothErrorEstimators object:

mfem::ConstantCoefficient amr_coef{1.0};
mfem::DiffusionIntegrator amr_integ{amr_coef};
SlothErrorEstimators estimator(ErrorEstimatorType::KELLY, &amr_integ);
  • amr_integ is a standard MFEM integrator (here mfem::DiffusionIntegrator, built from a constant coefficient) used to evaluate the estimator on each mesh face.
  • ErrorEstimatorType::KELLY selects the Kelly error estimator, which flags elements for refinement based on the jump of the estimated quantity across element faces.

Available error estimators

SLOTH currently provides two error estimators built on top of MFEM: ErrorEstimatorType::KELLY (shown above) and ErrorEstimatorType::L2_ZIENKIEWICZ_ZHU (Zienkiewicz–Zhu). More estimators may be added in the future. See the Adaptive Mesh Refinement page of the User Manual for a complete description of each estimator and how to configure it.

docs.title: Step 1 – Create the AMR object
docs.text:
The SingleVariableAMR object drives the refinement/coarsening of the shared mesh, based on one "driving" variable of the coupling:

SingleVariableAMR<VARS> amr(*spatial_phi.get_mesh(), spatial_phi.is_nc_simplices(), 0);

Its arguments are:

  1. The shared mesh (dereferenced mfem::ParMesh returned by get_mesh()).
  2. Whether non-conforming refinement was allowed on simplex elements when the mesh was built, obtained with is_nc_simplices() — this must simply mirror the allow_nc_simplices value passed to the SPA constructor (see Step 1); for quadrangle/hexahedron meshes such as the one used here, it is left at its default (false).
  3. The variable used to drive the refinement (the pilot variable), given by its index within VARS (0 here refers to the first variable declared in vars, i.e. phi) or by its name ("phi").

Driving the refinement with several variables

When a single variable is not sufficient to characterize where the mesh should be refined, SLOTH also provides MultiVariableMaxAMR<VARS>, which considers several pilot variables at once: every variable of VARS by default, or the variables whose names are given as a third argument (e.g. std::vector<std::string>{"phi", "c"}). For each element, the per-variable errors are combined by taking their maximum, and the mesh is refined/derefined once from this combined criterion, so an element is a candidate as soon as any pilot variable needs it resolved there. Refer to the Adaptive Mesh Refinement page of the User Manual for details.

docs.title: Step 2 – Set the refinement criteria
docs.text:
auto amr_params = Parameters(Parameter("max_elem_error", 1.e-4), Parameter("amr_max_level", 4),
                               Parameter("nc_limit", 0), Parameter("max_preref_cycles", 4));
amr.SetCriteria(/*estimator*/ &estimator, amr_params);
Argument/Parameter Type Description estimator SlothErrorEstimators* The error estimator defined in Section 2. max_elem_error double Error threshold above which an element is flagged for refinement. amr_max_level int Maximum number of refinement levels allowed for any element. nc_limit int Maximum allowed level difference between two neighboring elements (0 = no limit enforced). max_preref_cycles int Maximum number of refinement cycles applied to the mesh, based on the initial condition of the driving variable, before the first time step is solved.

Parallel computations: load balancing

Refinement concentrates the elements on the MPI processes that own the interfaces. Adding Parameter("rebalance", true) to amr_params redistributes the mesh between processes after each AMR pass that modified it. See the Load balancing section of the User Manual.

docs.title: Step 3 – Attach the AMR driver to the problem
docs.text:
problem1.set_amr(&amr);

Once attached, SLOTH automatically checks the refinement criteria and updates the shared mesh (and every finite element space and variable built on it) as the simulation progresses — no further action is required from the user during time integration.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Enabling AMR on a SLOTH simulation consists of:

  1. Building the first SPA object with enable_nc_mesh set to true (and allow_nc_simplices too, for triangle/tetrahedron meshes), then building every other SPA object of the coupling from its shared mesh (spatial.get_mesh()).
  2. Defining an error estimator (SlothErrorEstimators) from an MFEM integrator.
  3. Creating a SingleVariableAMR (or MultiVariableMaxAMR) object, setting its refinement criteria with SetCriteria, and attaching it to the problem with set_amr.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
A complete working example is available in the SLOTH repository:

  • 2D spinodal decomposition (Cahn-Hilliard) with AMR: https://github.com/Collab4Sloth/SLOTH/blob/master/tests/CahnHilliard/2D/test2_amr/main.cpp
  • 2D rising bubble (Cahn-Hilliard + advection) with AMR and load balancing: https://github.com/Collab4Sloth/SLOTH/blob/master/tests/CahnHilliard/2D/test6/main.cpp
  • 2D grain growth (one problem per grain, one AMR object per problem): https://github.com/Collab4Sloth/SLOTH/blob/master/tests/Studies/multigrains/test1_amr/main.cpp

docs.title: Tutorial: Coefficients with Sympy
docs.text:
This tutorial explains how the physics of a SLOTH problem is described with Coefficient objects, and how to write your own coefficients with the Sympy interface.

The running example goes from the double-well potential of the Allen-Cahn equation to the free energy of two sintering particles (Cahn-Hilliard + Allen-Cahn), taken from the tests/Studies/sintering/test1 case of the SLOTH repository. The structure of a main.cpp is assumed to be known (see the tutorial SLOTH Input Files in a Nutshell).

Slides

This tutorial is also available as a slide deck: download the PDF.

docs.title: Step 1 – The physics lives in coefficients
docs.text:
In SLOTH, the equation is carried by the integrators: the AllenCahn integrator assembles the weak form, the residual and the Jacobian of

∂φ∂t=−M[ω W′(φ)−λ Δφ] \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t} = -M\left[\omega\,W'(\varphi) - \lambda\,\Delta\varphi\right] ∂t∂φ​=−M[ωW′(φ)−λΔφ]

What changes from one material to another is in the coefficients: the mobility MMM (Glossary::Mobility), the free energy ωW\omega WωW (Glossary::FreeEnergy) and the capillarity λ\lambdaλ (Glossary::Capillary). For an energy, the integrator also needs the first and second derivatives, used in the residual and the Jacobian of the Newton solver: this is why SLOTH generates coefficients with Sympy, which differentiates the formula exactly.

docs.title: Step 2 – Quantity, scheme and function
docs.text:
Coefficient energy(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, W(omega));

A Coefficient is made of three ingredients:

QuantitySchemeFunction

A Glossary quantity says what the coefficient is: FreeEnergy, Mobility, Capillary, GradEnergy, Temperature, Dirichlet, Neumann, …

Integrators look a coefficient up by its quantity: the AllenCahn integrator searches the coefficients of the problem for a FreeEnergy, a Mobility and a Capillary.

The scheme says at which state the function is evaluated:

Scheme Evaluated with Derivatives in the Jacobian Scheme::Implicit the current Newton iterate yes Scheme::Explicit the fields of the previous time step tnt^ntn no Scheme::SemiImplicit both, see explicit_variables for the implicit variables

A constant takes no scheme.

A constant, a function provided by SLOTH such as W(omega), or your own class generated by Sympy from a JSON file. The latter is the topic of this tutorial.

docs.title: Step 3 – Three ways to give the function
Step 1 – From a formula to a C++ class
docs.text:
You write the formulas in a JSON file. The script GenerateCoefficient.py (in the scripts folder of SLOTH, or provided by an installed SLOTH as Sloth_COEFFICIENT_SCRIPT) parses each entry with Sympy, computes the first and second derivatives, and writes one C++ class per entry in the header named by outputfile. The header is then included in main.cpp.

By handWith CMake 
python3 GenerateCoefficient.py -r -f coefficients.json

The -r option overwrites existing files. Python 3 and Sympy are required (see the ExprTk and Sympy installation page).

add_custom_command(
  OUTPUT ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/MyCoefficients.hpp
  COMMAND ${Python3_EXECUTABLE} ${Sloth_COEFFICIENT_SCRIPT} -r -f ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/coefficients.json
  WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}
  DEPENDS ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/coefficients.json)

The header is regenerated whenever the JSON file changes (see Using an installed SLOTH).

docs.title: Step 2 – The double well, written by you
docs.text:
[
    {
    "expression": "phi*phi*(1-phi)*(1-phi)",
    "variables": "phi",
    "class_name": "DoubleWell",
    "outputfile": "MyCoefficients"
    }
]

This entry defines W(φ)=φ2(1−φ)2W(\varphi)=\varphi^2(1-\varphi)^2W(φ)=φ2(1−φ)2. The four keys used here are required:

Key Meaning expression the formula, in Sympy syntax variables the unknowns; derivatives are taken with respect to them (separated by spaces or commas) class_name name of the generated C++ class outputfile basename of the generated .hpp file

The optional keys constants, auxiliary_variables, coordinates and gradient are introduced below. In main.cpp, the generated class is used like any built-in:

#include "MyCoefficients.hpp"

Coefficient energy(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, DoubleWell(omega));

The prefactor

Every generated class accepts one optional argument, the prefactor (omega above, default 1). It multiplies the function and all its derivatives. It is convenient for sensitivity studies, or to reuse one formula for several coefficients.

docs.title: Step 3 – What Sympy writes
docs.text:
For each entry, the generator writes a class deriving from FunctionCoefficient with three functions: the value, the first derivatives (one per variable) and the Hessian. An extract of the class generated for the double well:

class DoubleWell : public FunctionCoefficient { … };

// value
double phi = input_vector[0];
double F = std::pow(phi, 2) * std::pow(1 - phi, 2);
return this->prefactor_ * F;

// first derivatives, one per variable
gradient[0] = this->prefactor_ *
  (std::pow(phi, 2) * (2 * phi - 2) + 2 * phi * std::pow(1 - phi, 2));
  • The derivatives are exact, computed symbolically by Sympy, not by finite differences.
  • The unknowns are read by position: the i-th variable of the JSON entry is input_vector[i], the i-th auxiliary variable is auxiliary_vector[i]. This is the origin of the ordering convention.
  • The header is a build product: never edit it by hand, change the JSON file and regenerate.

docs.title: Step 4 – Constants, physical constants and time
docs.text:
[
    {
    "expression": "a*x*x + b*x*y + c*z*x*y",
    "variables": "x, y z",
    "constants": "(a:2.0),(b:30.0),(c:0.1)",
    "class_name": "FunctionA",
    "outputfile": "MyCoefficients"
    }
]

Constants are written as (name:value) pairs separated by commas. They are substituted when the class is generated: changing one means regenerating. A value can also be the name of a SLOTH physical constant:

Value Meaning H Planck constant (Physical::H) NA Avogadro constant (Physical::NA) K Boltzmann constant (Physical::K) R molar gas constant (Physical::R) T current time, updated by SLOTH

The constant T makes a coefficient time-dependent, for example "constants": "(a:2.0),(t:T)" with "expression": "a*x*x*t".

Constant or prefactor?

A constant is frozen when the class is generated; the prefactor is chosen in main.cpp for each Coefficient. Use the prefactor for a parameter you want to vary between runs or between coefficients.

docs.title: Step 1 – Variables and auxiliary variables
docs.text:
The running example is the sintering of two particles: Cahn-Hilliard solves the density ccc, Allen-Cahn solves the grain fields η1,η2\eta_1, \eta_2η1​,η2​. The same free energy enters both problems:

f(c,η1,η2)=A c2(1−c)2+B[c2+6(1−c)∑iηi2−4(2−c)∑iηi3+3(∑iηi2)2] f(c,\eta_1,\eta_2) = A\,c^2(1-c)^2 + B\Big[c^2 + 6(1-c)\sum_{i}\eta_i^2 - 4(2-c)\sum_{i}\eta_i^3 + 3\Big(\sum_{i}\eta_i^2\Big)^2\Big] f(c,η1​,η2​)=Ac2(1−c)2+B[c2+6(1−c)i∑​ηi2​−4(2−c)i∑​ηi3​+3(i∑​ηi2​)2]

A coefficient must therefore say which fields are unknowns and which are only read:

  • variables: the unknowns of the problem that uses the coefficient. Sympy differentiates with respect to them; they are read, in order, from the problem's VARS.
  • auxiliary_variables: fields solved by another problem. They are only read, with no derivative; they are read, in order, from the auxiliary variables passed as the last argument of the problem.

docs.title: Step 2 – One energy, one class per problem
docs.text:
The same formula is therefore generated twice, once per problem, with different roles for the fields:

For Cahn-HilliardFor Allen-Cahn 
{
"expression": "A*c*c*(1-c)*(1-c) + B*(c*c + 6*(1-c)*Sum(eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)) - 4*(2-c)*Sum(eta[i]*eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)) + 3*(Sum(eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)))^2)",
"variables": "c",
"auxiliary_variables": "eta(1..2)",
"constants": "(A:16.0),(B:1.0)",
"class_name": "Fc",
"outputfile": "SinteringCoefficients"
}

TransientPB ch_pb("CahnHilliard", ch_oper,
                  ch_vars,             // c, mu   → input_vector
                  {ch_coef, ch_coef}, ch_pst,
                  ac_vars);            // η1, η2 → auxiliary_vector

{
"expression": "A*c*c*(1-c)*(1-c) + B*(c*c + 6*(1-c)*Sum(eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)) - 4*(2-c)*Sum(eta[i]*eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)) + 3*(Sum(eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)))^2)",
"variables": "eta(1..2)",
"auxiliary_variables": "c",
"constants": "(A:16.0),(B:1.0)",
"class_name": "Feta",
"outputfile": "SinteringCoefficients"
}

TransientPB ac_pb("AllenCahn", ac_oper,
                  ac_vars,             // η1, η2 → input_vector
                  {ac_coef, ac_coef}, ac_pst,
                  ch_vars);            // c, mu   → auxiliary_vector

Cahn-Hilliard solves c and mu: c comes first, so it is input_vector[0], and mu is simply not used by Fc. Allen-Cahn receives c and mu as auxiliary fields: c is auxiliary_vector[0].

Ordering convention

  • The variables of the JSON entry follow the order of the problem's VARS.
  • The auxiliary variables of the JSON entry follow the order of the problem's auxiliary VARS.

A wrong order is not detected: the wrong field is silently read. See Use of coefficients in SLOTH problems.

docs.title: Step 3 – N fields: indexed variables and sums
docs.text:
[
    {
    "expression": "Sum( -(x[i]*x[i])/2.0 + (x[i]*x[i]*x[i]*x[i])/4.0 , (i, 1, 30) )",
    "variables": "x(1..30)",
    "class_name": "Gw",
    "outputfile": "GrainsCoefficients"
    }
]

This entry defines

∑i=130(14xi4−12xi2) \sum_{i=1}^{30}\Big(\tfrac{1}{4}x_i^4-\tfrac{1}{2}x_i^2\Big) i=1∑30​(41​xi4​−21​xi2​)

  • x(1..30) declares the family x1,…,x30x_1, \dots, x_{30}x1​,…,x30​, in variables or auxiliary_variables.
  • Sum(expression, (i, 1, 30)) sums over it, with x[i] inside the expression; several index ranges give double sums.
  • The bounds of the sum must be consistent with the declaration.

In the sintering energy, the sums over the grains are written as Sum(eta[i]*eta[i], (i,1,2)): the same JSON describes NNN grains by changing the bounds. See Defining a summation.

docs.title: Step 4 – Gradient energies
docs.text:
[
    {
    "expression": "2.5*dot(x,x) + sdot(eta(1..2))",
    "variables": "x",
    "auxiliary_variables": "eta(1..2)",
    "class_name": "GradC",
    "outputfile": "SinteringCoefficients",
    "gradient": true
    }
]

With "gradient": true, each variable stands for the gradient of the field: dot(x,x) is ∇x⋅∇x\nabla x\cdot\nabla x∇x⋅∇x and sdot(eta(1..2)) is ∑i∇ηi⋅∇ηi\sum_i \nabla\eta_i\cdot\nabla\eta_i∑i​∇ηi​⋅∇ηi​ (a factor in front of sdot, numeric or constant, multiplies the whole sum). This entry defines the gradient energy of the Cahn-Hilliard problem of the sintering test,

52 ∇c⋅∇c+∑i=12∇ηi⋅∇ηi \tfrac{5}{2}\,\nabla c\cdot\nabla c + \sum_{i=1}^{2}\nabla\eta_i\cdot\nabla\eta_i 25​∇c⋅∇c+i=1∑2​∇ηi​⋅∇ηi​

used as

Coefficient ch_grad(Glossary::GradEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, GradC());

A gradient coefficient cannot depend on spatial coordinates. See Defining a scalar product.

docs.title: Step 5 – A field-dependent mobility
docs.text:
Kinetic coefficients can depend on the fields too. In the sintering test, the Cahn-Hilliard mobility combines volume, vapour, surface and grain-boundary diffusion:

D(c,η)=Dvol ϕ(c)+Dvap (1−ϕ(c))+Dsurf c(1−c)+Dgb∑i≠jηi ηj,ϕ(c)=c3 (10−15c+6c2) D(c,\eta) = D_{vol}\,\phi(c) + D_{vap}\,\big(1-\phi(c)\big) + D_{surf}\,c(1-c) + D_{gb}\sum_{i\neq j}\eta_i\,\eta_j, \qquad \phi(c)=c^3\,(10-15c+6c^2) D(c,η)=Dvol​ϕ(c)+Dvap​(1−ϕ(c))+Dsurf​c(1−c)+Dgb​i=j∑​ηi​ηj​,ϕ(c)=c3(10−15c+6c2)

[
    {
    "expression": "dvol*c*c*c*(10.0-15.0*c+6.0*c*c) + dvap*(1.0-c*c*c*(10.0-15.0*c+6.0*c*c)) + dsurf*c*(1-c) + dgb*(Sum(eta[i],(i,1,2))*Sum(eta[i],(i,1,2)) - Sum(eta[i]*eta[i],(i,1,2)))",
    "variables": "c",
    "auxiliary_variables": "eta(1..2)",
    "constants": "(dvol:0.04),(dvap:0.002),(dsurf:16.0),(dgb:1.6)",
    "class_name": "D",
    "outputfile": "SinteringCoefficients"
    }
]

Coefficient ch_mobility(Glossary::Mobility, Scheme::Explicit, D());

With Scheme::Explicit, the mobility is evaluated with the fields of the previous time step and adds no derivative to the Jacobian. Sympy still generates the derivatives, so Scheme::Implicit remains possible.

docs.title: Step 1 – One collection per variable
docs.text:
// Cahn-Hilliard (sintering test)
Coefficient ch_energy(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, Fc());
Coefficient ch_grad(Glossary::GradEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, GradC());
Coefficient ch_capillary(Glossary::Capillary, ch_lambda);
Coefficient ch_mobility(Glossary::Mobility, Scheme::Explicit, D());
Coefficients ch_coef(ch_energy, ch_capillary, ch_mobility, ch_grad);

TransientPB ch_pb("CahnHilliard", ch_oper, ch_vars, {ch_coef, ch_coef}, ch_pst, ac_vars);
  • Found by quantity: the integrator picks the FreeEnergy, Mobility, Capillary… it needs in the Coefficients collection; their order inside the collection is free.
  • One collection per variable: the problem takes a vector of Coefficients, as many as variables and in the same order. Cahn-Hilliard has two unknowns, c and mu, which both receive ch_coef.
  • Which quantities? Each integrator lists the quantities it reads on the PDEs page of the User Manual.

Names in the test

In tests/Studies/sintering/test1, the classes called Fc and Feta here are named Gc and Geta.

docs.title: Step 2 – Going further
docs.text:
Space-dependentConditionalSemi-implicitCombined 
"expression": "-pi*t*cos(pi*x)",
"coordinates": "x,y",

The coordinates key makes a coefficient depend on the position, typically for non-uniform boundary conditions attached to edges with set_bdr_index_coef (see tests/HeatTransfer/2D/test5). Coordinates are not unknowns. See coefficients depending on spatial coordinates.

"expressions": [
    {"expression": "…", "lower": 0.0, "upper": 0.75},
    {"expression": "…", "default": true}],
"range_variable": "x1",

Piecewise formulas on one range variable, with a default expression outside the ranges. See Defining a conditional coefficient.

"variables": "x(1..30)",
"explicit_variables": "xn(1..30)",

The xn variables are taken at the previous time step; the coefficient is used with Scheme::SemiImplicit. See Defining a semi-implicit coefficient.

auto P = ProductCoefficient({&A, &B});
auto S = SumCoefficient({&P, &P});

Products and sums of generated classes, built in main.cpp. See Defining a product or a sum.

docs.title: Step 3 – Six checks before running
docs.text:
Checklist

  1. Variable order: the JSON variables follow the order of the problem's VARS.
  2. Auxiliary order: the JSON auxiliary_variables follow the order of the problem's auxiliary VARS.
  3. Every symbol declared: once, as a variable, an auxiliary variable, a constant or a coordinate.
  4. Regenerate: after any change to the JSON file (CMake does it with a custom command).
  5. The right scheme: Implicit for energies, Explicit to freeze a coefficient at tnt^ntn, SemiImplicit with explicit_variables.
  6. The right quantity: the Glossary type the integrator expects.

docs.title: 5. Where to Find Information
docs.text: Where What Coefficients page of the User Manual every key of the JSON file PDEs page of the User Manual the quantities read by each integrator ExprTk and Sympy, Using an installed SLOTH installing Sympy; generating coefficients with CMake tests/Studies/sintering/test1 multiphase energy, gradient energy, mobility tests/HeatTransfer/2D/test5 coefficients depending on spatial coordinates tests/Coefficients/test2 constants SLOTH Input Files in a Nutshell the rest of the main.cpp

docs.title: Tutorial: SLOTH Input Files in a Nutshell
docs.text:
This tutorial explains how a SLOTH simulation is built, independently of any application: the philosophy of the code, the structure of an input file in four parts, then each part in detail.

It is the natural companion of the Basic features page: Basic features walks through one complete example (Allen-Cahn in 1D), while this tutorial gives the general pattern behind every SLOTH input file, including multiphase and multiphysics cases.

Slides

This tutorial is also available as a slide deck: download the PDF.

docs.title: 1. The SLOTH Philosophy
docs.text:
Four ideas are enough to understand a SLOTH input file.

The input file is a programOne equation = one operator + integratorsPhysics is specified analyticallyA multiphysics scheme built by nesting

There is no text input file: a SLOTH input file is a compiled main.cpp that assembles SLOTH objects. C++ typing catches many inconsistencies at compile time, and any function can be written. The same file runs on a workstation or on a cluster.

Neither the weak form, nor the assembly, nor the nonlinear solver are written by the user. One chooses an operator, TransientOPE for a transient simulation or SteadyOPE for a steady one, and names its integrators, which carry the variational formulation of the problem.

The energy functional and the kinetic parameters (mobilities) are SLOTH Coefficient objects, written as formulas in a JSON file and differentiated by Sympy. This is what makes multiphase simulations simple.

TimeDiscretization ⊃ { Coupling ⊃ { Problem } }: a time step solves couplings, each coupling solves problems. Adding a physics means adding a Problem.

docs.title: 2. An Input File in Four Parts
docs.text:
Every SLOTH main.cpp follows the same skeleton, whatever the problem:

  1. Headers and parallelism: includes, MPI and Hypre, namespace and aliases, footer.
  2. Spatial discretization: mesh (SPA) and boundary conditions (BCS).
  3. Multiphysics coupling: coefficients, variables, operators and integrators, post-processing, problems, coupling. This is where the physics comes in.
  4. Time marching and resolution: TimeDiscretization, then time.solve().

Parameters

Options are almost always passed through Parameters(Parameter(name, value), ...).

docs.title: 3. Part 1 – Headers and Parallelism
docs.text:
Part 1 is identical from one simulation to the next: it opens and closes the simulation.

// ── header ──
#include "Sloth/sloth.hpp"      // all of SLOTH
#include "Sloth/tests.hpp"      // test utilities
#include "MyCoefficients.hpp"   // your Sympy-generated .hpp
int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
  setVerbosity(Verbosity::Normal);   // output level
  mfem::Mpi::Init(argc, argv);       // MPI
  mfem::Hypre::Init();               // Hypre solvers
  Profiling::getInstance().enable();
  using namespace Sloth2D;           // dimension, aliases

  // … parts 2, 3 and 4 …

// ── footer ──
  Profiling::getInstance().print();  // timings
  MPI_Finalize();
  return 0;
}

using namespace Sloth2D; (or Sloth1D, Sloth3D) sets the dimension and gives access to the main aliases:

Alias Meaning SPA spatial discretization SPAS vector of SPA BCS boundary conditions VAR / VARS one variable / a set of VAR PST post-processing TransientOPE / SteadyOPE an operator type TransientPB / SteadyPB a problem type

See the Aliases page of the User Manual for the full list. When the factories of Part 2 are used, deleteSpatialDiscretization is added to the footer.

docs.title: Step 1 – The mesh: a SPA object
docs.text:
A mesh is built with one call and (at least) four arguments:

SPA spatial("InlineSquareWithQuadrangles", 1, 0, std::make_tuple(200, 200, 50., 50.));
  1. mesh type: "GMSH" to read a .msh file (ASCII v2), or an MFEM "inline" mesh: InlineLineWithSegments (1D), InlineSquareWithQuadrangles / InlineSquareWithTriangles (2D), InlineSquareWithTetraedres / InlineSquareWithHexaedres (3D);
  2. element order: 1 = linear;
  3. uniform refinements: 0 = none;
  4. dimensions: number of cells then lengths in each direction (or the file name for GMSH).

Optional arguments:

  • periodic mesh: a vector of translations;
  • AMR: enable_nc_mesh = true for a non-conforming mesh, which cannot be switched on afterwards (see the AMR tutorial);
  • GMSH file: SPA("GMSH", 1, 0, "mesh.msh").

See the Meshing page of the User Manual for all the meshing options.

docs.title: Step 2 – Boundary conditions: a BCS object
docs.text:
Boundary conditions are a BCS object built on a SPA, with exactly one Boundary per edge:

BCS bcs(&spatial, {
  Boundary("lower", 0, "Neumann"),
  Boundary("right", 1, "Dirichlet", 1.),
  Boundary("upper", 2, "Neumann"),
  Boundary("left",  3, "Dirichlet", 0.)});

A Boundary is made of a free name, an index, a type (Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin, Periodic) and, for a uniform Dirichlet condition, its value.

The right index

The name is free, but the index must match the edge attribute in the mesh. For the MFEM square: 0 bottom, 1 right, 2 top, 3 left. For a GMSH mesh, use the attributes defined in the file.

Each variable receives its BCS when it is created (see Part 3). See the Boundary Conditions page of the User Manual for all condition types.

docs.title: Step 3 – Going further: several fields on one mesh
docs.text:
In multiphase simulations, or with AMR, several fields often share one mesh. The same result can be obtained by hand or with factories:

Two fields, by handN fields, factory 
// shared, non-conforming mesh
SPA spatial_phi("InlineSquareWithQuadrangles",
                1, 0, std::make_tuple(200, 200, 50., 50.),
                true);
SPA spatial_mu(spatial_phi.get_mesh(), 1);
// one common list of edges
auto boundaries = {
  Boundary("lower", 0, "Neumann"),
  Boundary("right", 1, "Neumann"),
  Boundary("upper", 2, "Neumann"),
  Boundary("left",  3, "Neumann")};
// one BCS per variable
BCS bcs_phi(&spatial_phi, boundaries);
BCS bcs_mu(&spatial_mu, boundaries);

Each variable gets its own SPA, built on the mesh of the first one with get_mesh(). Orders may differ. This is required for AMR, since all variables must follow the same refinements.

const int N = 5;  // 5 grains
// N spaces, one mesh
SPAS spatials = setSpatialDiscretization(
    N, "InlineSquareWithQuadrangles",
    1, 0, std::make_tuple(200, 200, 50., 50.),
    true);
// same list of edges
auto bcs = setBoundaryConditions(N, spatials, boundaries);

// … variables, problems, time …

// in the footer
deleteSpatialDiscretization(spatials);

setSpatialDiscretization(N, ...) takes, after N, the arguments of the SPA constructor (setPeriodicSpatialDiscretization for a periodic mesh). setBoundaryConditions builds the N BCS from a single list of Boundary: bcs[i] goes with spatials[i]. Objects created by the factory are freed in the footer.

Non-uniform boundary values

A non-uniform boundary value is a Coefficient of type Glossary::Dirichlet, Neumann or Robin, attached to the edges with set_bdr_index_coef, and written in a JSON file like the energies (x, y as auxiliary, t for time):

Coefficient bc(Glossary::Dirichlet, …);
bc.set_bdr_index_coef({1});

See the factory sections of the Meshing and Boundary Conditions pages.

docs.title: Overview – One time step: nested boxes
docs.text:
At each time step, TimeDiscretization solves one or more Coupling, one after another. Each Coupling solves its Problem one after another (partitioned scheme). Each Problem gathers its coefficients, its primary variables, its operator with its integrators and its post-processing; it reads the fields of the other problems through its auxiliary variables, without solving them.

In the file, objects are written from the inside out, always in the same order:

Coefficients → Variables → Operator → PostProcessing → Problem → Coupling → Resolution (Part 4)

docs.title: Step 1 – Physics: Coefficient objects
docs.text:
Coefficients carry the physics, kept separate from the numerics:

// a constant
Coefficient capillary(Glossary::Capillary, lambda);
// a function provided by SLOTH
Coefficient w(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, W(omega));
// a function written in coefficients.json, generated by Sympy
Coefficient f(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, Gc());
// the collection given to the problem
Coefficients ch_coef(f, capillary, mobility, grad_energy);

A Coefficient combines:

  • a type: a quantity of the Glossary (FreeEnergy, Mobility, Capillary, GradEnergy, …);
  • a scheme: Implicit, Explicit or SemiImplicit (not needed for constants);
  • a function: a constant, a function provided by SLOTH such as the double well W(omega) or a class generated by Sympy from coefficients.json with its first and second derivatives (FunctionCoefficient from JSON), or an ExprTk expression written directly as a string.

The coefficients given to a problem are gathered in a Coefficients object.

Convention

In a function, the unknowns follow the order of the problem's Variables, then that of the auxiliary variables.

See the Coefficients page of the User Manual and the ExprTk and Sympy installation page.

docs.title: Step 2 – The unknowns: VAR and VARS
docs.text:
auto phi = VAR(&spatial, bcs, "phi", Glossary::PhaseField, 2, phi_ic);
auto mu  = VAR(&spatial, bcs, "mu", Glossary::ChemicalPotential, 2, mu_ic);
auto ch_vars = VARS(phi, mu);    // the Cahn-Hilliard unknowns

A VAR is built on:

  • a SPA and its BCS: the space and its boundary conditions (Part 2);
  • a name: the one used in the ParaView outputs;
  • a type: a Glossary quantity;
  • a storage depth (2 in the example);
  • an initial condition: a constant, a predefined AnalyticalFunctions, a user-written std::function, or an MFEM file for a restart.

The variables of a problem are gathered in a VARS. SLOTH distinguishes two kinds of variables, defined the same way:

  • primary variables, solved by the problem: φ and μ for Cahn-Hilliard;
  • auxiliary variables, solved by another problem and only read; they are passed as the problem's last argument. This is the coupling mechanism.

See the Variables page of the User Manual.

docs.title: Step 3 – One physics = one operator + integrators
docs.text:
Every PDE is written

F(U)=G(U) F(U) = G(U) F(U)=G(U)

where FFF is the form associated with the time derivative and GGG with the spatial operators (F=0F=0F=0 for a steady problem). The operator solves this system with a unified Newton-Raphson, even for linear equations; an LBFGS solver is also available. Each term is an integrator providing its contribution to the residual and the Jacobian.

TransientOPE · transientSteadyOPE · steady, F = 0 
TransientOPE(spatials, {"CahnHilliard"}, scheme, "SplitTimeDerivative")

The spaces, the list of GGG integrators, the time scheme and the FFF integrator.

SteadyOPE(spatials, {"AllenCahn"})

The spaces and the list of GGG integrators only.

Family Term Integrators Time FFF TimeDerivative, SplitTimeDerivative, HeatTimeDerivative,... Phase field GGG AllenCahn, SplitAllenCahn, CahnHilliard,... Diffusion, heat GGG Fick, MassFlux, Fourier,... Sources GGG MeltingConstant, MeltingCalphad, LatentHeat,...

Several integrators can be combined in GGG, for example AllenCahn + MeltingConstant.

Required pairings

  • CahnHilliard and SplitAllenCahn go with SplitTimeDerivative;
  • melting terms go with AllenCahn;
  • LatentHeat goes with Fourier.

Coefficients (mobility, energy) are given to the problem, not to the operator.

See the PDEs page of the User Manual for all integrators and their equations.

docs.title: Step 4 – Post-processing: a PST object
docs.text:
auto pst_params = Parameters(
  Parameter("main_folder_path", "Saves"),
  Parameter("calculation_path", "CahnHilliard"),
  Parameter("frequency", 100));
auto ch_pst = PST(&spatial, pst_params);

A PST is built on a space and a list of parameters: the root folder, the problem's sub-folder and the output frequency (iterations_list or times_list can be used instead of frequency). The variables of the associated problem(s) are written in ParaView format (VTK).

  • Optional: with no PST, there is no ParaView output for the problem.
  • Shareable: one PST for several problems gives a single ParaView file.
  • Specialized: integrals over the domain can be computed, and coefficients can be exported to the VTK.

See the Post-Processing page of the User Manual for all output parameters.

docs.title: Step 5 – Putting it together: a Problem
docs.text:
TransientPB ch_pb("CahnHilliard",   // name
    ch_oper,                        // operator + integrators
    ch_vars,                        // primary variables φ, μ
    {ch_coef, ch_coef},             // one Coefficients per variable
    ch_pst,                         // post-processing (optional)
    ac_vars);                       // auxiliary η1 … ηN (optional)

TransientPB (or SteadyPB with a SteadyOPE) takes a name, the operator, the primary variables, a vector of Coefficients, then optionally the post-processing and the auxiliary variables as last argument.

The vector of Coefficients

  • As many Coefficients as variables: the vector has the size of VARS.
  • In the same order: the i-th Coefficients goes with the i-th variable.

Optionally, a Convergence object (one PhysicalConvergence criterion per variable) stops the simulation when the steady state is reached (see the Convergence page).

See the Problems page of the User Manual.

docs.title: Step 6 – Chaining problems: a Coupling
6. Part 4 – Time Marching and Resolution
docs.text:
auto params = Parameters(
  Parameter("initial_time", 0.),
  Parameter("final_time", t_final),
  Parameter("time_step", dt));
auto time = TimeDiscretization(params, cc);
time.solve();    // runs the simulation

TimeDiscretization takes a list of parameters (initial time, final time, time step) and one or more Coupling, solved one after another at each step: TimeDiscretization(params, cc1, cc2, …). time.solve() starts the loop. Then comes the footer of Part 1.

Two useful options:

  • Variable time step (but not adaptive): a std::function<double(double)> replaces time_step;
  • Restart: initial_iteration restarts from a saved state (see the Save/Restart tutorial).

See the Time page of the User Manual for all the time-loop options.

docs.title: 7. From the Simple Case to the Multiphase Case
docs.text:
A multiphase Cahn-Hilliard + Allen-Cahn simulation keeps exactly the same skeleton as the simple case of Basic features. Parts 1, 2 and 4 only change with the dimension (Sloth2D or Sloth3D, square, cube or GMSH mesh); only Part 3 changes:

Simple case Multiphase case One problem per equation One Problem: Allen-Cahn Cahn-Hilliard (ϕ\phiϕ, μ\muμ) + Allen-Cahn (η1…ηN\eta_1 \dots \eta_Nη1​…ηN​), in one Coupling Auxiliary variables None Each problem reads the other's fields without solving them Energy W(omega), H(): provided by SLOTH f(ϕ,η1…ηN)f(\phi, \eta_1 \dots \eta_N)f(ϕ,η1​…ηN​) in the JSON file, differentiated by Sympy
