docs.title: Tutorial: Performing a Save/Restart Simulation
docs.text: This tutorial explains how to save the state of a simulation and restart it from a previously saved iteration.

docs.title: 1. Saving Variables
docs.text:
The iterations_list_save_gf parameter (type std::vector<int>) of the PostProcessing object specifies the iterations at which variables are saved as MFEM GridFunction files. By default, the files are written to a directory named GF. This location can be customized using the gf_folder_path parameter (type std::string):

std::string gf_folder_path = "Restart";
Parameter("gf_folder_path", gf_folder_path);

Each saved file follows the naming convention: 

<variable_name>_<iteration>.gf.<MPI_rank>

For example, the following file corresponds to the variable eta saved at iteration 2 on MPI rank 10: 

eta_2.gf.000010

Restart Requirements

To successfully restart a simulation, the following conditions must be satisfied:

  • The spatial discretization (mesh and finite element spaces) must be identical.
  • The number of MPI ranks must be the same.
  • Variable names must exactly match those used when the files were generated.

docs.title: 2. Reading Variables
docs.text:
Restarting a simulation requires two steps:

  1. Specify the iteration from which the simulation should restart.
  2. Initialize the variables from the corresponding saved GridFunction files.

docs.title: Step 1 – Set the Initial Iteration
docs.text:
The initial_iteration parameter (type int) must be added to the Time object:

Parameters(
    Parameter("initial_time", t_initial),
    Parameter("final_time", t_final),
    Parameter("time_step", dt),
    Parameter("initial_iteration", 2));

This indicates that the simulation resumes from iteration 2.

docs.title: Step 2 – Initialize the Variables
docs.text:
Each restarted variable must be initialized from its corresponding saved file: 

std::string file_restart = "eta_" + std::to_string(2) + ".gf";

ac_eta = VAR(
    &spatial,
    ac_bcs,
    "eta",
    Glossary::PhaseField,
    2,
    std::make_tuple(file_restart, gf_folder_path));

When initial_iteration is set to 2, SLOTH automatically loads the distributed files:

eta_2.gf.000000
eta_2.gf.000001
...
eta_2.gf.000010
...

from the directory specified by gf_folder_path. Each MPI rank reads its own GridFunction, allowing the simulation to continue exactly from the saved state.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A save/restart workflow consists of:

  1. Saving the variables at selected iterations using iterations_list_save_gf.
  2. Setting initial_iteration to the desired restart iteration.
  3. Initializing each variable from the corresponding .gf file.

Provided that the mesh, Finite Element spaces, MPI decomposition, and variable names remain unchanged, the simulation resumes seamlessly from the saved state.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
A complete working example is available in the SLOTH repository:

  • Ostwald test case: https://github.com/Collab4Sloth/SLOTH/tree/master/tests/Studies/ostwald/test1/main.cpp

docs.title: Installation guide
docs.text:
SLOTH is written in C++20. It can be built under Linux and MacOS using CMake.

Two mandatory prerequisites for building SLOTH

  • SLOTH is built on top of the MFEM Finite Element library developed in C++ by LLNL1.
  • SLOTH uses Sympy to handle physical properties.

Please ensure that both MFEM and Sympy are properly installed before building SLOTH.

MFEM

MFEM can be installed in several ways but the use of spack on Linux and Homebrewon MacOS is recommended for sake of simplicity.

Installing SLOTH therefore consists of first installing MFEM and compiling SLOTH. The basic procedure is then provided for the Linux platforms using spack, the Linux platforms from source files and the MacOs platforms, but also for supercomputers where SLOTH is intended to be used.

On Linux, SLOTH itself can also be installed with spack (see Using an installed SLOTH).

Once installed, SLOTH is used in your own projects through find_package(Sloth): see Using an installed SLOTH in your own project, which also provides a ready-to-build example.

Sympy

SLOTH provides an advanced interface based on Sympy to manage physical properties. The basic procedure also includes instructions for installing SLOTH with this dependency.

Optional dependencies for building SLOTH

  • SLOTH utilizes C++ APIs contained within the library libTorch to load PyTorch models. The basic procedure also includes instructions for installing libTorch.
  • While SLOTH primarily uses Sympy to handle physical properties, it also provides an interface based on ExprTk (see instructions for installing SLOTH with ExprTk).

  1. Robert Anderson, Julian Andrej, Andrew Barker, Jamie Bramwell, Jean-Sylvain Camier, Jakub Cerveny, Veselin Dobrev, Yohann Dudouit, Aaron Fisher, Tzanio Kolev, and others. Mfem: a modular finite element methods library. Computers & Mathematics with Applications, 81:42–74, 2021. ↩

docs.title: Installing SLOTH On Supercomputers Without Internet Access
docs.text:
This guide provides detailed steps to install SLOTH on a supercomputer without internet access using provided scripts. It includes using Spack for package management and compiling dependencies required by SLOTH.

Installing SLOTH on a supercomputer without internet access involves preparing the environment, downloading necessary components, creating a local Spack mirror, and building SLOTH with all dependencies.

docs.title: Use And Adapt Scripts
docs.text:
The installation is performed in two parts, with the scripts provided in the scripts directory of SLOTH:

  1. sloth-topaze-part1.sh: run on a local machine with internet access. It gathers Spack, its package recipes, the sources of MFEM and its dependencies, and SLOTH into an archive, and copies it to the supercomputer.
  2. sloth-topaze-part2.sh: run on the supercomputer. It installs MFEM with Spack from this archive, then builds and tests SLOTH.

Adapt the variables at the top of sloth-topaze-part1.sh (MY_LOG, DEST_DIR, SLOTH_TAG) and the modules loaded in sloth-topaze-part2.sh to your own settings.

On your local machine:

bash sloth-topaze-part1.sh

On the supercomputer (Topaze in our example), in DEST_DIR:

bash sloth-topaze-part2.sh

Same MFEM specification in both parts

Both scripts define the same MFEM_SPEC (by default mfem@4.9.0+mpi+mumps): the mirror created in part 1 only contains the sources needed by this specification. For problems with more than about 2 billion unknowns, add ^hypre+mixedint (64-bit global indices) to MFEM_SPEC in both scripts.

docs.title: Part 1: Preparing the Archive (sloth-topaze-part1.sh)
docs.text:
1. Spack and its package recipes. Spack is cloned, together with the spack-packages repository: since Spack 1.0, package recipes are no longer shipped with Spack and would otherwise be downloaded at first use, which is impossible on the supercomputer. 

    git clone https://github.com/spack/spack.git
git clone https://github.com/spack/spack-packages.git
source spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh
spack repo set --destination $WORK_DIR/spack-packages builtin

  2. SLOTH, at the tag given by SLOTH_TAG: 

    git clone --branch $SLOTH_TAG <SLOTH repository>

  3. Bootstrap mirror: binary packages of the tools Spack needs to work offline. 

    spack bootstrap mirror --binary-packages my_bootstrap

  4. Source mirror of MFEM and all its dependencies: 

    spack mirror create -d mirror-mfem -D "$MFEM_SPEC %gcc@11.2.0"

  5. Archive and copy to the supercomputer: 

    tar czvf archive.tar.gz sloth-topaze-dir/
scp archive.tar.gz $MY_LOG@topaze.ccc.cea.fr:$DEST_DIR/

docs.title: Part 2: Building on the Supercomputer (sloth-topaze-part2.sh)
docs.text:
1. Extract the archive and use the package recipes it contains: 

    tar xzvf archive.tar.gz
source $WORK_DIR/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh
spack repo set --destination $WORK_DIR/spack-packages builtin

  2. Offline bootstrap: the local bootstrap mirror is added and the online sources are disabled. 

    spack bootstrap reset -y
spack bootstrap add --scope=site --trust local-binaries $PWD/my_bootstrap/metadata/binaries/
spack bootstrap disable --scope=site github-actions-v0.5
spack bootstrap disable --scope=site github-actions-v0.4
spack bootstrap disable --scope=site spack-install
spack bootstrap now
    The names of the bootstrap sources depend on the Spack version: check them with spack bootstrap list and adapt the disable commands if needed.

  3. Modules, compilers and external packages, then MFEM from the local mirror: 

    module load gnu/11.2.0 mpi cmake/3.29.6
spack mirror add SLOTH $WORK_DIR/mirror-mfem/
spack compiler find
spack external find openmpi cmake openssh gmake
spack install $MFEM_SPEC

  4. SLOTH, built with envSloth.sh (which finds MFEM and HYPRE with spack location -i), then tested: 

    cd $WORK_DIR/sloth
mkdir -p build && cd build
bash ../envSloth.sh --portable --np=10
make -j 10 tests
ctest
    --portable avoids -march=native: the login node may not have the same CPU as the compute nodes.

Running tests on a supercomputer

Tests use mpiexec. Running them on a login node may be forbidden or limited by the compute centre: run ctest from an interactive allocation on compute nodes, with the same modules loaded.

docs.title: Run Your Simulation On Topaze
docs.text:
Script example of a simulation running on milan partition over 8192 mpi processes with a duration limit of about 24 hours:

#!/bin/bash
#MSUB -r sloth_big_run
#MSUB -n 8192
#MSUB -c 1
#MSUB -T 86000
#MSUB -m scratch
#MSUB -o sloth_big_run_%I.o
#MSUB -e sloth_big_run_%I.e
#MSUB -q milan

set -x
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
ccc_mprun ./test3D

docs.title: Cluster from source files
docs.text:
The following installation procedure describes how to install SLOTH from source files on a supercomputer. Here, the description is based on an installation done on CCRT Topaze.

This procedure is mainly based on the installation procedure from source files on local computer.

Why clone locally?

Compute centres usually have no outbound internet access. Source files are therefore cloned on a local computer and copied to the supercomputer.

docs.title: Getting source files on local computer
docs.text:
The first step consists in cloning MFEM, METIS, HYPRE and, optionally, Voro++.

Clone of the default branch

  • The current installation procedure assumes that the clone of the source files is based on the default branch of each repository.
  • Users are free to consider different branches for their installation.

All sources are collected in a global directory called MFEM4SLOTH.

cd $HOME
mkdir MFEM4SLOTH
cd MFEM4SLOTH

docs.title: MFEM
docs.text:
MFEM's source files are obtained by running the following command:

git clone https://github.com/mfem/mfem.git

docs.title: HYPRE
docs.text:
HYPRE's source files are obtained by running the following command:

git clone https://github.com/hypre-space/hypre.git

docs.title: METIS
docs.text:
METIS's source files are obtained by running the following commands:

git clone https://github.com/mfem/tpls.git
mv tpls/metis-4.0.3.tar.gz .
tar -zxvf metis-4.0.3.tar.gz
rm -fr metis-4.0.3.tar.gz tpls

docs.title: Voro++ (optional)
docs.text:
Voro++ is only required if SLOTH is built with the --voro option. Its source files are obtained by running the following command:

git clone https://github.com/chr1shr/voro.git

docs.title: Copy of source files on the supercomputer
docs.text:
Copy the MFEM4SLOTH folder on the supercomputer by running the following command:

rsync --info=progress2 -e ssh -avz MFEM4SLOTH <login>@<remote_host>:$DEST_DIR

docs.title: Building dependencies on the supercomputer
docs.text:
The second step consists in building METIS, HYPRE and, optionally, Voro++ on the supercomputer. From now on, all commands are run on the supercomputer.

In the following, MFEM4SLOTH denotes the absolute path of the copied folder:

export MFEM4SLOTH=$DEST_DIR/MFEM4SLOTH   # absolute path, no trailing slash

docs.title: Load required modules
docs.text:
Before building dependencies, it is necessary to load some modules. Please keep in mind that versions depend on the targeted environment.

gnu, mpi, cmake are required to build MFEM with METIS and HYPRE. python3 is required to build SLOTH (Sympy is used to generate the physical properties).

module load gnu/11.1.0
module load mpi/openmpi/4.1.4
module load cmake/3.29.6
module load python3/3.12

Same environment everywhere

The same modules must be loaded when building the dependencies, MFEM and SLOTH, and when running SLOTH (tests included). Mixing compilers or MPI implementations leads to link or ABI errors.

Environment file

To avoid reloading the environment at each session, create a file ~/sloth_env.sh: 

module load gnu/11.1.0 mpi/openmpi/4.1.4 cmake/3.29.6 python3/3.12
export MFEM4SLOTH=/path/to/MFEM4SLOTH
and run source ~/sloth_env.sh before any build or run.

Find available modules

The list of available modules can be obtained using the following command: 

module avail [optional_string]
where an optional string can be specified to refine the search for modules. This string can be a partial name.

docs.title: METIS
docs.text:
To build METIS, the following commands must be run:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/metis-4.0.3
make OPTFLAGS=-Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration
mkdir include
cp Lib/*.h include/
cd ..
ln -s metis-4.0.3 metis-4.0

The fourth instruction differs from the installation procedure from source files on local computer.

docs.title: HYPRE
docs.text:
To build HYPRE, the following commands must be run:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/hypre/src
./configure --disable-fortran
make -j N
cd ../..
where N is a user defined number of CPUs.

docs.title: Voro++ (optional)
docs.text:
To build Voro++, the following commands must be run:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/voro
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALL
cmake --build build -j N
cmake --install build
cd ..
where N is a user defined number of CPUs.

Using Voro++ in SLOTH

Voro++ is not handled by the --mfem option. Its installation prefix must be given explicitly when building SLOTH: 

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS] --mfem=$MFEM4SLOTH --voro=$MFEM4SLOTH/voro/INSTALL

docs.title: Building MFEM with dependencies
docs.text:
Here, we assume that all dependencies are well built according to the previous directives. At this stage, MFEM can be installed by running the following commands:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/mfem
make -j N parallel
make install PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALLDIR
cd ..

Checking the MFEM configuration

make parallel configures MFEM with MFEM_USE_MPI=YES and builds the library. The resulting configuration can be checked with: 

grep -E "^MFEM_CXX|^MFEM_USE_MPI" config/config.mk
MFEM_CXX must be mpicxx and MFEM_USE_MPI must be YES. If a previous build exists, run make clean before make parallel.

Always reinstall after rebuilding MFEM

SLOTH reads the installed configuration (INSTALLDIR/share/mfem/config.mk), not config/config.mk. After any rebuild of MFEM, run make install PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALLDIR again, otherwise SLOTH keeps using the previous flags.

Installation directory

envSloth.sh --mfem=DIR expects MFEM to be installed in DIR/mfem/INSTALLDIR (with DIR/hypre and DIR/metis-4.0 next to it). The PREFIX above follows this convention.

docs.title: SLOTH compilation
docs.text:
Once MFEM is installed, SLOTH can be built using the envSloth.sh shell script. This script loads MFEM, defines several environment variables, and compiles SLOTH.

Build SLOTH using the envSloth.sh shell script

The envSloth.sh shell script cannot be run directly from the root of the SLOTH repository. Users must create a separate build directory to compile SLOTH.

Installing Sympy

Please ensure that Sympy is installed for the python3 loaded above. Sympy is a mandatory prerequisite to build SLOTH as it is used to handle physical properties.

Once MFEM and Sympy are installed, please run the following commands to build SLOTH:

mkdir build
cd build

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS]  --mfem=$MFEM4SLOTH --voro=$MFEM4SLOTH/voro/INSTALL
where $MFEM4SLOTH is the absolute path of the folder containing mfem/, hypre/ and metis-4.0/ (not the MFEM installation directory itself). The --voro option is only needed if Voro++ has been built (see above). [OPTIONS] are: 
Build type (default: --release):
  --release          Release, with -march=native
  --portable         Release without -march=native (generic x86-64 target on x86)
  --debug | --coverage | --optim | --minsizerel | --relwithdebinfo

Dependencies:
  --mfem=DIR         local MFEM build (instead of spack on Linux / Homebrew on macOS)
  --exprtk=DIR       ExprTk (directory containing exprtk.hpp)
  --voro=DIR         Voro++ installation prefix
  --libtorch=DIR     LibTorch installation prefix
  --external=EXT_LIBDIR,EXT_LIBNAME
                     link Sloth with an external library

Other options:
  --shared           build Sloth as a shared library
  --install=DIR      installation directory (default: ../SlothInstall)
  --np=N             number of parallel compilation jobs (default: 4)
  -h | --help        print this help

Everything after "--" is passed unchanged to CMake, e.g.:
  bash ../envSloth.sh --exprtk=../../exprtk -- -DMATOOLS_VERBOSITY_LEVEL_1=ON
The up-to-date list is printed by bash ../envSloth.sh --help.

By default, this command builds a static library of SLOTH with release compiler options.

--release vs --portable

--release uses -march=native: the binary is optimised for the CPU of the node where it is compiled. If login and compute nodes have different CPUs, prefer --portable or compile on a compute node.

Building a shared library of SLOTH

The --shared option enables building a shared library of SLOTH. However, the user must ensure that the library type used for MFEM is compatible. Certain combinations of static and shared libraries may require specific compiler options, such as -fPIC.

The make command within the envSloth.sh script does not compile the tests. To compile tests after SLOTH has been built, run the following command:

make tests -j N

where N is a number of CPUs to use for building the tests in parallel.

Once the tests are compiled, users can verify the build by running all tests with ctest:

ctest -j N

Running tests on a supercomputer

Tests use mpiexec. Running them on a login node may be forbidden or limited by the compute centre. Run ctest from an interactive allocation on compute nodes (see the CCRT documentation for ccc_mprun), with the same modules loaded.

docs.title: SLOTH installation
docs.text:
Users can install the SLOTH library, headers, and scripts into the SlothInstall directory by running:

make install

Installing SLOTH in user-defined repository

By default, SLOTH is installed in a SlothInstall directory at the same level as the repository.

Users can specify another directory with the --install option of the envSloth.sh script.

Reinstalling after a dependency change

The installed CMake files (SlothInstall/lib/cmake/Sloth/SlothTargets.cmake) keep the link flags of MFEM at the time SLOTH was built. If MFEM is rebuilt, SLOTH must be rebuilt and reinstalled from an empty build directory, and the build directories of the installed examples must be removed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Compilation with g++ instead of mpicxx MPI not enabled in MFEM make clean, then make parallel (not make alone) MFEM configuration file (share/mfem/config.mk) not found MFEM not installed, or --mfem points to the wrong folder make install PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALLDIR in mfem/; --mfem must point to MFEM4SLOTH mpiexec was unable to launch ... allen_cahn Executable not built (previous link error) Fix the link error, rebuild the example from an empty build

docs.title: Sympy and ExprTk
docs.text:
SLOTH provides interfaces with the C++ Mathematical Expression Toolkit Library ExprTk and the Python library for symbolic mathematics Sympy to handle physical properties with Coefficient.

Installing Sympy

Sympy is a mandatory prerequisite to build SLOTH. Please ensure that Sympy is well installed.

This page presents the instructions for installing these dependencies.

docs.title: ExprTk
docs.text: The following installation procedure describes how to install and link the library ExprTk to SLOTH applications.

docs.title: Getting ExprTk
docs.text:
The C++ Mathematical Expression Toolkit Library ExprTk is contained in the C++ file name exprtk.hpp which can be downloaded either from the ExprTk website or with spack by running the following instructions in a terminal:

spack install exprtk

Other approaches exist as, for example, the use of conda.

docs.title: Linking SLOTH and ExprTk
docs.text:
To link SLOTH with ExprTk, the user must run the envSloth.sh script file with the --exprtk option:

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS] --exprtk=$EXPRTK_PATH

where EXPRTK_PATH is an environment variable setting the path toward the exprtk folder containing the file exprtk.hpp and [OPTIONS] are: 

Build type (default: --release):
  --release          Release, with -march=native
  --portable         Release without -march=native (generic x86-64 target on x86)
  --debug | --coverage | --optim | --minsizerel | --relwithdebinfo

Dependencies:
  --mfem=DIR         local MFEM build (instead of spack on Linux / Homebrew on macOS)
  --exprtk=DIR       ExprTk (directory containing exprtk.hpp)
  --voro=DIR         Voro++ installation prefix
  --libtorch=DIR     LibTorch installation prefix
  --external=EXT_LIBDIR,EXT_LIBNAME
                     link Sloth with an external library

Other options:
  --shared           build Sloth as a shared library
  --install=DIR      installation directory (default: ../SlothInstall)
  --np=N             number of parallel compilation jobs (default: 4)
  -h | --help        print this help

Everything after "--" is passed unchanged to CMake, e.g.:
  bash ../envSloth.sh --exprtk=../../exprtk -- -DMATOOLS_VERBOSITY_LEVEL_1=ON
The up-to-date list is printed by bash ../envSloth.sh --help.

With spack, this environment variable can be defined as:

export EXPRTK_PATH=$(spack location -i exprtk)/include/exprtk

docs.title: Sympy
docs.text:
The Python script GenerateCoefficient.py (see the script folder in the SLOTH repository) used to build coefficients from a mathematical expression is built on top of Sympy.

To install Sympy and use the Python script GenerateCoefficient.py, the following instruction can be run in a terminal:

pip install Sympy

Users are free to use other installation procedures as described in the Sympy website.

docs.title: PyTorch C++ API
docs.text: The following installation procedure describes how to install and link the library libTorch that contains C++ APIs used to load PyTorch models in some SLOTH applications. The procedure focuses on the CPU-only libTorch

docs.title: Getting libTorch
docs.text:
The library libTorch can be downloaded either from the PyTorch website or by running the following instructions in a terminal:

wget https://download.pytorch.org/libtorch/nightly/cpu/libtorch-shared-with-deps-latest.zip

unzip libtorch-shared-with-deps-latest.zip

This will result in an uncompressed folder named libtorch that can be linked to SLOTH during the configuration of the project.

docs.title: Linking SLOTH and libTorch
docs.text:
To link SLOTH with libTorch, the user must run the envSloth.sh script file with the --libtorch option:

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS] --libtorch=$LIBTORCH_PATH

where LIBTORCH_PATH is an environment variable containing the path toward the libtorch folder previously uncompressed and [OPTIONS] are: 

Build type (default: --release):
  --release          Release, with -march=native
  --portable         Release without -march=native (generic x86-64 target on x86)
  --debug | --coverage | --optim | --minsizerel | --relwithdebinfo

Dependencies:
  --mfem=DIR         local MFEM build (instead of spack on Linux / Homebrew on macOS)
  --exprtk=DIR       ExprTk (directory containing exprtk.hpp)
  --voro=DIR         Voro++ installation prefix
  --libtorch=DIR     LibTorch installation prefix
  --external=EXT_LIBDIR,EXT_LIBNAME
                     link Sloth with an external library

Other options:
  --shared           build Sloth as a shared library
  --install=DIR      installation directory (default: ../SlothInstall)
  --np=N             number of parallel compilation jobs (default: 4)
  -h | --help        print this help

Everything after "--" is passed unchanged to CMake, e.g.:
  bash ../envSloth.sh --exprtk=../../exprtk -- -DMATOOLS_VERBOSITY_LEVEL_1=ON
The up-to-date list is printed by bash ../envSloth.sh --help.

docs.title: On Linux with Spack
docs.text:
A straightforward way to install MFEM is to use spack.

Installing spack

To install spack on Linux, the first step consists in cloning and loading it into a $SPACK directory (see spack for more details).

Assuming spack is well installed into the $SPACK directory, the following command installs a parallel MFEM, which is all SLOTH requires:

source $SPACK/share/spack/setup-env.sh

spack install mfem+mpi

Optional MFEM features

  • +mumps enables the MUMPS direct solver in SLOTH: spack install mfem+mpi+mumps.
  • For problems with more than about 2 billion unknowns, use 64-bit global indices in HYPRE: spack install mfem+mpi ^hypre+mixedint.

Other MFEM options are accepted (SLOTH reads MFEM's configuration) but are not needed.

Installing a given version of MFEM

The user is free to install a different version of MFEM. By default, the latest release is installed. Otherwise, @<version> must be added to the spec, e.g.: 

spack install mfem@4.9+mpi

Once MFEM is installed, SLOTH can be built using the envSloth.sh shell script. This script loads MFEM, defines several environment variables, and compiles SLOTH.

Build SLOTH using the envSloth.sh shell script

The envSloth.sh shell script cannot be run directly from the root of the SLOTH repository. Users must create a separate build directory to compile SLOTH.

Installing Sympy

Please ensure that Sympy is installed. Sympy is a mandatory prerequisite to build SLOTH as it is used to handle physical properties.

If the system Python cannot be modified, Sympy can also be installed with Spack: 

spack install py-sympy
spack load py-sympy

Once MFEM and Sympy are installed, please run the following commands to build SLOTH:

mkdir build
cd build

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS]
where [OPTIONS] are: 
Build type (default: --release):
  --release          Release, with -march=native
  --portable         Release without -march=native (generic x86-64 target on x86)
  --debug | --coverage | --optim | --minsizerel | --relwithdebinfo

Dependencies:
  --mfem=DIR         local MFEM build (instead of spack on Linux / Homebrew on macOS)
  --exprtk=DIR       ExprTk (directory containing exprtk.hpp)
  --voro=DIR         Voro++ installation prefix
  --libtorch=DIR     LibTorch installation prefix
  --external=EXT_LIBDIR,EXT_LIBNAME
                     link Sloth with an external library

Other options:
  --shared           build Sloth as a shared library
  --install=DIR      installation directory (default: ../SlothInstall)
  --np=N             number of parallel compilation jobs (default: 4)
  -h | --help        print this help

Everything after "--" is passed unchanged to CMake, e.g.:
  bash ../envSloth.sh --exprtk=../../exprtk -- -DMATOOLS_VERBOSITY_LEVEL_1=ON
The up-to-date list is printed by bash ../envSloth.sh --help.

By default, this command builds a static library of SLOTH with release compiler options.

Building a shared library of SLOTH

The --shared option enables building a shared library of SLOTH. However, the user must ensure that the library type used for MFEM is compatible. Certain combinations of static and shared libraries may require specific compiler options, such as -fPIC.

spack builds a static library of MFEM unless the user enables shared ones (see +shared in the spack command): 

spack install mfem+shared+mpi

The make command within the envSloth.sh script does not compile the tests. To compile tests after SLOTH has been built, run the following command:

make tests -j N

where N is a number of CPUs to use for building the tests in parallel.

Once the tests are compiled, users can verify the build by running all tests with ctest:

ctest -j N

Finally, users can install the SLOTH library, headers, and scripts into the SlothInstall directory by running:

make install

Installing SLOTH in user-defined repository

By default, SLOTH is installed in a SlothInstall directory at the same level as the repository.

Users can specify another directory with the --install option of the envSloth.sh script.

Reinstalling after a dependency change

The installed CMake files (SlothInstall/lib/cmake/Sloth/SlothTargets.cmake) keep the link flags of MFEM at the time SLOTH was built. If MFEM is reinstalled or updated with Spack, SLOTH must be rebuilt and reinstalled from an empty build directory.

Using the installed SLOTH

To build your own programs with the installed SLOTH (find_package(Sloth)) and try the example provided with the installation, see Using an installed SLOTH in your own project.

docs.title: Alternative: installing SLOTH itself with Spack
docs.text:
SLOTH provides its own Spack package. Spack then installs MFEM and all the dependencies, and SLOTH:

source $SPACK/share/spack/setup-env.sh
spack repo add /path/to/SLOTH/spack_repo
spack install sloth
spack load sloth

See spack info sloth for the versions and variants, and Using an installed SLOTH in your own project to build programs with it.

docs.title: On MacOS with Homebrew
docs.text:
Following the MFEM website, the simplest way to install MFEM on MacOS consists in using the package manager Homebrew (see https://brew.sh for more details):

brew install mfem

By default, this MFEM installation depends on hypre, metis, openblas and suite-sparse. SLOTH only requires a parallel MFEM (MPI, HYPRE, METIS): the Homebrew formula can be used as is.

Adding dependencies to MFEM (optional)

This is not needed by SLOTH, only for your own extensions. It is possible to rebuild MFEM with additional dependencies (see https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/mfem for more details). Here, let us consider the petsc dependency. Two changes are needed in the formula file mfem.rb:

  • Get the formula: run brew edit mfem to open the default mfem.rb file, or get it from GitHub.
  • Add the dependency with the depends_on directive: 
    depends_on "cmake" => :build
depends_on "hypre"
depends_on "metis"
depends_on "openblas"
depends_on "suite-sparse"
depends_on "petsc"
  • Enable it in the MFEM configuration, by adding the corresponding option to the CMake arguments of the install block of the formula: 
    -DMFEM_USE_PETSC=YES
    depends_on only installs the package: without the CMake option, MFEM is built without PETSc.
  • Save the file and run: 
    brew install --build-from-source --formula ./mfem.rb

The installation with PETSc can be checked in the installed MFEM configuration: 

grep MFEM_USE_PETSC $(brew --prefix mfem)/share/mfem/config.mk
which must return YES. Each dependency can be installed easily using Homebrew.

Local formula files

Recent versions of Homebrew may refuse to install a formula from a local file. In that case, create a local tap and install the formula from it: 

brew tap-new $USER/local
cp mfem.rb $(brew --repository)/Library/Taps/$USER/homebrew-local/Formula/
brew install --build-from-source $USER/local/mfem

Once MFEM is installed, SLOTH can be built using the envSloth.sh shell script. This script loads MFEM, defines several environment variables, and compiles SLOTH.

Build SLOTH using the envSloth.sh shell script

The envSloth.sh shell script cannot be run directly from the root of the SLOTH repository. Users must create a separate build directory to compile SLOTH.

Installing Sympy

Please ensure that Sympy is installed. Sympy is a mandatory prerequisite to build SLOTH as it is used to handle physical properties.

The Python provided by Homebrew may refuse a global pip install. In that case, install Sympy in a dedicated environment and activate it before building SLOTH, either with a virtual environment: 

python3 -m venv $HOME/sloth-venv
source $HOME/sloth-venv/bin/activate
pip install sympy
or with a conda-like package manager (conda, mamba, micromamba...). For example, with micromamba: 
brew install micromamba
micromamba create -n sloth -c conda-forge python sympy
micromamba activate sloth
The environment must be activated in the shell where envSloth.sh is run.

Once MFEM and Sympy are installed, please run the following commands to build SLOTH:

mkdir build
cd build

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS]
where [OPTIONS] are: 
Build type (default: --release):
  --release          Release, with -march=native
  --portable         Release without -march=native (generic x86-64 target on x86)
  --debug | --coverage | --optim | --minsizerel | --relwithdebinfo

Dependencies:
  --mfem=DIR         local MFEM build (instead of spack on Linux / Homebrew on macOS)
  --exprtk=DIR       ExprTk (directory containing exprtk.hpp)
  --voro=DIR         Voro++ installation prefix
  --libtorch=DIR     LibTorch installation prefix
  --external=EXT_LIBDIR,EXT_LIBNAME
                     link Sloth with an external library

Other options:
  --shared           build Sloth as a shared library
  --install=DIR      installation directory (default: ../SlothInstall)
  --np=N             number of parallel compilation jobs (default: 4)
  -h | --help        print this help

Everything after "--" is passed unchanged to CMake, e.g.:
  bash ../envSloth.sh --exprtk=../../exprtk -- -DMATOOLS_VERBOSITY_LEVEL_1=ON
The up-to-date list is printed by bash ../envSloth.sh --help.

By default, this command builds a static library of SLOTH with release compiler options.

Building a shared library of SLOTH

The --shared option enables building a shared library of SLOTH. However, the user must ensure that the library type used for MFEM is compatible. Certain combinations of static and shared libraries may require specific compiler options, such as -fPIC.

The make command within the envSloth.sh script does not compile the tests. To compile tests after SLOTH has been built, run the following command:

make tests -j N

where N is a number of CPUs to use for building the tests in parallel.

Once the tests are compiled, users can verify the build by running all tests with ctest:

ctest -j N

Finally, users can install the SLOTH library, headers, and scripts into the SlothInstall directory by running:

make install

Installing SLOTH in user-defined repository

By default, SLOTH is installed in a SlothInstall directory at the same level as the repository.

Users can specify another directory with the --install option of the envSloth.sh script.

Reinstalling after a dependency change

The installed CMake files (SlothInstall/lib/cmake/Sloth/SlothTargets.cmake) keep the link flags of MFEM at the time SLOTH was built. Homebrew may upgrade MFEM or its dependencies automatically (brew upgrade): in that case, SLOTH must be rebuilt and reinstalled from an empty build directory. To prevent automatic upgrades of MFEM, run brew pin mfem.

Using the installed SLOTH

To build your own programs with the installed SLOTH (find_package(Sloth)) and try the example provided with the installation, see Using an installed SLOTH in your own project.

docs.title: On Linux from source files
docs.text:
The following installation procedure describes how to install SLOTH from source files.

It is assumed that the user has a Unix environment with a recent GCC compiler (C++20 compatible), MPI libraries, CMake and Python 3. Obviously, Git is also needed to clone source files.

The following procedure is mainly based on the installation procedure of a parallel MPI version of MFEM. Only the installation of Voro++ (optional) is added.

System packages

On Ubuntu, most prerequisites can be installed with: 

sudo apt-get install build-essential cmake git libopenmpi-dev openmpi-bin \
    python3 python3-sympy
Package names may differ on other distributions.

Installing on a supercomputer

For an installation on a supercomputer (modules, no internet access...), see the dedicated procedure on a cluster from source files.

docs.title: Getting source files
docs.text:
The first step consists in cloning MFEM, METIS, HYPRE and, optionally, Voro++.

Clone of the default branch

  • The current installation procedure assumes that the clone of the source files is based on the default branch of each repository.
  • Users are free to consider different branches for their installation.

All sources are collected in a global directory called MFEM4SLOTH:

export MFEM4SLOTH=$HOME/MFEM4SLOTH   # absolute path, no trailing slash
mkdir -p $MFEM4SLOTH
cd $MFEM4SLOTH

docs.title: MFEM
docs.text:
MFEM's source files are obtained by running the following command:

git clone https://github.com/mfem/mfem.git

docs.title: HYPRE
docs.text:
HYPRE's source files are obtained by running the following command:

git clone https://github.com/hypre-space/hypre.git

docs.title: METIS
docs.text:
METIS's source files are obtained by running the following commands:

git clone https://github.com/mfem/tpls.git
mv tpls/metis-4.0.3.tar.gz .
tar -zxvf metis-4.0.3.tar.gz
rm -fr metis-4.0.3.tar.gz tpls

docs.title: Voro++ (optional)
docs.text:
Voro++ is only required if SLOTH is built with the --voro option. Its source files are obtained by running the following command:

git clone https://github.com/chr1shr/voro.git

docs.title: Building dependencies
docs.text: The second step consists in building METIS, HYPRE and, optionally, Voro++.

docs.title: METIS
docs.text:
To build METIS, the following commands must be run:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/metis-4.0.3
make OPTFLAGS=-Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration
cd ..
ln -s metis-4.0.3 metis-4.0

docs.title: HYPRE
docs.text:
To build HYPRE, the following commands must be run:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/hypre/src
./configure --disable-fortran
make -j N
cd ../..
where N is a user defined number of CPUs.

docs.title: Voro++ (optional)
docs.text:
To build Voro++, the following commands must be run:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/voro
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALL
cmake --build build -j N
cmake --install build
cd ..
where N is a user defined number of CPUs.

Using Voro++ in SLOTH

Voro++ is not handled by the --mfem option. Its installation prefix must be given explicitly when building SLOTH: 

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS] --mfem=$MFEM4SLOTH --voro=$MFEM4SLOTH/voro/INSTALL

docs.title: Building MFEM with dependencies
docs.text:
Here, we assume that all dependencies are well built according to the previous directives. At this stage, MFEM can be installed by running the following commands:

cd $MFEM4SLOTH/mfem
make -j N parallel
make install PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALLDIR
cd ..

Checking the MFEM configuration

make parallel configures MFEM with MFEM_USE_MPI=YES and builds the library. The resulting configuration can be checked with: 

grep -E "^MFEM_CXX|^MFEM_USE_MPI" config/config.mk
MFEM_CXX must be mpicxx and MFEM_USE_MPI must be YES. If a previous build exists, run make clean before make parallel.

Always reinstall after rebuilding MFEM

SLOTH reads the installed configuration (INSTALLDIR/share/mfem/config.mk), not config/config.mk. After any rebuild of MFEM, run make install PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALLDIR again, otherwise SLOTH keeps using the previous flags.

Installation directory

envSloth.sh --mfem=DIR expects MFEM to be installed in DIR/mfem/INSTALLDIR (with DIR/hypre and DIR/metis-4.0 next to it). The PREFIX above follows this convention.

docs.title: SLOTH compilation
docs.text:
Once MFEM is installed, SLOTH can be built using the envSloth.sh shell script. This script loads MFEM, defines several environment variables, and compiles SLOTH.

Build SLOTH using the envSloth.sh shell script

The envSloth.sh shell script cannot be run directly from the root of the SLOTH repository. Users must create a separate build directory to compile SLOTH.

Installing Sympy

Please ensure that Sympy is installed. Sympy is a mandatory prerequisite to build SLOTH as it is used to handle physical properties.

Once MFEM and Sympy are installed, please run the following commands to build SLOTH:

mkdir build
cd build

bash ../envSloth.sh [OPTIONS]  --mfem=$MFEM4SLOTH
where $MFEM4SLOTH is the absolute path of the folder containing mfem/, hypre/ and metis-4.0/ (ie $HOME/MFEM4SLOTH in the current description, not the MFEM installation directory itself). If Voro++ has been built, add --voro=$MFEM4SLOTH/voro/INSTALL. [OPTIONS] are: 
Build type (default: --release):
  --release          Release, with -march=native
  --portable         Release without -march=native (generic x86-64 target on x86)
  --debug | --coverage | --optim | --minsizerel | --relwithdebinfo

Dependencies:
  --mfem=DIR         local MFEM build (instead of spack on Linux / Homebrew on macOS)
  --exprtk=DIR       ExprTk (directory containing exprtk.hpp)
  --voro=DIR         Voro++ installation prefix
  --libtorch=DIR     LibTorch installation prefix
  --external=EXT_LIBDIR,EXT_LIBNAME
                     link Sloth with an external library

Other options:
  --shared           build Sloth as a shared library
  --install=DIR      installation directory (default: ../SlothInstall)
  --np=N             number of parallel compilation jobs (default: 4)
  -h | --help        print this help

Everything after "--" is passed unchanged to CMake, e.g.:
  bash ../envSloth.sh --exprtk=../../exprtk -- -DMATOOLS_VERBOSITY_LEVEL_1=ON
The up-to-date list is printed by bash ../envSloth.sh --help.

By default, this command builds a static library of SLOTH with release compiler options.

Building a shared library of SLOTH

The --shared option enables building a shared library of SLOTH. However, the user must ensure that the library type used for MFEM is compatible. Certain combinations of static and shared libraries may require specific compiler options, such as -fPIC.

The make command within the envSloth.sh script does not compile the tests. To compile tests after SLOTH has been built, run the following command:

make tests -j N

where N is a number of CPUs to use for building the tests in parallel.

Once the tests are compiled, users can verify the build by running all tests with ctest:

ctest -j N

docs.title: SLOTH installation
docs.text:
Users can install the SLOTH library, headers, and scripts into the SlothInstall directory by running:

make install

Installing SLOTH in user-defined repository

By default, SLOTH is installed in a SlothInstall directory at the same level as the repository.

Users can specify another directory with the --install option of the envSloth.sh script.

Reinstalling after a dependency change

The installed CMake files (SlothInstall/lib/cmake/Sloth/SlothTargets.cmake) keep the link flags of MFEM at the time SLOTH was built. If MFEM is rebuilt, SLOTH must be rebuilt and reinstalled from an empty build directory.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Compilation with g++ instead of mpicxx MPI not enabled in MFEM make clean, then make parallel (not make alone) MFEM configuration file (share/mfem/config.mk) not found MFEM not installed, or --mfem points to the wrong folder make install PREFIX=$PWD/INSTALLDIR in mfem/; --mfem must point to MFEM4SLOTH

docs.title: Using an installed SLOTH in your own project
docs.text:
Once SLOTH is installed, a program using SLOTH can be built outside the SLOTH sources, with a short CMakeLists.txt based on find_package(Sloth). The procedure is the same whichever way SLOTH was installed:

SLOTH installed with Make it visible to CMake envSloth.sh + make install (Linux, macOS) export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/path/to/SlothInstall Spack (Linux) spack load sloth

docs.title: Installing SLOTH
docs.text:
envSloth.sh + make installSpack (Linux)

Follow the Linux or macOS guide, then install:

mkdir build && cd build
bash ../envSloth.sh                 # --install=DIR to choose the installation directory
make install                        # default directory: ../SlothInstall
export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$PWD/../../SlothInstall

SLOTH is available in Spack's builtin repository (Spack 1.0 or later):

spack install sloth
spack load sloth

If spack info sloth finds no package (Spack older than 1.0, or SLOTH not yet in your copy of the builtin repository), use the package shipped with the sources (see below).

spack info sloth lists the versions and variants (+shared, +mumps, +voro, +bigint, +native). For instance, to enable Voro++ (Voronoi tessellations):

spack install sloth +voro

To build the development version from a local clone instead, use the package shipped with the sources (directory spack_repo):

spack repo add /path/to/SLOTH/spack_repo
spack install sloth@master
spack load sloth

The installation contains the static (or shared) library, the headers, the CMake package files (lib/cmake/Sloth), the coefficient generator (scripts/GenerateCoefficient.py) and a ready-to-build example (share/sloth/examples/minimal).

Python and SymPy

The coefficient generator needs Python 3 with SymPy. With Spack, spack load sloth provides both; otherwise install SymPy (pip install sympy) or activate an environment (venv, conda) that provides it.

docs.title: The minimal example
docs.text:
The example is organised as for a practical session: one sub-directory per case.

minimal/
├── CMakeLists.txt        find_package(Sloth), MPI, Python + SymPy, add_subdirectory(...)
└── allen_cahn/
    ├── CMakeLists.txt    executable, coefficient generation, tests
    ├── coefficients.json double-well potential phi^2 (1 - phi)^2
    ├── main.cpp          1D Allen-Cahn interface at equilibrium (tanh profile)
    └── verify.py         check against the analytical solution

Copy it, build it and run its tests:

cp -r $CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH/share/sloth/examples/minimal .           # envSloth.sh installation
cp -r $(spack location -i sloth)/share/sloth/examples/minimal .   # Spack installation

cd minimal
cmake -B build
cmake --build build
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure

Two tests are run: allen_cahn_run (the simulation) and allen_cahn_verify (the interface must stay at equilibrium: tanh profile kept and interfacial energy equal to the input σ\sigmaσ).

docs.title: Writing your own CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
The top-level CMakeLists.txt only needs:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.13)
project(my_project LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(Sloth REQUIRED)

add_executable(main main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(main PRIVATE Sloth::Sloth)

Sloth::Sloth brings everything needed to compile and link: C++20, SLOTH and MFEM headers, MFEM and its dependencies (HYPRE, METIS, MPI, ...). In main.cpp, include Sloth/sloth.hpp and Sloth/tests.hpp (the latter defines the Sloth1D, Sloth2D and Sloth3D namespaces).

find_package(Sloth) also defines:

Variable Content Sloth_COEFFICIENT_SCRIPT coefficient generator GenerateCoefficient.py (Python + SymPy) Sloth_COMPARE_SCRIPT col_compare.py, comparison of CSV result files (Python standard library only) Sloth_USE_SHARED, Sloth_USE_VORO, Sloth_USE_LIBTORCH, ... options SLOTH was built with

docs.title: Coefficients generated from a JSON file
docs.text:
A coefficient described in a JSON file is turned into a C++ class at build time, and regenerated whenever the JSON file changes:

add_custom_command(
  OUTPUT ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/AllenCahnCoefficients.hpp
  COMMAND ${Python3_EXECUTABLE} ${Sloth_COEFFICIENT_SCRIPT} -r -f ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/coefficients.json
  WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}
  DEPENDS ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/coefficients.json)

add_executable(allen_cahn main.cpp ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/AllenCahnCoefficients.hpp)
target_include_directories(allen_cahn PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR})
target_link_libraries(allen_cahn PRIVATE Sloth::Sloth)

with, for instance, the double-well potential of the example:

[
    {
    "expression":"phi*phi*(1.0 - phi)*(1.0 - phi)",
    "variables":"phi",
    "class_name":"DoubleWell",
    "outputfile":"AllenCahnCoefficients"
    }
]

The generated class DoubleWell (with its first and second derivatives) is then used as any SLOTH coefficient: Coefficient(Glossary::FreeEnergy, Scheme::Implicit, DoubleWell(omega)).

Adding a case

Copy allen_cahn/, rename it (and its targets and tests in its CMakeLists.txt), and add an add_subdirectory() line at the end of the top-level CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: Static code analyis
docs.text:
CppLint is used to check code quality according to Google's C++ style guide.

CppLint is a static code checker that can be easily installed from PyPI:

pip install cpplint

The options considered for static code analysis are:

  • linelength=100 to set the maximum allowed line length for your code
  • filter=-runtime/references,-build/header_guard,-runtime/string

These options are placed in the file CPPLINT.cfg, available in the root of the SLOTH repository.

In practice, after loading the SLOTH environement file, using the CMake target lint enables to run the static code analysis:

make lint

docs.title: Code coverage analysis
docs.text:
Performing code coverage analysis consists of three simple steps:

  • Compilling SLOTH in coverage mode 
    mkdir build
cd build
source ../envSloth.sh --coverage
make -j N
  • Running the tests (here, for example, all cases stored in the folder tests): 
    ctest -j N
  • Running the CMake target cc to generate the code coverage analysis within the Coverage folder: 
    make cc

Code quality control before contributing

It is a prerequisite that both static code analysis and code coverage analysis are conducted prior to the incorporation of new functionalities in SLOTH. The results of these two analyses should get better or at least stay the same.
